title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
A forensic expert tells the court: “The DNA profile matches the defendant, and only one person in a million would match by chance.” The prosecutor concludes: “So there is only a one-in-a-million chance the defendant is innocent.”
The conclusion does not follow. It swaps a conditional probability for its converse, and the error has contributed to real miscarriages of justice.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
Two different questions
Let \(E\) be the evidence (a DNA match) and \(I\) the event that the defendant is innocent. The expert can legitimately report
\[
P(E \mid I) = 10^{-6},
\]
the chance of a match if the defendant is innocent. The court needs a different quantity,
\[
P(I \mid E),
\]
the chance the defendant is innocent given the match. These are not equal in general, any more than “most cricketers are men” means “most men are cricketers”.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
section: Bayes’ theorem supplies the missing piece
text:
Bayes’ theorem supplies the missing piece
\[
P(I \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid I)\,P(I)}{P(E \mid I)\,P(I) + P(E \mid G)\,P(G)},
\]
where \(G\) is guilt. The missing ingredient is the prior \(P(I)\): how likely was this person to be the source before the match was known?
Suppose the crime happened in a city of \(N = 2{,}000{,}000\) possible suspects, and the defendant was found by trawling a database, with no other evidence. A sensible prior is that each person is equally likely to be the source, so \(P(G) = 1/N\). A true source always matches, so \(P(E \mid G) = 1\).

posterior_innocent <- function(prior_guilt, p_match_innocent, p_match_guilty = 1) {
  num <- p_match_innocent * (1 - prior_guilt)
  num / (num + p_match_guilty * prior_guilt)
}

N <- 2e6
posterior_innocent(1 / N, 1e-6)

[1] 0.6666666


The probability of innocence is about 67%, not one in a million.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
Natural frequencies
The same answer is easier to see by counting people. Among 2,000,000 people:

1 is the true source, and matches.
The other 1,999,999 are innocent, and about \(1{,}999{,}999 \times 10^{-6} \approx 2\) of them match by chance.

So roughly 3 people match, and only 1 of them is guilty. Picking one matching person at random, the chance they are innocent is about \(2/3\).

tibble(
  group = factor(c("Guilty source", "Innocent, matches by chance"),
                 levels = c("Guilty source", "Innocent, matches by chance")),
  count = c(1, (N - 1) * 1e-6)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(group, count, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(count, 2)), vjust = -0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#d95f0e", "#2c7fb8")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Expected matching people") +
  ylim(0, 2.6)







Figure 1: Expected matches in a population of 2,000,000: one true source and about two innocent people who match by chance.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
How much the prior matters
The match probability alone doesn’t fix the answer. It depends on how many people could plausibly have done it.

grid <- expand.grid(
  pool = 10^seq(2, 8, length.out = 200),
  rmp = c(1e-4, 1e-6, 1e-9)
) |>
  mutate(
    p_innocent = posterior_innocent(1 / pool, rmp),
    rmp = factor(format(rmp, scientific = TRUE), levels = c("1e-04", "1e-06", "1e-09"))
  )

ggplot(grid, aes(pool, p_innocent, colour = rmp)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  labs(x = "Number of possible suspects", y = "P(innocent | match)",
       colour = "Random-match\nprobability")







Figure 2: Posterior probability of innocence given a match, for several random-match probabilities, as the pool of possible suspects grows.





A one-in-a-million match is strong evidence when the pool is a few hundred people, and weak when it is millions. Strong evidence only becomes decisive once the prior is also taken into account.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
Simulation check
Simulate many “crimes” in a city of \(N\) people: pick the true source, test everyone, and look at the people who match. Then ask how often a randomly chosen matching person is innocent.

trials <- 20000
innocent_matches <- rbinom(trials, N - 1, 1e-6)  # innocent people who match, per crime
total_matches <- 1 + innocent_matches            # the true source always matches

c(simulated_pooled   = sum(innocent_matches) / sum(total_matches),
  bayes              = posterior_innocent(1 / N, 1e-6),
  naive_prosecutor   = 1e-6,
  mean_per_crime     = mean(innocent_matches / total_matches))

simulated_pooled            bayes naive_prosecutor   mean_per_crime 
       0.6655407        0.6666666        0.0000010        0.5645903 


Pooling all matching people across the simulated crimes reproduces the Bayes answer of roughly two-thirds, and is nowhere near \(10^{-6}\).
The last line is a different quantity: it averages the innocent fraction crime by crime. It comes out lower (about 0.57) because crimes with no innocent matcher count as a full 0, and averaging a ratio is not the ratio of averages. The Bayes calculation, and the question “of everyone who matches, how many are innocent?”, correspond to the pooled figure.

title: The Prosecutor’s Fallacy
text:
Takeaways

\(P(E \mid I)\) and \(P(I \mid E)\) are different quantities. Equating them is the prosecutor’s fallacy.
The prior (how many people could have done it) is needed to get from one to the other.
Natural frequencies, such as “about 2 innocent people would also match”, make the correct reasoning hard to miss.
The mirror image is the defence attorney’s fallacy: arguing that because several people would match, the match is worthless. It is still evidence; it just must be weighed against the prior.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
text:
Sclocchi, Favero and Wyart’s A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models Reveals the Hierarchical Nature of Data (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024) makes a simple, sharp claim about how diffusion models generate images. Take a real image, run the forward noising process partway to some timestep \(t\), then run the backward (denoising) process the rest of the way back to \(t=0\). If \(t\) is small, you get back almost exactly the image you started with. If \(t\) is large, you get a plausible image of the same rough kind but with different fine details. The paper’s finding is that the switch between these two regimes isn’t gradual — it’s a genuine phase transition, and it happens at different noise levels for different levels of an image’s hierarchy (fine texture destabilizes first, then object parts, then overall semantic class).
This post reproduces that experiment end to end: real pretrained weights, real ImageNet-derived images, run locally on a Mac (Apple Silicon, no CUDA) rather than the multi-GPU cluster the paper used. The code lives in forward-backward-diffusion, the paper’s own release — I had to fix a couple of bugs in it and add Apple GPU (MPS) support to get it running here; the how and why of that is at the bottom of the post.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
section: Where does the class identity break?
text:
Where does the class identity break?
For each reversal point \(t\), we forward-diffuse every starting image to \(t\), denoise it back to a clean image, and ask ConvNeXt-Base what class it thinks the result is — then compare that to what it originally said about the untouched image. sample_correct and start_correct track agreement with the true (Imagenette) label; pred_unchanged tracks whether reconstruction preserved the classifier’s own original prediction, which is the more direct read on “did the reverse process preserve identity” independent of whether the classifier was right to begin with.

summary_by_t <- accuracy_by_t |>
  group_by(step_reverse) |>
  summarise(
    sample_correct = mean(sample_correct),
    pred_unchanged = mean(pred_unchanged),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(c(sample_correct, pred_unchanged), names_to = "metric", values_to = "fraction")

baseline_acc <- baseline$accuracy_top1[1] / 100

ggplot(summary_by_t, aes(step_reverse, fraction, color = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = baseline_acc, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = max(summary_by_t$step_reverse), y = baseline_acc,
           label = "baseline accuracy (no diffusion)", vjust = -0.6, hjust = 1,
           size = 3, color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(sample_correct = "#2C7FB8", pred_unchanged = "#D95F02"),
    labels = c(sample_correct = "matches true label", pred_unchanged = "matches original prediction")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "reversal timestep (t, out of 25 respaced steps)",
    y = "fraction of images",
    color = NULL,
    title = "Identity survives small t, then degrades"
  )







Figure 1: Classification agreement after forward-backward diffusion, as a function of the reversal timestep. t=0 is a no-op (perfect reconstruction); higher t means more of the diffusion trajectory is re-randomized before reconstruction.

title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models
section: A hierarchy of breakdown, layer by layer
text:
A hierarchy of breakdown, layer by layer
The more interesting view is inside the classifier. Every image gets pushed through ConvNeXt-Base twice — once as the original, once as the forward-backward reconstruction — and we compare activations at every one of its ~45 internal layers, from the earliest convolutional stem (depth 0) to the final classification head (depth ≈44). If the paper’s hierarchical story is right, shallow layers (fine texture) should start diverging at small \(t\), while only the deepest layers (semantic class) diverge at large \(t\).

cosine_by_depth_t <- activation_diff |>
  filter(metric == "cosine") |>
  group_by(step_reverse, depth) |>
  summarise(cosine_distance = 1 - mean(value), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(cosine_by_depth_t, aes(step_reverse, depth, fill = cosine_distance)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", labels = percent_format()) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = pretty_breaks()) +
  labs(
    x = "reversal timestep (t)",
    y = "network depth (0 = input stem, ~44 = classification head)",
    fill = "cosine\ndistance",
    title = "Where in the network reconstruction diverges from the original"
  )







Figure 2: Mean cosine distance (1 - cosine similarity) between original and reconstructed activations, by network depth and reversal timestep. Warmer = more disrupted. A hierarchy would show the disruption front moving from shallow layers (bottom) to deep layers (top) as t increases.






depth_max <- max(cosine_by_depth_t$depth)
sample_depths <- unique(round(seq(0, depth_max, length.out = 6)))

cosine_by_depth_t |>
  filter(depth %in% sample_depths) |>
  mutate(depth = factor(depth)) |>
  ggplot(aes(step_reverse, cosine_distance, color = depth, group = depth)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "magma", end = 0.85) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format()) +
  labs(
    x = "reversal timestep (t)",
    y = "cosine distance",
    color = "depth",
    title = "Shallow layers move first, deep layers move last"
  )







Figure 3: The same data as a line plot: a handful of representative depths, cosine distance vs. t.

section: What actually broke in the code, and how I fixed it
text:
What actually broke in the code, and how I fixed it
The paper’s released code isn’t quite runnable as committed, and separately, nothing about it was written with Apple’s MPS backend in mind. Four fixes were needed:

A broken relative import. guided_diffusion/image_datasets.py did from ..datasets.imagenet_classes import IMAGENET_CLASSES, a relative import that reaches outside the installed guided_diffusion package. It fails immediately with ImportError: attempted relative import beyond top-level package — every one of the repo’s three custom scripts imports this module, so nothing in the repo could run at all. Fixed by making datasets its own installable package (setup.py) and importing it absolutely.
Two sampling methods that don’t exist. The actual forward-backward experiment script calls diffusion.p_sample_loop_forw_back and diffusion.ddim_sample_loop_forw_back — methods that appear nowhere in gaussian_diffusion.py, and never have, across the entire git history. I implemented both, as variants of the existing p_sample_loop_progressive / ddim_sample_loop_progressive that start the reverse process at a given timestep instead of at pure noise.
float64 on MPS. _extract_into_tensor moved the diffusion schedule’s coefficients — stored as float64 numpy arrays — directly onto the compute device. MPS doesn’t support float64 at all, so this crashed on first use; fixed by casting to float32 before the device transfer.
torch.distributed collectives on an MPS tensor. The scripts use dist.all_reduce/all_gather (inherited from the original multi-GPU design) even for a single-process laptop run. Those collectives run over the gloo backend here (no CUDA means no NCCL), and gloo only understands CPU tensors — so the handful of tensors that cross a collective call needed to be routed to CPU rather than MPS, while leaving NCCL’s CUDA path untouched for the cluster case.

None of this changes the paper’s method — it’s the same forward-then-partial-backward diffusion process, the same classifier, the same activation-comparison logic. The fixes just make the released code actually executable, and executable somewhere other than a CUDA cluster.
Related: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models connects this paper’s belief-propagation phase transition to the renormalization-group critical phenomena in my own dissertation · if any of the underlying math felt assumed rather than explained, Markov Chains, Concretely and A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve are refreshers written to fill exactly that gap.

title: Instrumenting Agent Cybernetics
text:
Wang et al. (2026) argue that cybernetics supplies the missing theoretical scaffold for foundation agents, and derive six design principles from six classical laws. Their Principle 2 (Requisite Variety) requires that \(\min(V(\mathcal{O}), V(\mathcal{I})) \geq V(\mathcal{W})\), and three of the failure modes they name are diagnosed as \(V(\mathcal{T}) < V(\mathcal{W})\). Their headline open question — how should an agent respond when its environment exceeds its representational capacity? — presupposes that this condition can be detected.
It cannot, as the framework currently stands. \(V(\mathcal{W})\) appears throughout as Ashby’s classical cardinality — a theoretical quantity Wang et al. never operationalise from deployment telemetry. An operator who tries to estimate it from observed disturbance classes defaults to plug-in (maximum-likelihood) coverage; that default systematically understates environmental variety and overstates coverage, worst where the distribution is heaviest-tailed. Agent Cybernetics is, as written, unmeasurable.
We supply the instrument. Our central result is the Enumeration Elasticity Theorem: the elasticity of unhandled traffic with respect to enumeration investment is exactly \(\eta = 1 - \beta\), where \(\beta\) is the Heaps exponent of the disturbance-class discovery curve — a directly measurable quantity. A \(\lambda\)-fold increase in the effort spent mapping disturbance classes to responses reduces the unhandled fraction by \(\lambda^{1-\beta}\). As \(\beta \to 1\), \(\eta \to 0\) and investment stops buying coverage: at \(\beta = 0.9\), halving the residual costs a thousandfold increase in effort. This gives an operational answer to Wang et al.’s open question. When \(\eta \approx 0\), requisite variety cannot be met by amplification at any ledger a rational operator will build, and the deficit must be met by attenuation or by a class-independent fallback — an architectural conclusion, not an engineering one.
We further contribute: an open-world estimator for \(V(\mathcal{W})\) combining Good–Turing missing-mass correction and Heaps tracking, and a demonstration that plug-in estimation errs on both sides of the inequality at once; a determinism instrument, \(H(R \mid D)\), that operationalises the Conant–Ashby good regulator theorem, which is absent from the six laws; an interventional test that renders feedback blindness — a named closed-loop reliability failure they diagnose but do not measure (one of their first four failure modes, ranked highest for cost–benefit) — falsifiable rather than merely diagnosable, and which we run on the demonstrator (\(\Phi = 0.55\) bits, \(\approx\) 90x the resampling-noise floor: the agent’s action distribution genuinely conditions on its observations); and a partition-refinement procedure with three admission gates, including a policy-improvement criterion that corrects a natural but wrong instinct about when a disturbance class should be split.
We also identify a hazard in our own instrument: attenuation lowers measured \(\beta\), so the treatment we recommend improves the diagnostic whether or not it improves the system. We give the mitigation and do not claim to resolve it.
Finally, the same interventional machinery yields an adversarial instrument: susceptibility \(\Sigma\), the probability that an agent complies with an instruction injected into its observation channel (indirect prompt poisoning). Measured end-to-end through an agent’s real data-input tools — file read, RAG retrieval, web fetch — against a matched clean control (\(\Sigma_{\text{clean}} = 0\)), \(\Sigma\) is strongly attack-class-dependent (0.83 for a blunt instruction-override, 0.00 for a system-prompt-exfiltration attempt) and inversely tracks content-sensitivity \(\Phi\) across vectors, the direction §5.2 predicts: an agent that treats tool output as evidence to be checked, not an instruction to obey, is harder to hijack through that output, while a feedback-blind one passes an injected payload straight through.
We package these as a variety ledger: a versioned registry of essential variables, disturbance classes, response repertoire, and channel specifications, recomputed from telemetry and enforced as a CI gate. §6 exercises the full ledger on a semi-synthetic benchmark with known ground truth — including a graded outcome signal that makes the partition-refinement gates non-vacuous, an interventional feedback-blindness measurement, and an end-to-end prompt-poisoning susceptibility measurement — and reports one incident: a latent regulatory defect that inverted the dithering measurement until it was found and fixed, which is itself the clearest available demonstration of why §4.5’s canary discipline is not optional.

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
text: Second of three short refreshers behind Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models. The first covered Markov chains; read it first only if that material feels unfamiliar — this one stands alone.

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
text:
The problem mean-field theory solves
A ferromagnet is a lattice of interacting spins: each one wants to align with its neighbours, but the neighbours are themselves fluctuating, coupled to their neighbours, and so on. Tracking the full joint distribution over every spin is intractable for anything but tiny systems.
The mean-field trick: replace each spin’s actual, fluctuating neighbours with their average value. A many-body problem becomes a single spin sitting in an effective field set by everybody else’s average behaviour — and that’s tractable, at the cost of ignoring fluctuation correlations between neighbours. Sclocchi et al. (2024) (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024) use exactly this move — under a different name, “annealed” approximation — to get a closed-form description of belief propagation on their Random Hierarchy Model, and it’s worth seeing the classical version first.

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
text:
Curie-Weiss, derived
Give each spin \(z\) neighbours, coupling strength \(J\), at inverse temperature \(\beta\). Averaging over its neighbours’ fluctuations, a spin’s effective field is proportional to the mean magnetization \(m\), and self-consistency (the average spin must reproduce the magnetization that produced its own field) gives:
\[
m = \tanh(Km), \qquad K \equiv \beta J z
\]
Folding \(\beta\), \(J\), \(z\) into the single parameter \(K\) is the standard textbook reduction — the actual critical temperature is \(\beta_c = 1/(Jz)\), i.e. \(K=1\) exactly. Below \(K=1\) the only solution is \(m=0\) (paramagnetic: no net alignment); above it, two new nonzero solutions appear (ferromagnetic: spontaneous alignment, sign chosen by symmetry breaking).

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
text:
Solving it
\(m=0\) satisfies \(\tanh(K \cdot 0) = 0\) for every \(K\) — it’s always a trivial root, present whether or not the interesting nonzero one exists. Searching for the nonzero branch means excluding it explicitly: bracket uniroot away from zero.

nontrivial_root <- function(K, lower = 1e-6, upper = 1 - 1e-9) {
  if (K <= 1) return(0)
  self_consist_gap <- function(m) tanh(K * m) - m
  if (sign(self_consist_gap(lower)) == sign(self_consist_gap(upper))) return(NA_real_)
  uniroot(self_consist_gap, c(lower, upper))$root
}

Ks <- seq(0.05, 3, by = 0.01)
df <- data.frame(K = Ks)
df$m_stable <- sapply(Ks, nontrivial_root)

ggplot(df, aes(K)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(y = m_stable), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_line(aes(y = -m_stable), colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 1, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  labs(x = expression(K == beta * J * z), y = "magnetization m",
       title = "Order emerges above the critical point")







Figure 1: Curie-Weiss magnetization vs. K. The nonzero branch only exists above the critical point K=1.





Below \(K=1\), only \(m=0\); above it, a genuine phase transition. Three independent checks on the nonzero branch agree: at \(K=2\), uniroot gives \(m=0.9575\), and simply iterating \(m \leftarrow \tanh(2m)\) a thousand times from \(m=0.5\) converges to \(0.957504\) — the same fixed point found two different ways. Near the critical point, mean-field theory predicts \(m \approx \sqrt{3(K-1)}\); at \(K=1.01\) that asymptotic gives \(0.1732\) against uniroot’s \(0.1717\) — agreement to about 1%, which is the classical mean-field critical exponent \(\beta=1/2\) showing up numerically.

title: Mean-Field Theory and Annealed Disorder
section: The same move, in belief propagation
text:
The same move, in belief propagation
The Random Hierarchy Model’s disordered production rules play the role of the Ising model’s disordered neighbour spins. Tracking every possible realization of the hierarchy’s rules exactly is just as intractable as tracking every spin’s actual neighbours. Sclocchi et al. take the identical shortcut: average over the ensemble of rule realizations (the “annealed” approximation) rather than conditioning on one specific (quenched) realization, and a complicated random recursion collapses into the single deterministic belief-propagation map
\[
p' = F(p)
\]
already implemented and solved in Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models — same recipe (disorder → ensemble average → deterministic self-consistency map), same qualitative payoff (a clean, analyzable bifurcation), different physical dressing. That post doesn’t re-derive the annealed approximation; this is the missing piece that justifies why \(F(p)\) is allowed to be written down as a plain deterministic function at all.
The same self-consistency structure — and the same \(\sqrt{K-1}\)-type critical scaling — also shows up throughout my own dissertation on renormalization-group critical phenomena, where the RG fixed point plays the role \(K=1\) plays here.

title: Bifurcation vs. Langevin Dynamics
text:
Note



This report was generated using AI under general human direction. At the time of generation, the contents have not been comprehensively reviewed by a human analyst.
Score-based diffusion models generate images (or other data) by starting from pure noise and running a stochastic process that flows toward the learned data distribution. Near the start of that process, a generated sample is maximally ambiguous about which class it will end up as; only later, as the process evolves, does it commit to one class or another. This explainer works through a small, fully analytic toy version of that story: a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) standing in for a learned multi-class data distribution, its exact score function, and simulated Langevin trajectories that visibly bifurcate from a shared, unstable point near the origin into one of several stable class basins.

title: Bifurcation vs. Langevin Dynamics
text:
The Gaussian mixture model
A Gaussian mixture model describes a density as a weighted sum of Gaussian components:
\[
p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi_k \, \mathcal{N}(x; \mu_k, \sigma^2 I), \qquad \sum_k \pi_k = 1,
\]
where each component is centered at \(\mu_k\) with shared isotropic variance \(\sigma^2\), and the weights \(\pi_k\) are prior probabilities of each component. Here we use three components (“classes”) arranged symmetrically around the origin in 2D, with slightly unequal weights to mimic real-world class imbalance:

modes <- tibble(
  class  = c("A", "B", "C"),
  name   = c("Class A (Leopard)", "Class B (Wolf)", "Class C (Eagle)"),
  mu_x   = c(1.0, -0.5, -0.5),
  mu_y   = c(0.0, 0.866, -0.866),
  weight = c(0.45, 0.30, 0.25),
  col    = c("#cc5500", "#0055cc", "#22aa55")
)

well_sigma <- 0.35       # width of each class well
noise_strength <- 0.15   # diffusion coefficient g

Why a GMM, specifically? Real generative models learn densities over very high-dimensional data (pixels, tokens, …), and their exact score function is intractable to write down. A GMM is one of the few densities whose score has a clean closed form, while still being genuinely multi-modal. That combination makes it a convenient minimal model for studying the qualitative behaviour of score-based generation — in particular, how a smooth, single density can nonetheless produce sharply distinct, discrete outcomes (the classes) when sampled dynamically. Nothing here is a claim that real data looks like a GMM; it is a controlled setting in which the mechanism of interest (symmetry breaking near an unstable point) can be derived and simulated exactly rather than approximated.

title: Bifurcation vs. Langevin Dynamics
Bifurcation vs. Langevin Dynamics
text:
Langevin dynamics
Langevin dynamics is a stochastic differential equation (SDE) that combines deterministic drift up the score field with injected noise:
\[
dX_t = s(X_t)\,dt + g\,dW_t,
\]
where \(W_t\) is a standard Wiener process and \(g\) is a (constant, here) diffusion coefficient. This is the overdamped limit of the physical Langevin equation for a particle in a potential \(U(x) = -\log p(x)\) subject to thermal noise, and it is the continuous-time process underlying score-based sampling: under mild conditions, its stationary distribution is exactly \(p(x)\). Two competing effects are at work: the drift term \(s(X_t)\,dt\) pulls the state toward high-density regions (deepening class wells), while the diffusion term \(g\,dW_t\) injects randomness that lets the state escape shallow or unstable regions — including, critically, the near-symmetric region around the origin.

title: Bifurcation vs. Langevin Dynamics
text:
Euler-Maruyama discretization
Simulating the SDE above requires discretizing it in time. The Euler-Maruyama method is the direct stochastic analogue of Euler’s method for ODEs: replace the continuous drift and diffusion with a single small step \(\Delta t\), and replace \(dW_t\) with a Gaussian increment of the correct variance:
\[
X_{t+1} = X_t + s(X_t)\,\Delta t + g\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z_t, \qquad Z_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, I).
\]
The \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\) scaling (rather than \(\Delta t\)) is essential and follows from the Wiener process’s defining property \(\mathrm{Var}(W_{t+\Delta t} - W_t) = \Delta t\): it is what keeps the discrete-time noise variance consistent with the continuous-time process as \(\Delta t \to 0\). Euler-Maruyama is only first-order accurate (weakly), but it is simple and sufficient for the qualitative picture here.

simulate_langevin_path <- function(x0, y0, steps = 150, dt = 0.01) {
  x <- numeric(steps + 1); y <- numeric(steps + 1)
  x[1] <- x0; y[1] <- y0
  for (t in seq_len(steps)) {
    s <- gmm_score(x[t], y[t])
    noise <- rnorm(2)
    nx <- x[t] + s[1] * dt + noise_strength * sqrt(dt) * noise[1]
    ny <- y[t] + s[2] * dt + noise_strength * sqrt(dt) * noise[2]
    # Cosmetic boundary cap so plotted paths stay within a fixed radius
    r2 <- nx^2 + ny^2
    if (r2 > 9) {
      scale <- 3 / sqrt(r2)
      nx <- nx * scale
      ny <- ny * scale
    }
    x[t + 1] <- nx; y[t + 1] <- ny
  }
  tibble(step = 0:steps, x = x, y = y)
}

title: Bifurcation vs. Langevin Dynamics
Bifurcation vs. Langevin Dynamics
Bifurcation vs. Langevin Dynamics
text:
Conclusion
Both figures illustrate the same mechanism from different angles: a smooth, unimodal-looking region of the density near the origin is not actually a stable point of the dynamics, but an unstable one. Under Langevin sampling, infinitesimal fluctuations there get amplified rather than damped, and the trajectory is swept into one of several well-separated, stable class basins. This is a simplified but exact picture of the qualitative claim behind score-based generative models: semantic categories emerge dynamically, as the resolution of instability near maximal noise, rather than being explicitly encoded anywhere in the model.






Note



This is a toy model, not a reproduction of any specific paper’s results: three 2D Gaussian components with hand-chosen weights and variance stand in for a real, high-dimensional, learned data distribution. The value of the exercise is that the score function, Langevin SDE, and Euler-Maruyama discretization are all exact and standard, so the qualitative bifurcation behaviour shown here is a real (if simplified) consequence of the same equations that govern actual diffusion models.

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
text: Almost every atom heavier than helium was made inside a star. The carbon in your cells, the oxygen you breathe and the iron in your blood were assembled by thermonuclear reactions in stellar cores and then scattered by stellar winds and supernovae. This post covers the physics that makes that possible, in three steps: why fusion happens at all at stellar temperatures, how the rates of the main reaction chains depend on temperature, and how Fred Hoyle used the existence of carbon-based life to predict a property of the carbon-12 nucleus before anyone had measured it.

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
text:
A short history
Why do stars shine? In 1920 Arthur Eddington argued that stars are powered by turning hydrogen into helium. Four hydrogen nuclei weigh about 0.7% more than one helium nucleus, so the conversion releases energy through \(E = mc^2\). The objection was that stellar cores seemed far too cool: at roughly \(10^7\) K, protons do not have nearly enough energy to climb the Coulomb barrier. The way out came with quantum mechanics. In 1928 George Gamow showed that nuclei can tunnel through the barrier, and by the late 1930s Hans Bethe (and independently Carl von Weizsäcker) had worked out the reaction chains that power ordinary stars. Bethe’s 1939 paper laid out the proton–proton chain and the carbon–nitrogen–oxygen cycle.
Where do the heavier elements come from? In the 1940s there were two rival ideas. George Gamow and collaborators (Alpher, Bethe, Gamow, 1948) proposed that all the elements were cooked in the first minutes of the Big Bang. That runs into a wall: there are no stable nuclei with mass number 5 or 8, so building up from helium one nucleon at a time stalls, and the Big Bang makes essentially only hydrogen, helium and traces of lithium.
Enter Fred Hoyle. Fred Hoyle (1915–2001), a Cambridge astronomer, argued in 1946 that the heavier elements are built inside stars as they evolve. He was, with Hermann Bondi and Thomas Gold, also the author of the steady-state cosmology (1948), a rival to the Big Bang picture. The phrase “Big Bang” itself is usually credited to Hoyle, from a 1949 BBC radio talk. He later said it was meant as a vivid image and not a sneer, though the claim is still debated. Whatever his view of cosmology, his work on nucleosynthesis was right, and it outlived the steady-state theory.
The bottleneck was carbon. Stars can make helium, but to get anything heavier they must fuse helium nuclei (alpha particles). Two alphas make beryllium-8, which is unbound and falls apart in about \(10^{-16}\) s. A third alpha has to arrive within that window. Hoyle realised that for this to work at a useful rate in stellar cores, carbon-12 must have an excited state at roughly 7.65 MeV that lines up with the energy of the three-alpha system. In 1953 he pressed this on Willy Fowler’s group at Caltech. Fowler’s team (Dunbar, Cook, Whaling and colleagues) measured it, and found a \(0^+\) state at about 7.65 MeV, now called the Hoyle state. Hoyle published the full programme in 1954.
In 1957 Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, Willy Fowler and Fred Hoyle published “Synthesis of the Elements in Stars”, universally known as B2FH. It laid out the processes of nucleosynthesis (hydrogen burning, helium burning, the alpha process, the s- and r-processes of neutron capture, and others) and connected them to observed abundances. Fowler shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics for this work (with Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, who was honoured for other research); Hoyle was not included, which many in the field regard as a serious omission.
There is also a famous gloss on the Hoyle state: that Hoyle predicted it because carbon-based life exists, as an early anthropic argument. Historians disagree about how much of that reasoning was in Hoyle’s mind in 1953 versus added in later retellings. The nuclear physics is on firmer ground than the narrative.

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
section: Why fusion happens at all: Gamow tunnelling
text:
Why fusion happens at all: Gamow tunnelling
Two nuclei with charges \(Z_1 e\) and \(Z_2 e\) repel each other with Coulomb energy \(Z_1 Z_2 e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0 r)\). At the nuclear radius (a few femtometres) this barrier is of order an MeV, while the thermal energy at the Sun’s core temperature of \(1.5\times10^7\) K is only \(kT \approx 1.3\) keV. Classical collisions would almost never get through.
Quantum tunnelling gives a small but non-zero probability. For relative energy \(E\) much below the barrier height, the penetration probability is approximately
\[
P(E) \approx \exp\!\left(-\sqrt{E_G/E}\right),
\qquad
E_G = 2 m_r c^2 \,(\pi \alpha Z_1 Z_2)^2,
\]
where \(m_r\) is the reduced mass, \(\alpha \approx 1/137\) is the fine-structure constant and \(E_G\) is the Gamow energy. It grows rapidly with the charges, which is why hydrogen burns first and heavier fuels need higher temperatures.

reactions <- tribble(
  ~reaction,        ~Z1, ~Z2, ~A1, ~A2, ~T,
  "p + p",            1,   1,   1,   1, 1.5e7,
  "p + 14N",          1,   7,   1,  14, 2.0e7,
  "alpha + alpha",    2,   2,   4,   4, 1.0e8,
  "alpha + 12C",      2,   6,   4,  12, 2.0e8
) |>
  mutate(E_G_keV = gamow_energy(Z1, Z2, A1, A2))
reactions |> mutate(E_G_keV = round(E_G_keV), kT_keV = round(kT_keV(T), 2)) |>
  select(reaction, T, kT_keV, E_G_keV)

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
text:
The Gamow peak
Particles in a hot plasma follow a Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distribution, \(\propto \exp(-E/kT)\), which favours low energies. Tunnelling probability favours high energies. The reaction rate per particle pair is the integral of their product,
\[
\langle\sigma v\rangle = \left(\frac{8}{\pi m_r}\right)^{1/2}\frac{1}{(kT)^{3/2}}
\int_0^\infty S(E)\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{E}{kT}-\sqrt{\frac{E_G}{E}}\right)dE,
\]
where the cross-section is written as \(\sigma(E) = \dfrac{S(E)}{E}\,e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}\) and the astrophysical S-factor \(S(E)\) absorbs the slowly varying nuclear physics. The exponent is minimised at the Gamow peak
\[
E_0 = \left(\frac{E_G\,(kT)^2}{4}\right)^{1/3},
\qquad
\Delta = \frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{E_0\,kT},
\]
with \(\Delta\) the \(1/e\) full width. For protons in the Sun’s core the peak sits at about 6 keV, many times the mean thermal energy of \(\sim 1.3\) keV, and only a thin slice of the distribution is doing any fusing.

T_sun <- 1.5e7
EG_pp <- gamow_energy(1, 1, 1, 1)
kT <- kT_keV(T_sun)
E <- seq(0.05, 20, length.out = 800)
mb  <- exp(-E / kT)
tun <- exp(-sqrt(EG_pp / E))
prod <- mb * tun
E0 <- (EG_pp * kT^2 / 4)^(1/3)

df <- tibble(
  E = E,
  `Maxwell–Boltzmann` = mb / max(mb),
  `Tunnelling` = tun / max(tun),
  `Product (Gamow peak)` = prod / max(prod)
) |> tidyr::pivot_longer(-E, names_to = "factor", values_to = "value")

ggplot(df, aes(E, value, colour = factor)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = E0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = E0 + 0.4, y = 0.55, label = sprintf("E0 = %.1f keV", E0),
           hjust = 0, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2c7fb8", "black", "#d95f0e")) +
  labs(x = "Relative energy E (keV)", y = "Relative magnitude (each curve normalised)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 1: Maxwell–Boltzmann tail (blue), tunnelling probability (orange) and their product, the Gamow peak (black), for p + p at the Sun’s core temperature. Each curve is normalised to its own maximum so that all three share one axis.





The peak is at 5.9 keV for a thermal energy of 1.29 keV.

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
section: How steeply do rates depend on temperature?
text:
How steeply do rates depend on temperature?
Near its maximum, the integrand is approximately a Gaussian, and the integral gives a rate that depends on temperature as \(\langle\sigma v\rangle \propto T^{\,n}\) with the local exponent
\[
n = \frac{\tau - 2}{3},
\qquad
\tau = \frac{3E_0}{kT} = 3\left(\frac{E_G}{4\,kT}\right)^{1/3}.
\]
This exponent explains why different stars burn different fuels in different regimes. Reactions with a larger Coulomb barrier have a larger \(\tau\), so they respond far more violently to temperature.

reactions |>
  mutate(
    tau = 3 * (E_G_keV / (4 * kT_keV(T)))^(1/3),
    n   = (tau - 2) / 3
  ) |>
  transmute(reaction, T, E_G_keV = round(E_G_keV), tau = round(tau, 1), n = round(n, 1))

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  reaction              T E_G_keV   tau     n

1 p + p          15000000     490  13.7   3.9
2 p + 14N        20000000   44779  56    18  
3 alpha + alpha 100000000   31332  29.1   9  
4 alpha + 12C   200000000  422984  54.9  17.6


The alpha + alpha row is the non-resonant value; the resonant triple-alpha process below is far steeper. For p + p at \(1.5\times10^7\) K the rate goes roughly as \(T^4\); for proton capture on nitrogen-14 it goes as a much higher power of \(T\). This is why the CNO cycle dominates over the pp chain in stars somewhat more massive than the Sun. It also shows up in stellar structure: a CNO-burning core has a steep temperature gradient, which drives convection.

grid <- expand.grid(T = 10^seq(6.8, 8.6, length.out = 200), i = seq_len(nrow(reactions))) |>
  mutate(
    reaction = reactions$reaction[i],
    EG = reactions$E_G_keV[i],
    n = (3 * (EG / (4 * kT_keV(T)))^(1/3) - 2) / 3
  )

ggplot(grid, aes(T, n, colour = reaction)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1e7, 3e7, 1e8, 3e8), labels = scales::label_scientific(digits = 1)) +

  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
section: Hydrogen burning: pp chain and CNO cycle
text:
Hydrogen burning: pp chain and CNO cycle
Both routes convert four protons into one helium-4 nucleus:
\[
4\,{}^{1}\mathrm{H} \;\to\; {}^{4}\mathrm{He} + 2e^{+} + 2\nu_e + \text{energy}.
\]
The energy released is the mass difference. Using atomic masses, \(m({}^1\mathrm{H}) = 1.007825\) u and \(m({}^4\mathrm{He}) = 4.002603\) u,

m_H1  <- 1.007825
m_He4 <- 4.002603
Q_MeV    <- (4 * m_H1 - m_He4) * amu_MeV
frac     <- (4 * m_H1 - m_He4) / (4 * m_H1)

# Sun: how long could hydrogen burning last?
L_sun <- 3.828e26; M_sun <- 1.989e30; c_ms <- 2.998e8; yr <- 3.156e7
t_ms <- 0.1 * frac * M_sun * c_ms^2 / L_sun / yr    # ~10% of mass burns on the main sequence
c(Q_MeV = Q_MeV, mass_fraction_released = frac, main_sequence_years = t_ms)

                 Q_MeV mass_fraction_released    main_sequence_years 
          2.673108e+01           7.118547e-03           1.053369e+10 


That is about 26.7 MeV per helium nucleus (a bit less reaches the star, since neutrinos carry some away), or 0.71% of the rest mass. Assuming the Sun burns about 10% of its hydrogen at its current luminosity, that gives a lifetime of roughly 11 billion years, in line with the Sun’s expected main-sequence life.
The pp chain begins with the slowest, weak-interaction step:
\[
p + p \to {}^{2}\mathrm{H} + e^{+} + \nu_e ,
\]
which is the bottleneck, with a characteristic time of billions of years per proton. This is why the Sun lasts so long. Deuterium then captures another proton, \({}^2\mathrm{H}(p,\gamma){}^3\mathrm{He}\), and two \({}^3\mathrm{He}\) nuclei combine to give \({}^4\mathrm{He}\) plus two protons (the dominant branch).
The CNO cycle uses carbon, nitrogen and oxygen as catalysts, never consumed overall. The slowest step is \({}^{14}\mathrm{N}(p,\gamma){}^{15}\mathrm{O}\), which sets the cycle’s overall speed and, given the high Coulomb barrier, its steep temperature dependence.

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
text:
A reaction network, in general
The abundance of each species \(i\) (written as a number fraction \(Y_i = n_i/(\rho N_A)\)) obeys a coupled system of ordinary differential equations. For a reaction \(a + b \to c + \dots\),
\[
\frac{dY_i}{dt} = \sum_{j,k} \frac{\rho N_A \langle\sigma v\rangle_{jk}}{1+\delta_{jk}}\,Y_j Y_k\,(\pm\text{stoichiometry}) \;+\; \text{decays}.
\]
Real codes solve hundreds of such equations simultaneously. The system is stiff: the fastest and slowest rates can differ by tens of orders of magnitude, so implicit integrators are needed.

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
section: Helium burning and the triple-alpha process
text:
Helium burning and the triple-alpha process
Once the core runs out of hydrogen it contracts and heats up. At around \(10^8\) K, helium can fuse. The reaction has to proceed through two steps:
\[
\alpha + \alpha \;\rightleftharpoons\; {}^{8}\mathrm{Be},
\qquad
{}^{8}\mathrm{Be} + \alpha \;\to\; {}^{12}\mathrm{C}^{*} \;\to\; {}^{12}\mathrm{C} + \gamma\ (\text{or } e^{+}e^{-}).
\]
\({}^8\mathrm{Be}\) lies only about 92 keV above two free alphas and lives for roughly \(10^{-16}\) s. At stellar temperatures a small equilibrium population of it nonetheless exists, given (up to order-unity factors) by the Saha equation,
\[
\frac{n_{\mathrm{Be}}}{n_\alpha^2} \sim \left(\frac{2\pi\hbar^2}{M_\alpha kT}\right)^{3/2} e^{-E_{\mathrm{Be}}/kT},
\qquad E_{\mathrm{Be}} \approx 92\ \text{keV}.
\]
At \(10^8\) K (\(kT \approx 8.6\) keV) the Boltzmann factor is only about \(e^{-10.7}\), so beryllium is rare, but not negligibly so. A third alpha capturing on this beryllium would normally be too weak to matter. The Hoyle state, however, sits just above the \({}^8\mathrm{Be} + \alpha\) threshold: at 7.654 MeV excitation energy in \({}^{12}\mathrm{C}\), it is about 0.287 MeV above the \({}^8\mathrm{Be}+\alpha\) threshold, or 0.379 MeV above the three-alpha threshold. Capture into it is a resonance, so the cross-section is enormously boosted.
For a narrow resonance, the resulting three-body rate per unit volume is
\[
r_{3\alpha} = 3^{3/2}\, n_\alpha^3 \left(\frac{2\pi\hbar^2}{M_\alpha kT}\right)^{3}\frac{\Gamma}{\hbar}\,
\exp\!\left(-\frac{Q}{kT}\right),
\]
with \(Q = 379.5\) keV the resonance energy above the three-alpha threshold and \(\Gamma\) the effective width. Most Hoyle-state nuclei fall apart again into \(^8\)Be + \(\alpha\); the quantity that matters is the small radiative width \(\Gamma_\gamma \approx 3.7\) meV (plus a smaller pair-emission contribution), because only decays by radiation or pair emission produce stable carbon.

hbar  <- 1.054572e-34      # J s
kB    <- 1.380649e-23      # J/K
M_a   <- 4.001506 * 1.66054e-27   # kg
eV    <- 1.602177e-19
N_A   <- 6.02214e23
Q_J   <- 379.5e3 * eV      # resonance energy above 3-alpha threshold
Gam_J <- 3.7e-3 * eV       # effective width ~ radiative width

# rate per unit volume (m^-3 s^-1); rho in g/cm^3, pure helium
r3a <- function(T, rho) {
  n_a <- (rho * 1e3 / 4.0026e-3) * N_A            # alphas per m^3 (rho in kg/m^3 / molar mass)
  thermal <- 2 * pi * hbar^2 / (M_a * kB * T)
  3^1.5 * n_a^3 * thermal^3 * (Gam_J / hbar) * exp(-Q_J / (kB * T))
}

# alpha-particle lifetime against destruction: n_alpha / (3 r)
tau_alpha_yr <- function(T, rho) {
  n_a <- (rho * 1e3 / 4.0026e-3) * N_A
  n_a / (3 * r3a(T, rho)) / yr
}

tau_demo <- tau_alpha_yr(1e8, 1e5)

# format a number as LaTeX scientific notation for inline use
sci_tex <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  e <- floor(log10(x)); m <- signif(x / 10^e, digits)
  sprintf("%s \\times 10^{%d}", format(m), e)
}

At \(T = 10^8\) K and \(\rho = 10^5\) g cm\(^{-3}\) (the sort of dense, degenerate core in which helium ignites in a low-mass star), this simple estimate gives a helium lifetime of roughly \(4.8 \times 10^{7}\) years. At the same temperature but \(10^3\) g cm\(^{-3}\) it would be \(10^4\) times longer, because the rate scales as \(\rho^3\) while the helium supply scales as \(\rho\). Helium burns only when the core is both hot and dense.

ta <- expand.grid(T = 10^seq(7.8, 8.6, length.out = 200), rho = c(1e4, 1e5, 1e6)) |>
  mutate(tau = tau_alpha_yr(T, rho), rho = factor(format(rho, scientific = FALSE, big.mark = ",")))

ggplot(ta, aes(T, tau, colour = rho)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1e8, 2e8, 4e8), labels = scales::label_scientific(digits = 1)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (K)", y = "Helium lifetime (years)",
       colour = expression(rho~"(g/cm"^3*")")) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 3: Helium lifetime against the triple-alpha reaction for a pure-helium plasma, at three densities. The lifetime falls by many orders of magnitude over a factor of a few in temperature.





The local exponent of this rate is enormous. Since \(r \propto T^{-3}e^{-Q/kT}\) (the \(T^{-3}\) coming from the thermal factor),
\[
\frac{d\ln r_{3\alpha}}{d\ln T} = \frac{Q}{kT} - 3.
\]

Texp <- 1e8
n_ta <- Q_J / (kB * Texp) - 3
n_ta

[1] 41.03916


At \(10^8\) K that is 41, so the rate scales as roughly \(T^{41}\). A 10% temperature rise speeds helium burning up by a factor of about 50. Helium ignition therefore happens abruptly, and in stars with degenerate cores it is explosive (the helium flash).

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
section: What if the resonance were somewhere else?
text:
What if the resonance were somewhere else?
The factor \(\exp(-Q/kT)\) makes the rate exponentially sensitive to the resonance energy. If the Hoyle state were shifted by \(\Delta E\) relative to its real position, the rate at fixed temperature would change by \(\exp(-\Delta E/kT)\) (holding all else fixed, which is an idealisation).

kT100 <- kT_keV(1e8)
shift <- tibble(dE = seq(-150, 150, length.out = 300)) |>
  mutate(rel = exp(-dE / kT100))

ggplot(shift, aes(dE, rel)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  labs(x = "Resonance shift ΔE (keV)", y = "Rate relative to actual")







Figure 4: Relative triple-alpha rate at 10^8 K if the resonance were displaced by ΔE from its true position, other properties unchanged. A shift of order 100 keV changes the rate by about five orders of magnitude.





This sensitivity is what gives the “fine-tuning” discussions their punch. Fairer treatments, though, vary underlying nuclear parameters and track how the resonance energy, the beryllium state and the later burning of carbon into oxygen all respond together. The conclusion that comes out of such studies is more nuanced than “the universe is exactly balanced”, and what to make of it is a matter of ongoing debate rather than a result.

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
section: After helium: carbon, oxygen and beyond
text:
After helium: carbon, oxygen and beyond
Once carbon exists, it can capture another alpha to form oxygen, \({}^{12}\mathrm{C}(\alpha,\gamma){}^{16}\mathrm{O}\). The competition between this and the triple-alpha process sets the carbon-to-oxygen ratio at the end of helium burning, which controls what a star does afterwards. That rate is known only to limited accuracy, and measuring it more precisely is still an active problem in nuclear astrophysics.
In more massive stars the sequence continues in shells and cores: carbon burning (\(\sim 6\times10^8\) K), neon, oxygen and silicon burning, each stage faster and hotter than the last. The chain stops at iron-group nuclei because they have the greatest binding energy per nucleon, so fusing them no longer releases energy. Elements beyond iron are mostly made by neutron capture: slowly (the s-process, in evolved stars) or rapidly (the r-process, in neutron-star mergers and perhaps some supernovae).

title: Stellar Nucleosynthesis
text:
Takeaways

Fusion in stars depends on quantum tunnelling. The reaction rate is the product of two competing exponentials, giving the narrow Gamow peak.
The temperature sensitivity of a reaction, \(n = (\tau-2)/3\), is set by the Coulomb barrier through the Gamow energy.
Hydrogen burning releases about 26.7 MeV per helium nucleus, enough for the Sun to shine for billions of years.
The triple-alpha process needs a resonance, the Hoyle state, to make carbon at a useful rate. Fred Hoyle inferred its existence in 1953, and Fowler’s group confirmed it.
B2FH (1957) put stellar nucleosynthesis on a systematic footing. Fowler received the Nobel Prize in 1983; Hoyle did not.

title: The Many-Worlds Interpretation
text:
When people say “the multiverse” they can mean two quite different things. One is cosmological: the idea, which Martin Rees takes seriously in the six-numbers post, that there may be many regions or universes with different values of constants such as \(N\), \(\varepsilon\) and \(Q\). The other comes from quantum mechanics: the many-worlds interpretation (MWI), which holds that the equations of quantum theory describe reality exactly as written, with no collapse, so that every possible outcome of a quantum measurement really occurs, each in its own branch of one enormous wave function.
This post is about the second. It covers who proposed it and why, the mathematics that makes it hang together (entanglement and decoherence, computed explicitly), the difficulty of recovering probabilities, who defends the idea today, and how it relates to the cosmological multiverse.

title: The Many-Worlds Interpretation
section: The problem Everett was trying to solve
text:
The problem Everett was trying to solve
Quantum mechanics has two rules for how a state changes. Between measurements, the state evolves smoothly and deterministically under the Schrödinger equation, \(i\hbar\,\partial_t|\psi\rangle = \hat H|\psi\rangle\). At a measurement, the textbook (Copenhagen) account adds a second rule: the state collapses at random to one of the possible outcomes, with probability given by the Born rule, \(p_i = |\langle i|\psi\rangle|^2\).
The trouble is that the second rule never says what counts as a “measurement”. A measuring device is made of atoms that themselves obey quantum mechanics, so why should a detector, a physicist, or a cat be exempt from the smooth evolution? Schrödinger’s cat (1935) and Wigner’s friend (1961) were designed to expose exactly this tension.
Everett’s answer was radical in its simplicity: drop the second rule. Keep only the Schrödinger equation, apply it to everything including the observer, and see what it predicts.

title: The Many-Worlds Interpretation
text:
Hugh Everett III
Hugh Everett III (1930–1982) was born in Washington, D.C., and studied chemical engineering at the Catholic University of America before moving to Princeton in 1953, where he turned to mathematics and physics. At Princeton he studied under John Archibald Wheeler, who had earlier supervised Richard Feynman and later coined the terms “black hole” and “wormhole”. Everett’s 1957 PhD thesis, originally titled “Wave Mechanics Without Probability” and later shortened to “On the Foundations of Quantum Mechanics”, is the founding document of the interpretation. A condensed version appeared the same year in Reviews of Modern Physics as “‘Relative State’ Formulation of Quantum Mechanics”, with a supportive note from Wheeler.
The reception was cool. In 1959 Everett travelled to Copenhagen to present the idea to Niels Bohr and his circle. The meeting went badly: Bohr’s school saw the idea as missing the point, and Everett came away discouraged. By then he had already begun a second career. He worked from 1956 for the Pentagon’s Weapons Systems Evaluation Group on nuclear-war modelling, and later at defence-analysis firms he co-founded, where he did influential work on optimisation (a generalised Lagrange-multiplier method) and on military operations research. He never held a physics professorship, and published almost nothing more on quantum foundations.
Everett did not use the phrase “many worlds”. It was Bryce DeWitt, who admired the idea and championed it, who popularised the name in a 1970 Physics Today article, and who with Neill Graham edited the 1973 collection The Many-Worlds Interpretation of Quantum Mechanics, which finally printed Everett’s long thesis. Everett died of a heart attack in 1982, aged 51, after years of heavy smoking and drinking. His son, the musician Mark Oliver Everett of the band Eels, made a 2007 BBC documentary about his father, Parallel Worlds, Parallel Lives. Everett’s theory was only taken seriously after his death.

title: The Many-Worlds Interpretation
text:
The mathematics: how branches appear

Measurement as entanglement
Take a system qubit in the state \(|\psi\rangle = c_0|0\rangle + c_1|1\rangle\) and a measuring device that starts in a “ready” state \(|R\rangle\). A good measurement is just an interaction that correlates the device with the system:
\[
\bigl(c_0|0\rangle + c_1|1\rangle\bigr)\otimes|R\rangle
\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{Schrödinger}\ }\;
c_0\,|0\rangle|D_0\rangle + c_1\,|1\rangle|D_1\rangle .
\]
The result is an entangled state. There’s no collapse here, just linear evolution. If the device is an observer, the right-hand side contains one term where the observer saw 0 and one where they saw 1. Each term is a self-consistent “world” in which the observer remembers a definite result. Everett called each term’s observer state relative to the system state, hence “relative-state formulation”.
We can check numerically that this entangled state is genuinely not a product state. Its entanglement entropy vanishes only for a product state:

entropy_bits <- function(p) { p <- p[p > 1e-12]; -sum(p * log2(p)) }

c0 <- sqrt(0.9); c1 <- sqrt(0.1)
# State of (system, device) as a 2x2 matrix Psi[system, device]
Psi <- matrix(c(c0, 0, 0, c1), 2, 2)     # c0|0>|D0> + c1|1>|D1>
schmidt <- svd(Psi)$d^2                  # squared Schmidt coefficients
c(schmidt_weights = schmidt, entanglement_entropy_bits = entropy_bits(schmidt))

         schmidt_weights1          schmidt_weights2 entanglement_entropy_bits 
                0.9000000                 0.1000000                 0.4689956 


The two Schmidt weights are 0.9 and 0.1, and the entropy is about 0.469 bits. A product state would have a single weight of 1 and zero entropy.


Why branches don’t interfere: decoherence
If the post-measurement state is just a quantum superposition, why can’t we see interference between the two terms, as we do in the double-slit experiment? The answer, developed from the 1970s by H. Dieter Zeh, Wojciech Zurek and others, is decoherence: the branches become entangled with the enormous number of microscopic degrees of freedom in their surroundings, and this makes interference between them unobservable in practice.
Here is a minimal model. Our system qubit interacts with \(N\) environment qubits, each initially \(|0\rangle\). If the system is \(|0\rangle\), the environment is untouched. If it is \(|1\rangle\), each environment qubit is rotated into \(|e_1\rangle = \cos\theta\,|0\rangle + \sin\theta\,|1\rangle\). The joint state is
\[
|\Psi\rangle = c_0\,|0\rangle\,|0\rangle^{\otimes N} + c_1\,|1\rangle\,|e_1\rangle^{\otimes N}.
\]
Tracing out the environment gives the system’s reduced density matrix. Its diagonal entries are \(|c_0|^2\) and \(|c_1|^2\), unchanged, but the off-diagonal “coherence” term that controls interference is
\[
\rho_{01} = c_0 c_1^{*}\,\langle e_1|0\rangle^{N} = c_0 c_1^{*}\,(\cos\theta)^{N}.
\]
Each extra environment qubit multiplies the coherence by \(\cos\theta < 1\), so it decays exponentially with environment size. I’ll verify this formula by building the full \(2^{N+1}\)-dimensional state vector explicitly and tracing out the environment numerically:

env_state <- function(N, theta) {
  e1 <- c(cos(theta), sin(theta))
  v <- 1
  for (k in seq_len(N)) v <- kronecker(v, e1)
  v
}
zero_env <- function(N) { v <- rep(0, 2^N); v[1] <- 1; v }

coherence_numeric <- function(N, theta, c0, c1) {
  # joint state as a matrix: rows = system (0,1), columns = environment basis
  Psi <- rbind(c0 * zero_env(N), c1 * env_state(N, theta))
  rho <- Psi %*% t(Psi)          # trace over environment (real amplitudes)
  abs(rho[1, 2])
}

theta <- 0.5
chk <- tibble(N = 0:10) |>
  mutate(
    numeric  = sapply(N, coherence_numeric, theta = theta, c0 = c0, c1 = c1),
    analytic = c0 * c1 * cos(theta)^N
  )
chk |> mutate(across(c(numeric, analytic), ~ round(.x, 5))) |> slice(c(1, 2, 3, 6, 11))

# A tibble: 5 × 3
      N numeric analytic
  <int>   <dbl>    <dbl>
1     0  0.3      0.3   
2     1  0.263    0.263 
3     2  0.231    0.231 
4     5  0.156    0.156 
5    10  0.0813   0.0813

max(abs(chk$numeric - chk$analytic))

[1] 2.775558e-17


The brute-force trace and the closed form agree to machine precision (maximum difference 2.8e-17). Even with only 10 environment qubits, the coherence has dropped to 27.1% of its initial value. Real environments contain something like \(10^{20}\) or more degrees of freedom:

curves <- expand.grid(N = 0:60, theta = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5)) |>
  mutate(rel = cos(theta)^N, theta = factor(paste0("θ = ", theta)))

ggplot(curves, aes(N, rel, colour = theta)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = chk |> mutate(theta = factor("θ = 0.5"), rel = numeric / numeric[1]),
             aes(N, rel), size = 2.5, colour = "black", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  labs(x = "Number of environment qubits N", y = "Relative coherence |ρ₀₁| / |ρ₀₁(0)|", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 1: Coherence between the two branches, relative to its starting value, as the number of environment qubits grows. Lines: analytic result (cos θ)^N for three coupling strengths. Points: brute-force numerical trace for N ≤ 10 (θ = 0.5). Decoherence is exponential in environment size.





This is the mechanism that makes the branches effectively independent. Once the off-diagonal terms are negligible, nothing that happens in one branch can be detected from another, and each branch evolves as though the others did not exist. This is what Everettians mean by saying the “worlds” are real but emergent: they are not added to the theory, they are patterns in the wave function that decoherence makes robust.
One common objection is that branching must violate energy conservation. It does not: the total state remains normalised, \(\sum_i|c_i|^2 = 1\), and each branch carries only its share. Branching does not copy the universe; it describes how a single wave function organises itself.

title: The Many-Worlds Interpretation
section: The hard part: where do the probabilities come from?
text:
The hard part: where do the probabilities come from?
If every outcome occurs, what does it mean to say that outcome 0 has probability 0.9? A tempting answer is to count branches. After a single measurement there are two branches, so each has “probability 1/2” regardless of the amplitudes. That gives the wrong answer.
The problem is sharper with repeated measurements. Prepare \(n\) copies of \(\sqrt{0.9}|0\rangle+\sqrt{0.1}|1\rangle\) and measure them all. There are \(2^n\) branches, one for each sequence of results. Counting branches treats all sequences as equally likely, so the number of zeros would follow a Binomial\((n, 1/2)\) distribution. The Born rule instead gives each sequence with \(k\) zeros a weight \(0.9^k\,0.1^{n-k}\), so the total weight of branches with \(k\) zeros is Binomial\((n, 0.9)\).

n <- 50
bc <- tibble(k = 0:n,
             `Count branches` = dbinom(k, n, 0.5),
             `Weight by |amplitude|²` = dbinom(k, n, 0.9)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-k, names_to = "rule", values_to = "p")

ggplot(bc, aes(k, p, fill = rule)) +
  geom_col(position = "identity", alpha = 0.65) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2c7fb8", "#d95f0e")) +
  labs(x = "Number of zeros in 50 measurements", y = "Probability / relative weight", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 2: Distribution of the number of zeros after measuring n = 50 identically prepared qubits with |c0|² = 0.9. Counting branches (blue) predicts about half zeros; weighting each branch by |amplitude|² (orange) gives the observed 90%.





Experiments see frequencies near 90% zeros, so the amplitude-squared weighting is the one that matches experience. The question is why that weighting, rather than branch-counting, should govern what an observer expects.
Everett’s own argument was a law-of-large-numbers result. Measure the weight (squared norm) of the branches whose relative frequency of zeros deviates from 0.9 by more than 0.05. That weight goes to zero as \(n\) grows, so the branches that carry almost all the weight are those in which the observed frequencies match the Born rule:

ns <- c(10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000)
atypical <- sapply(ns, function(n) {
  k <- 0:n
  sum(dbinom(k, n, 0.9)[abs(k / n - 0.9) > 0.05])
})
tibble(n = ns, weight_of_atypical_branches = round(atypical, 5))

# A tibble: 7 × 2
      n weight_of_atypical_branches
  <dbl>                       <dbl>
1    10                     0.613  
2    25                     0.508  
3    50                     0.234  
4   100                     0.0963 
5   250                     0.00836
6   500                     0.0003 
7  1000                     0      


By \(n = 1000\) the atypical branches carry a negligible weight. But critics, notably Adrian Kent, point out that this is circular: it assumes the squared-amplitude weighting is the right measure of “how much a branch matters” and then derives that observers will see Born frequencies. It does not independently justify the weighting.
The modern responses are:

Decision theory (Deutsch 1999, Wallace 2012). Show that a rational agent who accepts Everettian quantum mechanics and some plausible rationality axioms must bet as if branch probabilities equal \(|c_i|^2\).
Self-locating uncertainty (Sebens and Carroll 2018). Before learning which branch you are in, you have uncertainty about where you are, and symmetry arguments fix that uncertainty to the Born weights. This links to ordinary Bayesian reasoning, like the posterior calculations in the prosecutor’s fallacy post: the question is not “what will happen?” but “given everything I know, which of the observers that match my evidence am I?”.
Objective-weights or “measure” proposals. Treat \(|c_i|^2\) as a basic feature of the world, akin to a mass, not a probability to be derived.

Whether any of these succeeds is a matter of live disagreement. It remains the main technical objection to the interpretation.

title: The Many-Worlds Interpretation
text:
Who defends it today?
The interpretation was a fringe position for decades, but has found serious advocates:

David Deutsch (Oxford) is the most committed champion. He argues that the interpretation is demanded by quantum computing, since the computation seems to need explaining by many parallel computational histories, and made the case in The Fabric of Reality (1997). His 1999 decision-theoretic derivation of the Born rule started the modern probability debate.
David Wallace (philosopher of physics, now at the University of Pittsburgh) gave the most careful defence in The Emergent Multiverse (2012), which treats branches as emergent, decoherence-defined structures and develops the decision-theoretic argument.
Sean Carroll (Johns Hopkins and the Santa Fe Institute) brought the view to a wide readership in Something Deeply Hidden (2019) and, with Charles Sebens, developed the self-locating-uncertainty approach.
Simon Saunders (Oxford) has contributed foundational work on branching and probability, and Lev Vaidman (Tel Aviv) is another long-standing advocate, and the author of the standard encyclopedia entry on the topic.
Max Tegmark (MIT) treats many-worlds as one level of a hierarchy of multiverses (below), and has argued that the interpretation follows naturally from taking the Schrödinger equation seriously.
Wojciech Zurek and H. Dieter Zeh built the decoherence framework that makes the interpretation precise, although neither is a straightforward Everettian.

It remains a minority view. A 2013 survey of conference participants by Schlosshauer, Kofler and Zeilinger found roughly 42% favouring Copenhagen-style views and about 18% favouring Everett, with the rest split among other approaches. The main rivals each have prominent supporters and each has costs:

Collapse theories (GRW, Penrose) modify the dynamics, adding a physical collapse mechanism, with testable differences.
Pilot-wave (Bohmian) mechanics adds definite particle positions guided by the wave function, at the cost of non-locality.
QBism and relational views treat the quantum state as an agent’s information, not a feature of the world.

Critics such as Tim Maudlin, David Albert and Adrian Kent press the probability problem and ask whether “worlds” are well defined.

title: The Many-Worlds Interpretation
text:
How it connects to cosmology
It is not the same as Rees’s multiverse. Tegmark organises the possibilities into levels:








Level
What exists
Source




I
Regions beyond our cosmic horizon, same laws and constants
Infinite or very large space


II
Other “bubble” universes with different constants and perhaps different physics
Eternal inflation, string landscape


III
Branches of the quantum wave function
Everett’s many-worlds


IV
All mathematically consistent structures
Mathematical universe hypothesis



The multiverse that bears on the six numbers is Level II: different regions can have different \(N\), \(\varepsilon\), \(Q\) and \(\lambda\), so an anthropic selection effect can explain why we see values that permit observers. That is the argument Carr and Rees made in 1979, and it is the cosmological version of the carbon-resonance reasoning behind the Hoyle state.
Level III does not do that job. Every Everettian branch obeys the same Schrödinger equation with the same constants. Many-worlds therefore gives no anthropic explanation for why \(N \approx 10^{36}\) or why \(\varepsilon\approx0.007\). The two ideas are logically independent: one can accept either, both or neither. Deutsch and Tegmark have argued that if you believe in an inflating universe, the two views end up looking more alike.
A place where they meet: the origin of structure. The amplitude \(Q\approx10^{-5}\) of primordial density fluctuations is, in the inflationary picture, set by quantum fluctuations that were stretched to cosmic size. On the Everettian reading, the specific pattern of hot and cold spots in the microwave background is one of an enormous number of branches, each with a different realisation of the same statistics. The galaxies in our branch sit where they do because of one such history; our measured \(Q\) describes the statistics that all branches share.
Probability again. Questions like “which observers am I?” echo the counting problems in the birthday paradox post, where the right answer came from counting the right things (pairs, not people). Here the analogous question, what to count and how to weight it, is exactly what the Born-rule debate is about.

title: The Many-Worlds Interpretation
text:
Takeaways

Everett (1957) removed the collapse postulate and kept only unitary evolution; measurement becomes entanglement, and each outcome corresponds to a branch.
Decoherence explains why branches don’t interfere: coherence falls as \((\cos\theta)^N\) with environment size, as the numerical check shows.
The unresolved issue is probability. Counting branches gives the wrong answer; the Born weights come from decision theory, self-locating arguments or a postulate, and critics contest each.
Many-worlds is not the cosmological multiverse. It does not explain fine-tuned constants, which belong to Level II arguments of the kind Rees discusses.
It remains a minority but serious position, with prominent defenders such as Deutsch, Wallace, Carroll, Saunders, Vaidman and Tegmark.

title: Inside a Meade LX90: Ray Tracing an 8-inch Schmidt–Cassegrain
text:
The Meade LX90 8-inch is a Schmidt–Cassegrain telescope (SCT): a Cassegrain reflector with a thin aspheric glass corrector plate across the front. That is a slight correction to calling it a “Cassegrain”: a plain Cassegrain has no corrector, and the plate is what lets this design use cheap spherical mirrors. This post builds a ray-trace model of such a telescope in Python, follows the light from a star to the eye, and then uses the model to look at the qualities that make a telescope good or bad: diffraction, off-axis aberrations, field curvature, and chromatic focus (including how an SCT compares with an achromatic and an apochromatic refractor).
What this model is, and is not. Meade does not publish the lens and mirror prescription, so I have not reproduced the real instrument. Instead I built a representative 8-inch f/10 SCT from the published specifications (203 mm aperture, f/10, a central obstruction of roughly a third of the aperture) and designed the corrector plate myself by optimisation. The behaviour is therefore realistic, but individual numbers (for example the exact field curvature) will differ from a particular telescope. The LX90 also comes in an “ACF” version, whose optics Meade describes as having a hyperbolic secondary mirror and an aspheric corrector to reduce coma. I have modelled the classic spherical-mirror SCT, which is the simpler case.

title: Inside a Meade LX90: Ray Tracing an 8-inch Schmidt–Cassegrain
text:
How a Schmidt–Cassegrain works
Light enters through the corrector plate (nearly flat glass with a subtle aspheric figure on its inner face), travels down the tube to a concave primary mirror, returns to a convex secondary mirror mounted on the back of the corrector, and then passes back through a hole in the primary to a focus behind the telescope. The light crosses the tube three times, which is how a 2032 mm focal length fits into a tube about half a metre long.
Geometry. Let the primary have focal length \(f_1\) (for these telescopes it is about \(f/2\), so \(f_1 = 406.4\) mm) and let the secondary magnify the primary’s image by a factor \(m\), so that the system focal length is \(f = m f_1\). For \(f = 2032\) mm we need \(m = 5\). If the focus is to lie a distance \(b\) behind the primary and the mirrors are separated by \(d\), then
\[
m = \frac{d+b}{f_1 - d}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
d = \frac{m f_1 - b}{m + 1},
\]
and the mirror equation for the convex secondary, with virtual object distance \(s = f_1 - d\) and image distance \(s' = d + b\), gives its radius of curvature
\[
\frac{2}{R_2} = \frac{1}{s'} - \frac{1}{s}\ (<0,\ \text{convex}).
\]


Show code

d  = (m * f1 - b) / (m + 1)     # mirror separation
s, sp = f1 - d, d + b
R1 = -2 * f1                    # primary radius (concave; negative in Optiland's convention)
R2 = 2 / (1/sp - 1/s)           # secondary radius (convex)
sec_diam = 2 * (D/2) * s / f1   # marginal-ray footprint on the secondary, mm

section: Building the optical model in Python
text:
Building the optical model in Python
I’ll use Optiland, an open-source Python package for sequential ray tracing, aberration analysis, wavefront and MTF calculation, and optimisation. A sequential model lists surfaces in the order the light meets them, including the reflections: corrector front, corrector back, primary, secondary, image. Mirrors use material="mirror", and after each reflection the thickness changes sign.


Show code
FIELD_MAX = 0.5   # maximum field half-angle in degrees (image circle about 35 mm across)

def Hn(deg):
    """Optiland wants normalised field coordinates (maximum field = 1)."""
    return deg / FIELD_MAX

def build_sct(coeffs=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), t_back=None, r_image=np.inf, glass="N-BK7"):
    """Representative 8-inch f/10 Schmidt-Cassegrain.

    coeffs: even-asphere coefficients (r^2, r^4, r^6) on the back face of the corrector plate.
    t_back: secondary-to-focus distance (mm); r_image: radius of the image surface.
    """
    t_back = d + b if t_back is None else t_back
    o = Optic()
    o.surfaces.add(index=0, radius=be.inf, thickness=be.inf)
    # 1: corrector front face, flat; this is the aperture stop. The secondary's housing blocks the centre.
    o.surfaces.add(index=1, radius=be.inf, thickness=4.0, material=glass, is_stop=True,
                   aperture=physical_apertures.RadialAperture(r_max=be.inf, r_min=obs * D / 2))
    # 2: corrector back face, aspheric
    o.surfaces.add(index=2, radius=be.inf, thickness=d, surface_type="even_asphere",
                   coefficients=list(coeffs))
    # 3: spherical primary mirror (light now travels in the -z direction)
    o.surfaces.add(index=3, radius=R1, thickness=-d, material="mirror")
    # 4: spherical convex secondary, mounted on the corrector; light returns in +z through the primary's hole
    o.surfaces.add(index=4, radius=R2, thickness=t_back, material="mirror",
                   aperture=physical_apertures.RadialAperture(r_max=33.0, r_min=0))
    # 5: image surface
    o.surfaces.add(index=5, radius=r_image)
    o.set_aperture(aperture_type="EPD", value=D)
    o.fields.set_type(field_type="angle")
    for ang in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5):
        o.fields.add(y=ang)
    for wl, primary in ((0.45, False), (0.55, True), (0.65, False)):
        o.wavelengths.add(value=wl, is_primary=primary)
    return o

sct0 = build_sct()
print(f"Paraxial focal length: {float(sct0.paraxial.f2()):.1f} mm,  f/{float(sct0.paraxial.FNO()):.2f}")


Paraxial focal length: 2032.0 mm,  f/10.00


The paraxial focal length comes out at exactly 2032 mm and f/10, which confirms the geometry and the sign conventions.

Designing the corrector plate
Two spherical mirrors in this configuration have enormous spherical aberration: rays from the edge of the primary focus much closer than rays near the centre. Bernhard Schmidt’s 1930 insight was that a weak aspheric plate at the entrance can pre-compensate. Here I let a least-squares optimiser choose the plate’s figure. The variables are the coefficients of the \(r^2\), \(r^4\) and \(r^6\) terms on the plate’s back face, plus the focus position and the curvature of the image surface. The objective is the RMS spot radius at field angles of 0°, 0.1° and 0.2°.


Show code
def pupil_annulus(nr=7, nth=18):
    """Equal-area sampling of the pupil outside the central obstruction."""
    r = np.sqrt(np.linspace(obs**2, 1.0, nr + 1)[:-1] + (1 - obs**2) / nr / 2)
    th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, nth, endpoint=False)
    R, T = np.meshgrid(r, th)
    return (R * np.cos(T)).ravel(), (R * np.sin(T)).ravel()

PX, PY = pupil_annulus()

def rms_spot_um(o, field_deg, wl=0.55):
    """RMS spot radius about the centroid, in microns."""
    rays = o.trace_generic(Hx=0, Hy=Hn(field_deg), Px=PX, Py=PY, wavelength=wl)
    x, y = np.asarray(rays.x), np.asarray(rays.y)
    ok = np.isfinite(x) & np.isfinite(y)
    return 1000 * np.sqrt(np.mean((x[ok] - x[ok].mean())**2 + (y[ok] - y[ok].mean())**2))

SCALES = np.array([1e-6, 1e-10, 1e-15])     # typical size of each aspheric coefficient

def apply(o, p):
    for i, sc in enumerate(SCALES):
        o.set_asphere_coeff(p[i] * sc, 2, i)
    o.set_thickness(d + b + p[3], 4)
    curv = p[4] * 1e-3
    o.set_radius(1/curv if abs(curv) > 1e-12 else np.inf, 5)

FIELDS = [0.0, 0.1, 0.2]; WEIGHTS = [1.0, 0.8, 0.6]
sct = build_sct()
def residuals(p):
    apply(sct, p)
    return [w * rms_spot_um(sct, h) for h, w in zip(FIELDS, WEIGHTS)]

uncorrected_rms = rms_spot_um(sct, 0.0)             # all-zero start = no corrector figure
fit = least_squares(residuals, np.zeros(5), diff_step=1e-3, max_nfev=200)
apply(sct, fit.x)

c2, c4, c6 = fit.x[:3] * SCALES
t_focus   = d + b + fit.x[3]
R_image   = 1 / (fit.x[4] * 1e-3)
sag_edge  = (c2 * 101.6**2 + c4 * 101.6**4 + c6 * 101.6**6) * 1000   # plate sag at the aperture edge, microns

 f"| RMS spot radius on axis, with corrector | {rms_spot_um(sct, 0.0):.1f} µm |"))

The optimiser turns an uncorrected blur of more than a millimetre into a few microns, using a plate whose sag at the edge is only about 70 µm (roughly a tenth of the thickness of a sheet of paper). That the correction needs so little glass is why the corrector can be a thin, cheap plate.
