title: Inside a Meade LX90: Ray Tracing an 8-inch Schmidt–Cassegrain
text:
The eyepiece and the eye
The model so far stops at the focal plane, where a camera sensor would sit. For visual use we add an eyepiece. I designed a 26 mm Plössl, the classic eyepiece that comes with many telescopes: two identical cemented crown/flint doublets, mounted with their flint faces toward each other. The radii were found by optimising, from the eye side, for small spots at field angles up to 26° (a 52° apparent field), with the focal length held at 26 mm.


Show code
FE, EYE_RELIEF, EYE_PUPIL = 26.0, 18.0, 3.0

def eyepiece_design(R1, R2, R3, gap=1.0, tc=5.0, tf=2.0):
    """Eyepiece traced from the eye side with a collimated beam (object at infinity)."""
    o = Optic()
    o.surfaces.add(index=0, radius=be.inf, thickness=be.inf)
    o.surfaces.add(index=1, radius=be.inf, thickness=EYE_RELIEF, is_stop=True)    # eye pupil
    o.surfaces.add(index=2, radius=R1,  thickness=tc, material="N-BK7")
    o.surfaces.add(index=3, radius=R2,  thickness=tf, material="N-F2")
    o.surfaces.add(index=4, radius=R3,  thickness=gap)
    o.surfaces.add(index=5, radius=-R3, thickness=tf, material="N-F2")
    o.surfaces.add(index=6, radius=-R2, thickness=tc, material="N-BK7")
    o.surfaces.add(index=7, radius=-R1, thickness=10.0)
    o.surfaces.add(index=8)
    o.set_aperture(aperture_type="EPD", value=EYE_PUPIL)
    o.fields.set_type(field_type="angle")
    for h in (0, 13, 21, 26): o.fields.add(y=h)
    for wl, primary in ((0.4861, False), (0.5876, True), (0.6563, False)): o.wavelengths.add(value=wl, is_primary=primary)
    return o

def eye_spot_um(o, h_deg, wl=0.5876):
    r = np.sqrt((np.arange(8) + 0.5) / 8); th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 16, endpoint=False)
    R, T = np.meshgrid(r, th)
    rays = o.trace_generic(Hx=0, Hy=h_deg / 26.0, Px=(R*np.cos(T)).ravel(), Py=(R*np.sin(T)).ravel(), wavelength=wl)
    x, y = np.asarray(rays.x), np.asarray(rays.y); ok = np.isfinite(x) & np.isfinite(y)
    return 1000 * np.sqrt(np.mean((x[ok]-x[ok].mean())**2 + (y[ok]-y[ok].mean())**2))

def eye_residuals(p):
    o = eyepiece_design(*p); o.image_solve()
    return [3.0 * (float(o.paraxial.f2()) - FE)] + [eye_spot_um(o, h) / 10 for h in (0, 13, 21, 26)]

# a few starting points; keep the best physically sensible biconvex-crown solution
best = None
for start in ([37.1, -15.9, -47.4], [50.0, -18.0, -60.0], [30.0, -20.0, -100.0]):
    try:
        r = least_squares(eye_residuals, np.array(start), bounds=([12, -80, -400], [120, -8, -25]),
                          diff_step=1e-3, max_nfev=150)
        if best is None or r.cost < best.cost: best = r
    except Exception:
        pass
# the optimiser's best result sits on a bound; use the neighbouring interior solution
R1e, R2e, R3e = 51.0, -16.45, -37.25
eye_design = eyepiece_design(R1e, R2e, R3e); eye_design.image_solve()
fe_actual = float(eye_design.paraxial.f2()); focal_dist = float(eye_design.surfaces[7].thickness)
spots = [eye_spot_um(eye_design, h) for h in (0, 13, 21, 26)]

full.surfaces.add(index=0, radius=be.inf, thickness=be.inf)

                  aperture=physical_apertures.RadialAperture(r_max=33.0, r_min=0))
# eyepiece, light travelling toward the eye: field doublet first (radii and order reversed from the eye-side design)
full.surfaces.add(index=5,  radius=+R1e, thickness=5.0, material="N-BK7")
full.surfaces.add(index=6,  radius=+R2e, thickness=2.0, material="N-F2")

# reduced eye: one refracting surface and a retina

full.surfaces.add(index=12, radius=be.inf)
full.set_aperture(aperture_type="EPD", value=D)
full.fields.set_type(field_type="angle")
for ang in (0.0, 0.25): full.fields.add(y=ang)

# fine-tune the telescope-to-eyepiece spacing so a star focuses sharply on the retina
def retina_blur(dt):
    full.set_thickness(t_focus + focal_dist + dt, 4)
    r = np.sqrt((np.arange(6) + 0.5) / 6); th = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 12, endpoint=False)
    R, T = np.meshgrid(r, th)
    rays = full.trace_generic(Hx=0, Hy=0, Px=(obs + (1-obs)*R*R).ravel()**0.5*np.cos(T).ravel(),
                              Py=(obs + (1-obs)*R*R).ravel()**0.5*np.sin(T).ravel(), wavelength=0.55)
    x, y = np.asarray(rays.x), np.asarray(rays.y); ok = np.isfinite(x) & np.isfinite(y)
    return np.sqrt(np.mean((x[ok]-x[ok].mean())**2 + (y[ok]-y[ok].mean())**2))
res = minimize_scalar(retina_blur, bounds=(-3, 3), method="bounded")
full.set_thickness(t_focus + focal_dist + res.x, 4)

title: Inside a Meade LX90: Ray Tracing an 8-inch Schmidt–Cassegrain
text:
Diffraction: what perfection looks like
Even with no aberrations at all, a circular aperture produces an Airy pattern. The central obstruction changes it: it transfers a little energy from the central disk into the rings. To quantify that, I compute the point-spread function by Fourier transform of the pupil, for the clear 8-inch aperture and for the aperture with a 34% obstruction.


Show code
from scipy.special import j1

def airy_intensity(v, eps):
    """Normalised intensity of the diffraction pattern of an annular aperture with obstruction ratio eps.
    v = pi * r / (lambda * N) is the usual dimensionless focal-plane radius."""
    v = np.asarray(v, float)
    out = np.ones_like(v)
    nz = v > 0
    term = 2 * j1(v[nz]) / v[nz]
    if eps > 0:
        term = term - eps**2 * 2 * j1(eps * v[nz]) / (eps * v[nz])
    out[nz] = (term / (1 - eps**2))**2
    return out

r_lamN = np.linspace(0, 60, 240001)               # radius in units of lambda*N
to_um = lam * N_f * 1000                          # microns per unit of lambda*N
def enclosed_energy(eps):
    cum = np.cumsum(airy_intensity(np.pi * r_lamN, eps) * r_lamN)
    return cum / cum[-1]

ee_c, ee_o = enclosed_energy(0.0), enclosed_energy(obs)
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
rr = np.linspace(0, 6, 1500)
axs[0].semilogy(rr * to_um, airy_intensity(np.pi * rr, 0.0), color=BLUE, label="Clear aperture")
axs[0].semilogy(rr * to_um, airy_intensity(np.pi * rr, obs), color=ORANGE, label="34% obstruction")
axs[0].set_xlabel("Radius in the focal plane (µm)"); axs[0].set_ylabel("Relative intensity")
axs[0].set_ylim(1e-6, 1.5); axs[0].legend()
axs[1].plot(r_lamN * to_um, ee_c, color=BLUE, label="Clear aperture")
axs[1].plot(r_lamN * to_um, ee_o, color=ORANGE, label="34% obstruction")
axs[1].axvline(1.22 * to_um, ls="--", color=GREY)
axs[1].set_xlim(0, 40); axs[1].set_xlabel("Radius (µm)"); axs[1].set_ylabel("Enclosed energy"); axs[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

r_first = 1.22 * to_um
ee_clear_first = float(np.interp(1.22, r_lamN, ee_c)); ee_obs_first = float(np.interp(1.22, r_lamN, ee_o))








Figure 3: Left: radial profile of the diffraction pattern (log scale) for a clear circular aperture and for one with a 34% central obstruction. The obstruction narrows the central peak slightly and brightens the rings. Right: fraction of the light enclosed within a given radius. The dashed line marks the first dark ring of the clear aperture, 6.7 µm.





The dashed line is the radius of the first dark ring, 6.7 µm. A clear aperture puts about 84% of the light inside it, close to the textbook 84%. With the obstruction the figure falls to about 65%, because more light is pushed into the rings. This is why obstructed telescopes show slightly lower contrast on fine planetary detail.

The MTF
The modulation transfer function (MTF) says how much contrast the telescope preserves at each spatial frequency. For a perfect circular aperture it falls steadily to zero at the diffraction cutoff \(\nu_c = 1/(\lambda N)\), about 182 cycles/mm here. A central obstruction cuts contrast at low and mid frequencies, and gives a slight boost near the cutoff. I compute the ideal curves from the autocorrelation of the pupil, and then the actual model with its aberrations from Optiland’s FFT-based MTF.


Show code
def pupil_mask(eps, n=1024, R=128):
    y, x = np.mgrid[-n//2:n//2, -n//2:n//2]; r = np.hypot(x, y)
    return ((r <= R) & (r >= eps*R)).astype(float)

def ideal_mtf(eps, n=1024, R=128):
    mask = pupil_mask(eps, n, R)
    ac = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.ifft2(np.abs(np.fft.fft2(mask))**2).real); ac /= ac.max()
    prof = ac[n//2, n//2:]; nu = np.arange(len(prof)) / (2*R)
    return nu, prof

nu_c = 1 / (lam * N_f)   # cycles per mm
nu, mtf_clear = ideal_mtf(0.0); _, mtf_obs = ideal_mtf(obs)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 4.2))
ax.plot(nu * nu_c, mtf_clear, "--", color=GREY, label="Ideal, clear aperture")
ax.plot(nu * nu_c, mtf_obs, "--", color=ORANGE, label="Ideal, 34% obstruction")
for fd, alpha, lab in ((0.0, 1.0, "Model, on axis"), (0.1, 0.6, "Model, 0.1°"), (0.2, 0.35, "Model, 0.2°")):
    m = FFTMTF(sct, fields=[(0, Hn(fd))], wavelength=0.55, num_rays=64, grid_size=256, max_freq="cutoff")
    f_ = np.asarray(m.freq[0]); t_ = np.asarray(m.mtf[0][0])
    sel = f_ <= nu_c
    ax.plot(f_[sel], t_[sel], color=BLUE, alpha=alpha, label=lab)
ax.set_xlabel("Spatial frequency (cycles/mm)"); ax.set_ylabel("Modulation"); ax.set_xlim(0, nu_c); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 4: MTF of the 8-inch SCT. Dashed grey: ideal clear aperture. Dashed orange: ideal aperture with the 34% obstruction. Solid blue: the ray-traced model on axis; the lighter curves are 0.1° and 0.2° off axis (tangential). Contrast falls with both the obstruction and the residual aberrations.





On axis the model follows the ideal obstructed curve closely: the corrector and mirrors work as designed. Moving off axis, the curves peel away, which is the subject of the next section.

title: Inside a Meade LX90: Ray Tracing an 8-inch Schmidt–Cassegrain
text:
Off-axis performance and field curvature
Off axis, three things degrade the image: coma (stars become comet-shaped), astigmatism, and field curvature, where the sharpest focus lies on a curved surface instead of a flat sensor. To separate them I trace the model with a flat image plane and find, for each field angle, the focus position that minimises the RMS spot. The shift of that best focus from the axial focus measures the curvature of the focal surface.


Show code
angles = np.array([0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5])
curved = np.array([rms_spot_um(sct, a) for a in angles])

# flat image plane: same optics, image surface made flat and refocused over 0-0.2 degrees
flat = build_sct(coeffs=(c2, c4, c6))
def flat_cost(t):
    flat.set_thickness(t, 4)
    return sum(rms_spot_um(flat, a) for a in (0.0, 0.1, 0.2))
rt = minimize_scalar(flat_cost, bounds=(t_focus - 3, t_focus + 3), method="bounded")
flat.set_thickness(rt.x, 4)
flat_rms = np.array([rms_spot_um(flat, a) for a in angles])

# best-focus position at each field angle on a flat plane
def best_focus(a):
    f = lambda t: (flat.set_thickness(t, 4), rms_spot_um(flat, a))[1]
    return minimize_scalar(f, bounds=(t_focus - 4, t_focus + 4), method="bounded").x
bf = np.array([best_focus(a) for a in angles])
h_img = FL * np.tan(np.radians(angles))                   # image height, mm
dz = bf - bf[0]                                           # best-focus shift relative to the axis, mm
R_fit = np.sum(h_img**4) / (2 * np.sum(h_img**2 * dz))    # least-squares radius for dz = h^2 / (2R)

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.0))
axs[0].axhspan(0, r_first, color=GREY, alpha=0.2, label="Airy radius")
axs[0].plot(angles, curved, "o-", color=BLUE, label="Curved focal surface")
axs[0].plot(angles, flat_rms, "s-", color=ORANGE, label="Flat focal plane")
axs[0].set_xlabel("Field angle (degrees)"); axs[0].set_ylabel("RMS spot radius (µm)"); axs[0].legend()
axs[1].plot(h_img, dz, "o", color=BLUE, label="Ray-traced best focus")
hh = np.linspace(0, h_img.max(), 100)
axs[1].plot(hh, hh**2 / (2 * R_fit), "--", color=GREY, label=f"Sphere, R = {abs(R_fit):.0f} mm")
axs[1].set_xlabel("Image height (mm)"); axs[1].set_ylabel("Best-focus shift (mm)"); axs[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
edge_defocus_blur = abs(dz[-1]) / (2 * N_f) * 1000      # blur radius from edge defocus, microns








Figure 5: Left: RMS geometric spot radius against field angle for the optimiser’s curved focal surface (blue) and for a flat focal plane refocused for the best compromise over 0–0.2° (orange). The grey band is the Airy-disk radius (6.7 µm). Right: how far the best focus at each field angle sits from the axial focus; the dashed parabola corresponds to a focal surface of constant radius of curvature.





The best-focus surface is close to a sphere with radius of about 205 mm, about a tenth of the focal length. (The curved image surface the optimiser chose earlier, R ≈ 330 mm, is flatter than this because it balances curvature against coma.) At the field edge (0.5°, 17.7 mm from the axis) the focus has moved by about 0.77 mm, several times the ±0.11 mm depth of focus, so a flat sensor placed at the axial focus would show noticeably defocused stars in the corners. In this f/10 design, however, coma and astigmatism dominate the blur over most of the field: the curved focal surface only lowers the RMS spot noticeably beyond about 0.3°. Field curvature matters more once a focal reducer makes the system faster, which is why reducers are sold as combined “reducer/flatteners”.
The geometric blur passes the Airy radius at only about 0.06° (a few arcminutes) off axis, even on the curved surface. The wavefront view says the same thing. The Strehl ratio (the peak brightness compared with a perfect system) follows from the RMS wavefront error \(\sigma\) in waves through the Maréchal approximation \(S \approx e^{-(2\pi\sigma)^2}\), and 0.8 is the usual threshold for “diffraction limited”.


Show code
def wavefront_rms_waves(o, field_deg, wl=0.55):
    w = OPD(o, field=(0, Hn(field_deg)), wavelength=wl, num_rays=64, distribution="uniform")
    v = list(w.data.values())[0]
    keep = np.asarray(v.intensity) > 0           # drop rays blocked by the obstruction
    return float(np.std(np.asarray(v.opd)[keep]))

fa = np.array([0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.04, 0.06, 0.08, 0.1])
sig = np.array([wavefront_rms_waves(sct, a) for a in fa])
strehl = np.exp(-(2*np.pi*sig)**2)
dl_limit = float(np.interp(0.8, strehl[::-1], fa[::-1]))      # field angle where Strehl crosses 0.8

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
axs[0].plot(fa, sig, "o-", color=BLUE); axs[0].axhline(0.0745, ls="--", color=GREY)
axs[0].set_xlabel("Field angle (degrees)"); axs[0].set_ylabel("RMS wavefront error (waves)")
axs[1].plot(fa, strehl, "o-", color=BLUE); axs[1].axhline(0.8, ls="--", color=GREY)
axs[1].set_xlabel("Field angle (degrees)"); axs[1].set_ylabel("Strehl ratio (Maréchal)"); axs[1].set_ylim(0, 1.05)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
blur_edge_arcsec = float(np.interp(0.32, angles, curved)) * plate_scale / 1000   # RMS blur radius at the eyepiece field edge








Figure 6: Wavefront error and Strehl ratio against field angle (central obstruction excluded from the pupil). The Maréchal formula is only trustworthy for Strehl ratios near or above 0.8, so the plot stops at 0.1°; beyond it the image is simply far from diffraction limited.





The on-axis wavefront error is 0.043 waves RMS, a Strehl ratio of about 0.93, comfortably diffraction limited (the dashed line is the 0.075-wave Maréchal criterion). The Strehl ratio falls below 0.8 at about 0.016°, roughly 0.9 arcminute from the axis. That is a tiny diffraction-limited zone, and it is typical of a classic f/10 SCT, whose coma is set by the f-ratio of the combined system. Visually it is much less of a problem than it sounds: at the edge of a 26 mm Plössl’s field (about 0.32° from the axis, since the true field is 0.64°) the model’s RMS blur radius is about 3.0 arcseconds, comparable to typical atmospheric seeing. It does explain why the ACF design and aftermarket flatteners exist, and why astrophotographers see star shapes degrade toward the corners of a large sensor.

title: Inside a Meade LX90: Ray Tracing an 8-inch Schmidt–Cassegrain
text:
Colour: is an SCT apochromatic?
A refractor bends different colours by different amounts, so its focus depends on wavelength. A mirror reflects every wavelength identically, so the mirrors add no chromatic aberration at all. In an SCT the only refracting element is the thin corrector plate (plus the eyepiece), so the telescope should be nearly colour-free.
To test this I calculate the focal shift with wavelength for three 8-inch f/10 systems, using real glass dispersion data from Optiland’s catalogues:

The SCT model, from the ray trace (paraxial rays at each wavelength).
A refractor achromat, a thin crown/flint pair (N-BK7 with N-F2) whose focus is matched at 450 nm and 650 nm.
A refractor apochromat, a thin-lens triplet using fluorite-class S-FPL53 with N-LAK34 and N-KZFS11, with the focus matched at three wavelengths (450, 550, 650 nm). This is an idealised design for comparison, not a commercial prescription.

For the refractors, the focal length of thin lenses in contact follows from \(1/f(\lambda) = \sum_i c_i\,[\,n_i(\lambda) - 1\,]\) where \(c_i\) is each element’s curvature difference. Choosing the \(c_i\) so that \(f\) is equal at the matched wavelengths is the entire design.


Show code
wl_grid = np.linspace(0.40, 0.70, 61)

def n_of(name, catalog=None):
    mat = Material(name) if catalog is None else Material(name, catalog=catalog)
    return np.array([float(np.asarray(mat.n(w)).ravel()[0]) for w in wl_grid])

glass = {"N-BK7": n_of("N-BK7"), "N-F2": n_of("N-F2"), "S-FPL53": n_of("S-FPL53", "ohara"),
         "N-LAK34": n_of("N-LAK34"), "N-KZFS11": n_of("N-KZFS11")}
iw = [int(np.argmin(abs(wl_grid - x))) for x in (0.45, 0.55, 0.65)]

def thin_contact_focal(names, match):
    A = np.array([[glass[n][i] - 1 for n in names] for i in match]); rhs = np.ones(len(match)) / FL
    c = np.linalg.solve(A, rhs)
    return 1 / sum(c[j] * (glass[n] - 1) for j, n in enumerate(names))

f_achro = thin_contact_focal(["N-BK7", "N-F2"], [iw[0], iw[2]])
f_apo   = thin_contact_focal(["S-FPL53", "N-LAK34", "N-KZFS11"], iw)
ref = int(np.argmin(abs(wl_grid - 0.55)))
shift_achro = (f_achro - f_achro[ref]) * 1000      # microns, relative to 550 nm
shift_apo   = (f_apo   - f_apo[ref]) * 1000

# SCT: axis crossing of a near-axis ray at each wavelength
def sct_focus_shift(o, w_um):
    rays = o.trace_generic(Hx=0, Hy=0, Px=np.array([0.0]), Py=np.array([0.02]), wavelength=w_um)
    y = float(np.asarray(rays.y)[0]); M = float(np.asarray(rays.M)[0]); Nn = float(np.asarray(rays.N)[0])
    return -y / (M / Nn)
sh = np.array([sct_focus_shift(sct, w) for w in wl_grid])
shift_sct = (sh - sh[ref]) * 1000

dof_um = 2 * lam * N_f**2 * 1000     # +/- 2 lambda N^2 diffraction-limited depth of focus
ptp = lambda a: a.max() - a.min()
display(Markdown(
 "| System | Focal shift, peak-to-peak, 400–700 nm | Compared with ±2λN² = ±" + f"{dof_um:.0f} µm |\n|:--|:--|:--|\n"
 f"| Achromat refractor (BK7 + F2) | {ptp(shift_achro)/1000:.1f} mm | {ptp(shift_achro)/(2*dof_um):.0f}× the tolerance |\n"
 f"| Apochromat refractor (FPL53 + LAK34 + KZFS11) | {ptp(shift_apo):.0f} µm | {ptp(shift_apo)/(2*dof_um):.2f}× |\n"
 f"| Schmidt–Cassegrain model | {ptp(shift_sct):.0f} µm | {ptp(shift_sct)/(2*dof_um):.2f}× |"))

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.0))
x = wl_grid * 1000
axs[0].plot(x, shift_achro / 1000, color=RED, label="Achromat (BK7 + F2)")
axs[0].plot(x, shift_apo / 1000, color=GREEN, label="Apochromat triplet")

Figure 7: Longitudinal chromatic focal shift relative to 550 nm for three 8-inch f/10 telescopes. Left: the achromat refractor’s violet and red foci are millimetres away. Right: zoom on the SCT and the apochromat, with the shaded band showing the ±2λN² diffraction-limited depth of focus (±110 µm). Both stay inside the band over the whole visible range.





The result is striking. The achromat’s focus wanders by about 8.6 mm across the visible band, so bright stars wear a violet halo; a well-designed apochromat holds it to about 26 µm; and the SCT model sits at about 20 µm, within the same tolerance. For the telescope alone, a Schmidt–Cassegrain is effectively apochromatic in focus, because the only glass in the light path is a thin, nearly flat plate that barely bends the beam. (The last figure of this section shows the one residual, spherochromatism of the plate.)
Caveats. The corrector plate in a real instrument is a different glass and a different shape, and the eyepiece is a real source of colour error (a Plössl is only an achromat, and its lateral colour at the field edge is the dominant residual). Coatings and thermal effects also matter. The point is the contrast with a refractor, not the precise micron figure.
To see this as a picture, the next figure plots spots at three wavelengths on axis, at a single common focus.


Show code
def spot_xy(o, field_deg, wl):
    rays = o.trace_generic(Hx=0, Hy=Hn(field_deg), Px=PX, Py=PY, wavelength=wl)
    x, y = np.asarray(rays.x), np.asarray(rays.y)
    ok = np.isfinite(x) & np.isfinite(y)
    return 1000 * (x[ok] - x[ok].mean()), 1000 * (y[ok] - y[ok].mean())

# uncorrected comparison, refocused for the best RMS
unc = build_sct()
ru = minimize_scalar(lambda t: (unc.set_thickness(t, 4), rms_spot_um(unc, 0.0))[1], bounds=(d + b - 6, d + b + 6), method="bounded")
unc.set_thickness(ru.x, 4)

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.5, 4.6))
for ax, o, title, lim in ((axs[0], unc, "Uncorrected (spherical mirrors only)", 1500), (axs[1], sct, "With designed corrector plate", 14)):
    for wl, col in ((0.45, BLUE), (0.55, GREEN), (0.65, RED)):
        xs, ys = spot_xy(o, 0.0, wl); ax.scatter(xs, ys, s=7, color=col, alpha=0.7, label=f"{int(wl*1000)} nm")
    ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), r_first, fill=False, ls="--", color="k"))
    ax.set_xlim(-lim, lim); ax.set_ylim(-lim, lim); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("x (µm)"); ax.set_ylabel("y (µm)")
axs[1].legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
unc_rms_best = rms_spot_um(unc, 0.0)
rms_by_wl = {w: rms_spot_um(sct, 0.0, wl=w) for w in (0.45, 0.55, 0.65)}








Figure 8: On-axis spot diagrams at 450 nm (blue), 550 nm (green) and 650 nm (red), at one common focus. Left: the SCT without a corrector figure (a plain spherical-mirror pair). Right: the corrected SCT. The dashed circle is the Airy disk. At the design wavelength (550 nm) the corrected spots lie almost entirely within it; at 450 and 650 nm the outer pupil zones land farther out (spherochromatism).





Without the corrector plate the best-focus blur is still about 1344 µm in radius, roughly two hundred times the Airy disk; with it, the 550 nm spot sits inside the diffraction pattern.
A caveat on colour. The corrected spots are not identical at the three wavelengths. The RMS spot radius is 21.0 µm at 450 nm, 3.8 µm at 550 nm and 12.6 µm at 650 nm, because the plate’s spherical-aberration correction is exact only at the design wavelength (a residual called spherochromatism). The focus does not move appreciably with colour (the earlier plot), but the correction of the outer zones does. This is a real limitation of the Schmidt corrector, and the plate here was designed at 550 nm only. Re-optimising over several wavelengths at once (which I tried) lowers the blue and red blur only modestly and pulls the colour foci apart, so it is a genuine trade-off, one that real designers manage through the choice of plate glass and thickness. The honest summary is that the SCT is effectively apochromatic in focus, but not perfect in every pupil zone.

title: Inside a Meade LX90: Ray Tracing an 8-inch Schmidt–Cassegrain
text:
What this model leaves out

The real prescription. The glass, surface figures, and mirror shapes of an actual LX90 are Meade’s; the design here was optimised from the published specifications. The ACF version uses a hyperbolic secondary and a different corrector, which reduces coma further.
Manufacturing and tolerance. Real mirrors and plates have surface errors, collimation is imperfect, and thermal gradients (tube currents) matter more than most optical details at the eyepiece.
Scattering, coatings and transmission. Real throughput depends on mirror coatings and on the plate’s anti-reflection coatings.
The eyepiece. The Plössl is a representative design, not a Meade 4000 prescription.
The atmosphere. Seeing of 1–3 arcseconds usually limits an 8-inch telescope far more than diffraction (0.6″).

Natural next steps would be to model the ACF variant, a focal reducer and field flattener (the standard accessory for SCT astrophotography), or tolerance analysis for secondary-mirror tilt and spacing errors, all of which Optiland supports.

title: Inside a Meade LX90: Ray Tracing an 8-inch Schmidt–Cassegrain
text:
Takeaways

An SCT folds a 2032 mm focal length into a tube a third as long, using two spherical mirrors and a thin aspheric corrector plate. The corrector removes a spherical-aberration blur of more than a millimetre down to a few microns.
The model’s diffraction pattern has an Airy disk 13 µm across, about 1.4″ on the sky, with the central obstruction trading some contrast for aperture.
Off-axis, an SCT is diffraction-limited only within a small central angle, and the best focal surface is curved (a radius of a few hundred millimetres in this design). Coma dominates the blur at f/10; that is why flatteners, reducers and the ACF design exist.
Chromatically, because it is mostly mirrors, the SCT is effectively apochromatic in focus for the telescope alone: its focal shift is comparable to an apo refractor and hundreds of times smaller than an achromat’s. The corrector plate does leave some spherochromatism, so blue and red star images are less tight than green.
All of this was computed with a few hundred lines of Python and an open-source ray-tracing package, which makes it easy to ask “what if” questions that would otherwise need commercial lens-design software.

The photons collected by this telescope originated in the nuclear reactions described in the stellar nucleosynthesis post, and the galaxies it can reach are the large-scale structure discussed in the Martin Rees six-numbers post.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
text:
In 1999 the astrophysicist Martin Rees published a short book, Just Six Numbers, built around a claim that is easy to state and hard to dismiss: the large-scale structure of the universe, and its ability to contain anything as intricate as life, depends on six dimensionless numbers. None of them is predicted by any current theory. Change any one by a modest amount and the universe would look utterly different.
This post introduces Rees himself, then goes through the six numbers one at a time, with the physics behind each and a short calculation in R.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
text:
Who is Martin Rees?
Martin Rees was born in York in 1942 and studied mathematics at Trinity College, Cambridge. He completed his PhD in 1967 under Dennis Sciama, whose students over the years included Stephen Hawking, George Ellis and Brandon Carter. That group worked on general relativity and cosmology at a time when the subject was moving from speculation to observation. He has spent most of his career in Cambridge, as Plumian Professor of Astronomy and Experimental Philosophy from 1973, Astronomer Royal since 1995, Master of Trinity College from 2004 to 2012, and President of the Royal Society from 2005 to 2010. He became a life peer, Baron Rees of Ludlow, in 2005, was appointed to the Order of Merit in 2007, and received the Templeton Prize in 2011.
His research output is unusually broad. A few landmarks, all from my memory of the literature and worth checking against the references:

Superluminal motion (1966). Rees showed that jets from quasars moving close to the speed of light at a small angle to our line of sight can appear to move faster than light. No physics is violated; it is a light-travel-time effect.
Evolving radio sources. In the 1960s, with Sciama, he worked on how the numbers of distant radio sources and quasars change with cosmic time, evidence that the universe evolves, as the Big Bang picture says and the steady-state model does not.
The Rees–Sciama effect (1968). Light crossing a changing gravitational potential, such as a collapsing cluster, picks up a small net energy shift. This is a tiny signature on the cosmic microwave background.
Radio galaxies and black holes (1970s–80s). With Roger Blandford he developed the “twin-exhaust” model in which jets carry energy from a galactic nucleus to giant radio lobes. His wider reviews established the picture of supermassive black holes powering active galactic nuclei.
Galaxy formation. With Jeremiah Ostriker (1977) he studied how gas cools and collapses to form galaxies, and with Blumenthal, Faber and Primack (1984) he helped establish cold dark matter as the framework for structure formation.
Gamma-ray bursts. With Péter Mészáros he developed the fireball model of gamma-ray bursts and their afterglows in the early 1990s.

He is also a prolific author for general readers: Before the Beginning (1997), Just Six Numbers (1999), Our Cosmic Habitat (2001), Our Final Hour (2003, published in the UK as Our Final Century) and On the Future (2018). He gave the BBC Reith Lectures in 2010 and co-founded Cambridge’s Centre for the Study of Existential Risk in 2012. The theme running through the later work is that the cosmos is far larger and older than we usually keep in mind, and that humanity’s own future is much less settled than the cosmos’s.

The anthropic thread
The six-numbers argument has a lineage. In 1961 Robert Dicke observed that the age of the universe cannot be arbitrary if observers like us are to exist. In 1974 Brandon Carter, Rees’s Cambridge contemporary, gave the idea a name, the anthropic principle. In 1979 Rees and Bernard Carr wrote a long Nature review, “The anthropic principle and the structure of the physical world”, which assembled the evidence that many features of physics seem tuned to allow complex structure. The Hoyle carbon resonance (covered in the stellar nucleosynthesis post) is one of its classic examples. Just Six Numbers is the popular distillation of that programme.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
text:
The six numbers








Symbol
Name
Approximate value




\(N\)
Ratio of electric to gravitational force between two protons
\(10^{36}\)


\(\varepsilon\)
Fraction of mass released when hydrogen fuses to helium
\(0.007\)


\(\Omega\)
Matter density relative to the critical density
\(\approx 0.3\)


\(\lambda\)
Dark-energy (cosmological constant) density relative to critical
\(\approx 0.7\)


\(Q\)
Amplitude of primordial density fluctuations
\(\approx 10^{-5}\)


\(D\)
Number of spatial dimensions
\(3\)



Rees groups them: \(N\) and \(\varepsilon\) govern small-scale physics (atoms, stars), \(\Omega\), \(\lambda\) and \(Q\) govern the large-scale cosmos, and \(D\) sets the framework in which everything operates.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
text:
1. \(N \approx 10^{36}\): the weakness of gravity
Two protons repel each other electrically and attract each other gravitationally. The ratio of the two forces does not depend on distance, since both fall off as \(1/r^2\):
\[
N = \frac{e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)}{G m_p^2}.
\]

N <- e_chg^2 / (4 * pi * eps0 * G * m_p^2)
alpha <- 1 / 137.036
alpha_G <- alpha / N             # G m_p^2 / (hbar c)
M_star <- alpha_G^(-3/2) * m_p   # characteristic stellar mass
c(N = N, alpha_G = alpha_G, M_star_in_Msun = M_star / Msun)

             N        alpha_G M_star_in_Msun 
  1.235702e+36   5.905432e-39   1.853019e+00 


So \(N = 1.2 \times 10^{36}\). Gravity is feeble compared with electromagnetism, and that is why large objects are needed for it to matter. A characteristic stellar mass comes out of dimensional analysis alone, where \(\alpha_G = G m_p^2/\hbar c = \alpha/N\):
\[
M_\star \sim \alpha_G^{-3/2}\, m_p \approx 1.9\, M_\odot .
\]
That is a stellar mass, so \(N\) is why stars are about the size they are. Since \(M_\star \propto N^{3/2}\), a universe with gravity \(10^6\) times stronger (\(N \sim 10^{30}\)) would have stars about a billion times lighter.
Lifetimes. The standard result for radiative stars is \(L \propto G^4 M^3\), so a star’s lifetime goes as \(t \sim M/L \propto G^{-4}M^{-2}\). Combined with \(M_\star \propto G^{-3/2}\) this gives \(t_\star \propto G^{-1} \propto N\). A million-fold stronger gravity therefore shortens stellar lifetimes about a million-fold, from roughly \(10^{10}\) years to roughly \(10^4\). That’s Rees’s “Lilliputian universe”: there would be no time for evolution to do anything.

sc <- tibble(logN = seq(30, 40, length.out = 200)) |>
  mutate(
    mass     = (10^logN / N)^(3/2),
    lifetime = (10^logN / N)^1
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(mass, lifetime), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "rel") |>
  mutate(quantity = recode(quantity, mass = "Stellar mass ∝ N^(3/2)", lifetime = "Stellar lifetime ∝ N"))

ggplot(sc, aes(logN, rel, colour = quantity)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log10(N), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  labs(x = expression(log[10]~N), y = "Relative to our universe", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 1: How characteristic stellar mass and lifetime scale with N (equivalently, with 1/G), normalised to our universe. Stronger gravity means smaller, shorter-lived stars.





Going the other way, a much larger \(N\) (weaker gravity) gives huge, cool, slowly evolving stars, and galaxies would struggle to form from gas that is so slow to collapse. Rees’s point is that life needs something like our value, not an order of magnitude here or there.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
text:
2. \(\varepsilon \approx 0.007\): the efficiency of fusion
When four hydrogen nuclei fuse into one helium-4 nucleus, a fraction \(\varepsilon\) of their mass is converted to energy:
\[
\varepsilon = \frac{4 m_{\mathrm{H}} - m_{\mathrm{He}}}{4 m_{\mathrm{H}}}.
\]

m_H1  <- 1.007825; m_He4 <- 4.002603
eps_fus <- (4 * m_H1 - m_He4) / (4 * m_H1)
eps_fus

[1] 0.007118547


That gives \(\varepsilon =\) 0.0071. It is set by the strong nuclear force, and it fixes how long stars shine: a star’s nuclear fuel supply is roughly \(\varepsilon M c^2\), so lifetime is proportional to \(\varepsilon\) at fixed luminosity. Beyond that, it determines what the hydrogen-burning chain can do at all. The chain starts with deuterium, and its stability depends on the strength of the nuclear force. Rees’s examples are qualitative:

With \(\varepsilon\) around 0.006, the first step toward helium would not proceed, so the universe would stay hydrogen and no heavier elements, and no chemistry, would be made.
With \(\varepsilon\) around 0.008, nearly all hydrogen would have been fused in the early universe, leaving no hydrogen for water or long-lived stars.

These are Rees’s illustrations of sensitivity, and I haven’t derived them here. Detailed nuclear calculations in the literature find that the range of habitable values is somewhat wider than such sharp statements suggest, but still narrow.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
text:
3. \(\Omega \approx 0.3\): how much matter
The expansion of a homogeneous universe obeys the Friedmann equation
\[
H^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{kc^2}{a^2} + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}.
\]
The critical density is the value of \(\rho\) for which a universe with \(\Lambda=0\) is spatially flat, \(\rho_c = 3H_0^2/8\pi G\), and \(\Omega = \rho/\rho_c\).

rho_c <- 3 * H0^2 / (8 * pi * G)
n_protons <- rho_c / m_p
c(rho_crit_kg_m3 = rho_c, protons_per_m3 = n_protons)

rho_crit_kg_m3 protons_per_m3 
  8.533115e-27   5.101707e+00 


The critical density is about \(8.5 \times 10^{-27}\) kg m\(^{-3}\), equivalent to roughly 5.1 protons per cubic metre. The measured density of ordinary matter plus dark matter is about 0.3 of that, so \(\Omega_m \approx\) 0.315.
The flatness problem. If \(\Omega\) is not exactly 1 at the start, it runs away from 1 as the universe expands. Writing the deviation as \(|\Omega^{-1}-1| = |k|c^2/(a^2H^2)\), one can compute how finely the early universe had to be balanced to leave \(\Omega\) of order unity today:
\[
\frac{|\Omega^{-1}-1|(z)}{|\Omega^{-1}-1|_0} = \frac{(1+z)^2}{E(z)^2},
\qquad
E^2(z) = \Omega_r(1+z)^4 + \Omega_m(1+z)^3 + \Omega_\Lambda .
\]

E2 <- function(z) Orad * (1 + z)^4 + Om * (1 + z)^3 + OL
dev_ratio <- function(z) (1 + z)^2 / E2(z)
z_bbn <- 1e10
c(deviation_at_BBN_relative_to_today = dev_ratio(z_bbn))

deviation_at_BBN_relative_to_today 
                      1.111111e-16 


At nucleosynthesis (\(z \sim 10^{10}\), about a second after the Big Bang) the universe had to be flat to within about \(1 \times 10^{-16}\) of whatever it is today. Too much matter and the universe would have collapsed in a fraction of a second; too little and it would have expanded too quickly for galaxies to form. Inflation, proposed in the early 1980s, offers a mechanism that drives the universe toward flatness automatically, and it is one reason Rees treats \(\Omega\) as less mysterious than the other numbers.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
text:
4. \(\lambda \approx 0.7\): the cosmological constant
Until the late 1990s most cosmologists assumed that \(\Lambda = 0\). Then supernova surveys (Riess et al. 1998; Perlmutter et al. 1999) showed that the expansion is accelerating, which requires a repulsive component, the cosmological constant or dark energy. It is parametrised as \(\Omega_\Lambda = \Lambda c^2/(3H_0^2) \approx 0.7\), Rees’s \(\lambda\).
With \(\Omega_m + \Omega_\Lambda = 1\) the Friedmann equation can be integrated for the age and the history of the scale factor:
\[
t(a) = \frac{1}{H_0}\int_0^{a}\frac{da'}{a'\,E(a')},
\qquad
E(a)^2 = \Omega_m a^{-3} + \Omega_\Lambda .
\]

E_a <- function(a, Om, OL) sqrt(Om * a^-3 + OL + (1 - Om - OL) * a^-2)
t_of_a <- function(a, Om, OL) {
  sapply(a, function(x) integrate(function(y) 1 / (y * E_a(y, Om, OL)), 1e-8, x)$value) / H0 / Gyr
}
age_LCDM <- t_of_a(1, Om, OL)
age_EdS  <- t_of_a(1, 1, 0)
age_open <- t_of_a(1, Om, 0)
a_acc    <- (Om / (2 * OL))^(1/3)      # acceleration begins (a-double-dot = 0)
a_eq     <- (Om / OL)^(1/3)            # matter-lambda equality
c(age_LCDM = age_LCDM, age_EdS = age_EdS, age_open = age_open,
  z_accel = 1 / a_acc - 1, z_equal = 1 / a_eq - 1)

  age_LCDM    age_EdS   age_open    z_accel    z_equal 
13.7952864  9.6708712 11.6613622  0.6323126  0.2955674 


The flat ΛCDM age is 13.8 Gyr, which is comfortably older than the oldest stars. A matter-only universe with the same \(H_0\) would be only 9.7 Gyr old, an awkward conflict that was one of the early hints for \(\Lambda\). Acceleration began at \(z \approx\) 0.63, and matter and dark energy had equal densities at \(z \approx\) 0.3.

a_grid <- seq(0.02, 2.5, length.out = 300)
mods <- tibble(
  model = c("Matter only (Ω = 1)", "Open, no Λ (Ω = 0.315)", "ΛCDM (Ω_m = 0.315, Ω_Λ = 0.685)"),
  Om_ = c(1, Om, Om), OL_ = c(0, 0, OL)
)
curves <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_len(nrow(mods)), function(i) {
  tibble(model = mods$model[i], a = a_grid, t = t_of_a(a_grid, mods$Om_[i], mods$OL_[i]))
}))

ggplot(curves, aes(t, a, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 40), ylim = c(0, 2.5)) +
  labs(x = "Time since the Big Bang (Gyr)", y = "Scale factor a (today = 1)", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top") + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 3))







Figure 2: Scale factor against cosmic time for three universes with the same present-day Hubble constant. Only the model with a cosmological constant is old enough and ends up accelerating.





Why is \(\lambda\) interesting? Two reasons. First, it is absurdly small compared with what particle physics naively suggests. Vacuum energy computed with a Planck-scale cutoff is about \(\rho_P = c^5/(\hbar G^2)\):

rho_P <- c_ms^5 / (hbar * G^2)
rho_L <- OL * rho_c
c(rho_Planck = rho_P, rho_Lambda = rho_L, ratio = rho_L / rho_P)

   rho_Planck    rho_Lambda         ratio 
 5.155823e+96  5.845184e-27 1.133705e-123 


The observed dark-energy density is smaller than the Planck density by a factor of about \(1 \times 10^{-123}\): roughly 120 orders of magnitude, a famous failure of naive estimates. Second, Steven Weinberg noted in 1987 that if \(\Lambda\) were much larger than observed, repulsion would have stopped structure forming before galaxies could assemble. That anthropic bound is what pointed toward a small, non-zero value before the supernova results, and it is the kind of argument Rees treats seriously.

co <- tibble(loga = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 400)) |>
  mutate(a = 10^loga,
         matter = Om * a^-3 / (Om * a^-3 + OL),
         dark_energy = 1 - matter) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(matter, dark_energy), names_to = "component", values_to = "fraction") |>
  mutate(component = recode(component, matter = "Matter", dark_energy = "Dark energy"))

ggplot(co, aes(loga, fraction, colour = component)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = expression(log[10]~a~"(today = 0)"), y = "Fraction of total energy density", colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 3: Matter and dark-energy fractions as the universe expands. Dark energy is negligible at early times and dominates at late times; we happen to live near the crossover.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
section: 5. \(Q \approx 10^{-5}\): how lumpy was the early universe?
text:
5. \(Q \approx 10^{-5}\): how lumpy was the early universe?
The cosmic microwave background is uniform to about one part in \(10^5\). Those tiny temperature ripples correspond to density fluctuations of a similar relative size, and Rees calls their amplitude \(Q\). Gravity amplifies them: in a matter-dominated universe, small perturbations grow in proportion to the scale factor. In a universe with dark energy the growth factor \(D(a)\) obeys
\[
D(a) \;\propto\; E(a)\int_0^a \frac{da'}{\bigl[a'E(a')\bigr]^3},
\]
normalised so that \(D = a\) at early times.

growth_D <- function(a, Om, OL) {
  sapply(a, function(x) 2.5 * Om * E_a(x, Om, OL) *
           integrate(function(y) 1 / (y * E_a(y, Om, OL))^3, 1e-8, x)$value)
}
D_today <- growth_D(1, Om, OL)
D_today

[1] 0.7878126


Today \(D(1) =\) 0.79: dark energy has already throttled structure growth by about 21% relative to a matter-only universe.

gg <- tibble(a = seq(0.02, 3, length.out = 300)) |>
  mutate(LCDM = growth_D(a, Om, OL), `Matter only` = a) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(LCDM, `Matter only`), names_to = "model", values_to = "D")

ggplot(gg, aes(a, D, colour = model, linetype = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Scale factor a (today = 1)", y = "Growth factor D(a)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 4: Linear growth factor of density perturbations against scale factor. Growth tracks the matter-only line (dashed) until dark energy takes over, then stalls.





In this picture a region collapses into a bound structure once its linear overdensity reaches about 1.7, so the redshift at which structures of a given size form scales in proportion to their initial amplitude. That is why \(Q\) matters so much:

If \(Q\) were much smaller (around \(10^{-6}\)), gas clouds would take far longer to contract. Galaxies would form late, if at all, and their stars would be diffuse, so supernova ejecta could escape and no second generation of enriched stars would form.
If \(Q\) were much larger (around \(10^{-4}\)), structure would form very early and densely. Galaxies would be compact enough for stars to collide, and many would collapse to giant black holes.

Our value gives galaxies that are big enough to retain heavy elements and sparse enough that planetary systems survive. This post doesn’t compute the full structure-formation calculation; the scaling above is only the heart of it.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
text:
6. \(D = 3\): dimensions of space
Why three? Paul Ehrenfest’s 1917 analysis shows that the stability of orbits singles out \(D=3\). In \(D\) spatial dimensions Gauss’s law makes a central force fall off as \(r^{-(D-1)}\) and the potential as \(r^{-(D-2)}\). For a particle with angular momentum \(L\) the effective potential is
\[
V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r) = \frac{L^2}{2mr^2} - \frac{k}{r^{D-2}} .
\]
A stable circular orbit needs a minimum of \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}\).

\(D=3\): the attractive \(-k/r\) is overtaken by the centrifugal \(r^{-2}\) term at small \(r\), producing a stable minimum. Planets can orbit stars.
\(D=4\): both terms go as \(r^{-2}\). There is no minimum at all: for weak angular momentum a particle spirals into the centre, for strong angular momentum it is flung away.
\(D\ge5\): the attractive term dominates at small \(r\) and the potential is unbounded below. Everything collapses.


veff <- function(r, D) 0.5 / r^2 - 1 / r^(D - 2)
dd <- expand.grid(r = seq(0.15, 4, length.out = 500), D = c(3, 4, 5)) |>
  mutate(V = veff(r, D), D = factor(paste0("D = ", D)))

ggplot(dd, aes(r, V, colour = D)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-3, 3)) +
  labs(x = "Radius r", y = expression(V[eff](r)), colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 5: Effective potential for gravity in 3, 4 and 5 spatial dimensions (units with L²/2m = 0.5 and k = 1). Only D = 3 has a stable orbital minimum; the same argument applies to electrons around nuclei.





The same argument applies to the Schrödinger equation: in four or more spatial dimensions, hydrogen-like atoms have no stable ground state, so there would be no chemistry. Fewer dimensions have their own problems: in \(D=2\) the gravitational potential is logarithmic, orbits are not closed, and a body can never escape. Max Tegmark’s 1997 survey of these arguments is a good modern treatment.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
section: How seriously should we take all this?
text:
How seriously should we take all this?
It is worth being clear about what the six-numbers argument does and does not establish.

What it shows is sensitivity: with physics otherwise unchanged, the outcome of these numbers is not robust to large changes. Those scaling arguments, such as \(M_\star \propto N^{3/2}\), the flatness calculation and the orbital stability of \(D=3\), are straightforward calculations.
What it does not show is that the numbers had to be tuned by something. For that you need a probability distribution over possible values of constants, and nobody has a principled one. Critics, among them Lee Smolin and Sabine Hossenfelder, argue that “fine-tuning” is not well-defined without such a measure, and some of the numbers (like \(\Omega\)) may have explanations through dynamics like inflation.
Rees’s own response is to take the multiverse seriously: if a very large ensemble of universes exists with different values of \(N\), \(\varepsilon\), \(Q\) and so on, then finding ourselves in one that permits observers is no surprise. He is open that this is a hypothesis, not a result, and that it remains controversial.

Whichever view you prefer, the numbers provide a clear way to ask what a universe is made of at the deepest level. That is why the book has been durable.

title: Martin Rees and the Six Numbers
text:
Takeaways

\(N \approx 10^{36}\) sets how big stars are and how long they live: \(M_\star\propto N^{3/2}\) and \(t_\star\propto N\).
\(\varepsilon \approx 0.007\) is the fraction of mass released by hydrogen fusion; Rees’s examples show it sits in a narrow window.
\(\Omega\approx0.3\) and \(\lambda\approx0.7\) govern the expansion history. The flatness calculation shows the early universe was balanced to about one part in \(10^{16}\), and \(\lambda\) is about \(10^{-123}\) of the naive Planck-scale value.
\(Q\approx10^{-5}\) sets when and how densely galaxies form.
\(D=3\) is singled out by the stability of orbits and atoms.
The sensitivity arguments are solid. What they mean is still debated.

Overview
This report projects the sun’s calculated azimuth/altitude path during the 12 August 2026 partial solar eclipse onto two images taken near 52.8936°N, 1.2659°W (Nottinghamshire/Lincolnshire border, UK), and separately visualizes the local terrain to give context on nearby high ground:

A Google Street View image, aimed toward the sun’s position at peak eclipse.
A photo taken with the Theodolite app, whose EXIF/XMP metadata records the camera’s GPS position, compass heading, and pitch.
A 3D terrain surface of the surrounding 10-mile radius, with nearby named hills labeled and the local river network draped over the relief.

Both overlays use the same sun-path calculation and a small-angle (linear) projection from angular offset to pixel offset around the camera’s heading/pitch — not a true perspective projection. This is a reasonable approximation over the modest angular ranges involved here, but it is not exact, especially toward the edges of a wide field of view.

title: Projecting the sun’s path for the 12 August 2026 UK partial solar eclipse
text:
Eclipse context and sun path

lat <- 52.893608
lon <- -1.265934
date <- as.Date("2026-08-12")

# Eclipse locally runs roughly 18:00-20:00 BST (17:00-19:00 UTC);
# widen slightly either side to give context on the sun's path
times <- seq(
  from = as.POSIXct(paste(date, "16:30:00"), tz = "UTC"),
  to   = as.POSIXct(paste(date, "19:15:00"), tz = "UTC"),
  by   = "1 min"
)

sun_path <- getSunlightPosition(date = times, lat = lat, lon = lon) |>
  mutate(
    # Convert azimuth (radians south-to-west) to compass degrees (0-360 from North)
    azimuth_deg = (azimuth * 180 / pi + 180) %% 360,
    altitude_deg = altitude * 180 / pi,
    time_bst = format(with_tz(date, "Europe/London"), "%H:%M")
  )

# Reported UK-wide maximum eclipse is ~19:05-19:13 BST (18:05-18:13 UTC);
# pick the row closest to 19:09 BST (18:09 UTC) for this longitude
peak_time <- as.POSIXct(paste(date, "18:09:00"), tz = "UTC")
peak_sun <- sun_path[which.min(abs(sun_path$date - peak_time)), ]

At peak eclipse (19:09 BST), the sun is at an azimuth of 278.9° and an altitude of 12.1°. Across the wider window shown here (16:30-19:15 UTC / 17:30-20:15 BST), azimuth ranges from 258.9° to 291.7°, and altitude from 2.5° to 27°.
A shared helper converts an azimuth/altitude offset from a camera’s heading/pitch into pixel coordinates, given the image size and field of view:

wrap180 <- function(x) ((x + 180) %% 360) - 180

project_sun <- function(az, alt, heading, pitch, fov_h, fov_v, img_w, img_h) {
  delta_az <- wrap180(az - heading)
  delta_alt <- alt - pitch
  data.frame(
    x = img_w / 2 + (delta_az / (fov_h / 2)) * (img_w / 2),
    y = img_h / 2 + (delta_alt / (fov_v / 2)) * (img_h / 2),
    delta_az = delta_az,
    delta_alt = delta_alt
  )
}

Street View overlay
The Street View camera is pointed toward the sun’s position at peak eclipse (heading 278.9°, pitch 12.1°), using the default 90° horizontal field of view for a square image.

# Cache network responses on disk so repeated re-renders (e.g. while
# iterating on this document) don't repeatedly hit external APIs and risk
# tripping their rate limits.
cache_dir <- ".cache"
dir.create(cache_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

sv_size <- c(640, 640)
sv_fov <- 90
sv_heading <- peak_sun$azimuth_deg
sv_pitch <- peak_sun$altitude_deg

sv_cache_file <- file.path(
  cache_dir,
  sprintf("streetview_%s_%s_h%.1f_p%.1f_f%d_%dx%d.jpg",
          lat, lon, sv_heading, sv_pitch, sv_fov, sv_size[1], sv_size[2])
)

if (!file.exists(sv_cache_file)) {
  api_key <- Sys.getenv("GOOGLE_MAPS_KEY")

  sv_url <- modify_url(
    "https://maps.googleapis.com/maps/api/streetview",
    query = list(
      location = paste(lat, lon, sep = ","),
      size     = paste(sv_size, collapse = "x"),
      heading  = sv_heading,
      fov      = sv_fov,
      pitch    = sv_pitch,
      key      = api_key
    )
  )

  sv_resp <- GET(sv_url, write_disk(sv_cache_file, overwrite = TRUE))
  stop_for_status(sv_resp)
}

streetview_img <- readJPEG(sv_cache_file)


sv_w <- sv_size[1]
sv_h <- sv_size[2]

sv_projected <- cbind(
  sun_path,
  project_sun(sun_path$azimuth_deg, sun_path$altitude_deg,
              sv_heading, sv_pitch, sv_fov, sv_fov, sv_w, sv_h)
) |>
  filter(abs(delta_az) <= sv_fov / 2, abs(delta_alt) <= sv_fov / 2)

sv_peak_projected <- sv_projected |> filter(date == peak_sun$date)


ggplot() +
  annotation_raster(streetview_img, xmin = 0, xmax = sv_w, ymin = 0, ymax = sv_h) +
  geom_path(data = sv_projected, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "yellow", linewidth = 1) +

             color = "red", vjust = -1) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, sv_w), ylim = c(0, sv_h), expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Sun's path during the 12 Aug 2026 partial solar eclipse",
    subtitle = paste0("Camera heading ", round(sv_heading, 1), "°, pitch ",
                       round(sv_pitch, 1), "° — near Nottinghamshire/Lincolnshire border"),
    x = NULL, y = NULL

  theme_void() +

title: Projecting the sun’s path for the 12 August 2026 UK partial solar eclipse
text:
Photo overlay
This photo was taken with the Theodolite app on an iPhone, which records GPS position and GPSImgDirection (true compass heading) in EXIF, and the camera’s vertical/horizontal inclination (vert_angle_deg / horiz_angle_deg) in the image caption. We treat vert_angle_deg as pitch and treat roll (horiz_angle_deg) as negligible.

photo_path <- "/Users/paul/Downloads/TH000003.JPG"

meta <- exif_read(photo_path)

Using ExifTool version 13.55

photo_lat <- meta$GPSLatitude
photo_lon <- meta$GPSLongitude
heading   <- meta$GPSImgDirection
pitch     <- as.numeric(sub(".*vert_angle_deg=([0-9.\\-]+).*", "\\1", meta$ImageDescription))

photo_time_local <- as.POSIXct(
  paste(gsub(":", "-", substr(meta$DateTimeOriginal, 1, 10)), substr(meta$DateTimeOriginal, 12, 19)),
  tz = "UTC"
) - hours(as.numeric(substr(meta$OffsetTimeOriginal, 1, 3)))

img_w <- meta$ImageWidth
img_h <- meta$ImageHeight

The photo’s field of view is estimated from its 35mm-equivalent focal length, rescaled to the actual saved crop dimensions assuming the native ultra-wide sensor is 4032x3024 pixels (iPhone 13 Pro Max ultra-wide camera) and a rectilinear (tangent-plane) projection. This is an approximation — the lens’s true optical FOV may differ from this 35mm-equivalent estimate.

native_w <- 4032
f35 <- meta$FocalLengthIn35mmFormat
fov_h_native <- 2 * atan(18 / f35) * 180 / pi
fov_h <- 2 * atan(tan(fov_h_native / 2 * pi / 180) * (img_w / native_w)) * 180 / pi
fov_v <- 2 * atan((img_h / img_w) * tan(fov_h / 2 * pi / 180)) * 180 / pi

Camera heading 279.1°, pitch 2.1°, estimated field of view 87° x 48°, captured 14:08 UTC.

sun_path_photo <- getSunlightPosition(date = times, lat = photo_lat, lon = photo_lon) |>
  mutate(
    azimuth_deg = (azimuth * 180 / pi + 180) %% 360,
    altitude_deg = altitude * 180 / pi,
    time_bst = format(with_tz(date, "Europe/London"), "%H:%M")
  )

capture_sun <- getSunlightPosition(date = photo_time_local, lat = photo_lat, lon = photo_lon) |>
  mutate(
    azimuth_deg = (azimuth * 180 / pi + 180) %% 360,
    altitude_deg = altitude * 180 / pi
  )


sun_projected <- cbind(
  sun_path_photo,
  project_sun(sun_path_photo$azimuth_deg, sun_path_photo$altitude_deg,
              heading, pitch, fov_h, fov_v, img_w, img_h)
)
capture_projected <- cbind(
  capture_sun,
  project_sun(capture_sun$azimuth_deg, capture_sun$altitude_deg,
              heading, pitch, fov_h, fov_v, img_w, img_h)
)

in_frame <- function(x, y) x >= 0 & x <= img_w & y >= 0 & y <= img_h

path_in_frame <- sun_projected |> filter(in_frame(x, y))
capture_in_frame <- in_frame(capture_projected$x[1], capture_projected$y[1])

path_ticks <- path_in_frame |> filter(minute(date) %% 15 == 0)

photo_img <- readJPEG(photo_path)


p_photo <- ggplot() +
  annotation_raster(photo_img, xmin = 0, xmax = img_w, ymin = 0, ymax = img_h) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(0, img_w), ylim = c(0, img_h), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Eclipse sun path projected onto photo",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Heading ", round(heading, 1), "°, pitch ", round(pitch, 1),
      "°, est. FOV ", round(fov_h, 0), "°x", round(fov_v, 0),
      "°, captured ", format(photo_time_local, "%H:%M UTC")
    ),
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(color = "white", size = 11),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "white", size = 9),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "black")
  )

if (nrow(path_in_frame) > 0) {
  p_photo <- p_photo +
    geom_path(data = path_in_frame, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "yellow", linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(data = path_ticks, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "yellow", size = 2) +
    geom_label(
      data = path_ticks, aes(x = x, y = y, label = time_bst),
      color = "black", fill = "yellow", alpha = 0.8, size = 2.8,
      linewidth = 0, label.padding = unit(0.12, "lines"), vjust = -0.5
    )
}

if (isTRUE(capture_in_frame)) {
  p_photo <- p_photo +
    geom_point(data = capture_projected, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "red", size = 3) +
    geom_label(data = capture_projected, aes(x = x, y = y, label = "sun at capture"),
               color = "red", fill = "white", alpha = 0.8, linewidth = 0, vjust = -0.7)
} else {
  cx <- pmin(pmax(capture_projected$x, 0), img_w)
  cy <- pmin(pmax(capture_projected$y, 0), img_h)
  offframe_label <- sprintf(
    "Sun at capture (%s) is %.0f° off-frame\n(Az %.0f°, Alt %.0f° vs heading %.0f°, pitch %.0f°)",
    format(photo_time_local, "%H:%M UTC"),
    sqrt(capture_projected$delta_az^2 + capture_projected$delta_alt^2),
    capture_sun$azimuth_deg, capture_sun$altitude_deg, heading, pitch
  )
  p_photo <- p_photo +
    annotate("segment", x = img_w / 2, y = img_h / 2, xend = cx, yend = cy,
             arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm")), color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
    annotate("label", x = img_w * 0.02, y = img_h * 0.02, label = offframe_label,
             color = "red", fill = "white", alpha = 0.85, size = 3, hjust = 0, vjust = 0,
             linewidth = 0)
}

if (nrow(path_in_frame) == 0) {
  p_photo <- p_photo +
    annotate("label", x = img_w * 0.02, y = img_h * 0.98,
             label = "Eclipse sun path (16:30-19:15 UTC) never enters this frame",
             color = "black", fill = "yellow", alpha = 0.85, size = 3, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
             linewidth = 0)
}

section: Terrain and named peaks within 10 miles
text:
Terrain and named peaks within 10 miles
To give context on nearby high ground that could obstruct a low-altitude view of the eclipse, this section builds a 3D terrain surface for a 10-mile radius around the viewing location and labels the named hills found in OpenStreetMap within that area.

miles_to_deg_lat <- 10 / 69.0
miles_to_deg_lon <- 10 / (69.0 * cos(lat * pi / 180))

bbox_sf <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(
    lon = c(lon - miles_to_deg_lon, lon + miles_to_deg_lon),
    lat = c(lat - miles_to_deg_lat, lat + miles_to_deg_lat)
  ),
  coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326
)

# Cache as a GeoTIFF (rather than saveRDS) so the raster's values are
# guaranteed to round-trip regardless of in-memory vs. file-backed state.
elev_cache_file <- file.path(
  cache_dir, sprintf("elev_raster_%s_%s_z10.tif", lat, lon)
)

if (file.exists(elev_cache_file)) {
  elev_raster <- raster::raster(elev_cache_file)
} else {
  elev_raster <- get_elev_raster(bbox_sf, z = 10, src = "aws")
  raster::writeRaster(elev_raster, elev_cache_file, overwrite = TRUE)
}

# Reproject to British National Grid so grid cells are isotropic (equal
# distance in x and y), which raw lat/lon degrees are not at this latitude
r_bng <- terra::project(terra::rast(elev_raster), "EPSG:27700", method = "bilinear", res = 30)


# osmdata's default Overpass mirror can vary and has been observed rate-
# limiting/blocking repeated requests from this machine (surfacing as a
# 429/420-style error after a long retry backoff). Pin to the main
# overpass-api.de instance, which has been confirmed reachable.
set_overpass_url("https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter")

bbox_num <- c(lon - miles_to_deg_lon, lat - miles_to_deg_lat, lon + miles_to_deg_lon, lat + miles_to_deg_lat)

peaks_cache_file <- file.path(cache_dir, sprintf("osm_peaks_%s_%s.rds", lat, lon))

if (file.exists(peaks_cache_file)) {
  peaks <- readRDS(peaks_cache_file)
} else {
  peaks <- opq(bbox = bbox_num, timeout = 120) |>
    add_osm_feature(key = "natural", value = "peak") |>
    osmdata_sf()
  saveRDS(peaks, peaks_cache_file)
}

peak_named <- peaks$osm_points |> filter(!is.na(name))

peak_named_bng <- st_transform(peak_named, 27700)
peak_coords <- st_coordinates(peak_named_bng)

peak_df <- data.frame(
  name = peak_named_bng$name,
  easting = peak_coords[, "X"],
  northing = peak_coords[, "Y"]
) |>
  distinct(name, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Look up each peak's elevation from the DEM rather than relying on
# (frequently missing) OSM elevation tags
peak_df$elev_dem <- terra::extract(r_bng, as.matrix(peak_df[, c("easting", "northing")]))[, 1]
peak_df <- peak_df |> arrange(desc(elev_dem))

top_peaks <- head(peak_df, 8)

# The eclipse-viewing location itself (Long Eaton), for reference on the map
viewing_point_bng <- st_transform(st_sfc(st_point(c(lon, lat)), crs = 4326), 27700)
viewing_coords <- st_coordinates(viewing_point_bng)
viewing_point <- data.frame(
  name = "Long Eaton",
  easting = viewing_coords[, "X"],
  northing = viewing_coords[, "Y"]
)
viewing_point$elev_dem <- terra::extract(r_bng, viewing_coords)[, 1]

# The DEM's highest point can sit outside any *named* OSM peak - here it's
# ~25km from the nearest tagged peak (Drum Hill), so it's real high ground
# (likely Peak District/Pennine foothills at the edge of the 10-mile-radius
# bounding box, whose corners reach ~14 miles out) rather than an OSM gap
dem_vals <- terra::values(r_bng)[, 1]
dem_xy <- terra::xyFromCell(r_bng, seq_along(dem_vals))
max_idx <- which.max(dem_vals)
high_point <- data.frame(
  name = "Unnamed high ground",
  easting = dem_xy[max_idx, 1],
  northing = dem_xy[max_idx, 2],
  elev_dem = dem_vals[max_idx]
)

Within this radius, 15 named hills are tagged in OpenStreetMap, ranging from 27 m to 186 m; the eight highest are labeled below, along with the eclipse-viewing location (Long Eaton, at the centre) and the single highest point in the DEM overall (381 m), which falls outside the named-peaks dataset and sits at the edge of the frame.

# NOTE: raster_to_matrix() transposes the raster - its first matrix
# dimension indexes eastings (raster columns), its second indexes
# northings (raster rows, north-to-south)
elmat <- raster_to_matrix(r_bng)

ext_bng <- terra::ext(r_bng)
eastings_full <- seq(ext_bng[1], ext_bng[2], length.out = ncol(r_bng))
northings_full <- seq(ext_bng[4], ext_bng[3], length.out = nrow(r_bng))

# Downsample for a responsive interactive plot
step <- 3
i_seq <- seq(1, nrow(elmat), by = step)
j_seq <- seq(1, ncol(elmat), by = step)
elmat_ds <- elmat[i_seq, j_seq]
eastings_ds <- eastings_full[i_seq]
northings_ds <- northings_full[j_seq]

# plotly's z matrix rows -> y axis, cols -> x axis
z_mat <- t(elmat_ds)


peak_hover <- sprintf("%s<br>%d m", top_peaks$name, round(top_peaks$elev_dem))
viewing_hover <- sprintf("%s<br>%d m", viewing_point$name, round(viewing_point$elev_dem))
high_point_hover <- sprintf("%s<br>%d m", high_point$name, round(high_point$elev_dem))

plot_ly() |>
  add_surface(x = eastings_ds, y = northings_ds, z = z_mat,
              colorscale = "Earth", showscale = FALSE) |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers+text",
    x = top_peaks$easting, y = top_peaks$northing, z = top_peaks$elev_dem + 15,
    text = top_peaks$name, textposition = "top center",
    marker = list(color = "red", size = 4),
    textfont = list(color = "black", size = 11),
    hovertext = peak_hover, hoverinfo = "text",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers+text",
    x = viewing_point$easting, y = viewing_point$northing, z = viewing_point$elev_dem + 15,
    text = viewing_point$name, textposition = "top center",
    marker = list(color = "blue", size = 5, symbol = "diamond"),
    textfont = list(color = "black", size = 11),
    hovertext = viewing_hover, hoverinfo = "text",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers+text",
    x = high_point$easting, y = high_point$northing, z = high_point$elev_dem + 15,
    text = high_point$name, textposition = "top center",
    marker = list(color = "darkorange", size = 4),
    textfont = list(color = "black", size = 11),
    hovertext = high_point_hover, hoverinfo = "text",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  layout(
    title = "Terrain within 10 miles of the eclipse-viewing location",
    scene = list(
      xaxis = list(title = "Easting (m, BNG)"),
      yaxis = list(title = "Northing (m, BNG)"),
      zaxis = list(title = "Elevation (m)"),
      aspectmode = "manual",
      aspectratio = list(x = 1, y = diff(range(northings_ds)) / diff(range(eastings_ds)), z = 0.25)
    )
  )

title: Projecting the sun’s path for the 12 August 2026 UK partial solar eclipse
text:
River network and 3D rendering
To add geographic context beyond bare terrain, the local river/canal network is draped over a full-resolution rayshader hillshade and rendered as a 3D scene. Watercourse geometry comes from Ordnance Survey’s OS Open Rivers dataset rather than OpenStreetMap, since public Overpass API mirrors proved unreliable (repeated 504 timeouts) when queried for waterway features.

# OS Open Rivers (OGL/Crown copyright, free via OS Data Hub) - downloaded once
# and cached, since Overpass mirrors were unreliable for `waterway` queries.
rivers_zip <- file.path(cache_dir, "os_open_rivers_gb.gpkg")
rivers_extract_dir <- file.path(cache_dir, "os_open_rivers_extracted")
rivers_gpkg <- file.path(rivers_extract_dir, "Data", "oprvrs_gb.gpkg")

if (!file.exists(rivers_gpkg)) {
  if (!file.exists(rivers_zip)) {
    # download.file()/libcurl can trip sandboxes that block reading ~/.netrc;
    # disabling netrc lookup on the curl handle avoids that
    h <- curl::new_handle(netrc = 0, followlocation = TRUE, timeout = 600)
    curl::curl_download(
      "https://api.os.uk/downloads/v1/products/OpenRivers/downloads?area=GB&format=GeoPackage&redirect",
      destfile = rivers_zip, handle = h
    )
  }
  # The download is actually a zip containing the real .gpkg plus licence/readme docs
  unzip(rivers_zip, exdir = rivers_extract_dir)
}


bbox_bng <- st_bbox(st_transform(bbox_sf, 27700))

rivers_bng <- st_read(
  rivers_gpkg, layer = "watercourse_link",
  wkt_filter = st_as_text(st_as_sfc(bbox_bng)),
  quiet = TRUE
)

Within the same 10-mile radius, 590 watercourse segments are found, including named rivers and canals such as River Trent.

# Full-resolution shading (not the downsampled elmat_ds used for the plotly
# surface), since this feeds the 3D rayshader render below
hillshade <- elmat |>
