text:
Notes and caveats

Both photo overlays use a small-angle/linear projection from angular offset to pixel offset around the camera’s heading and pitch, rather than a true perspective (gnomonic) projection. This is a reasonable approximation for the field-of-view sizes and angular ranges involved here, but introduces increasing distortion toward the edges of wide fields of view.
The Street View camera’s field of view is assumed to be 90° both horizontally and vertically (the API default for a square image); the true vertical field of view for the Street View panorama projection may differ.
The photo’s field of view is estimated from its 35mm-equivalent focal length and an assumed native sensor resolution (4032x3024 for the iPhone 13 Pro Max ultra-wide camera), rescaled to the actual saved crop size. This is not a verified optical specification.
The photo’s pitch is taken directly from the Theodolite app’s vert_angle_deg caption field, and roll (horiz_angle_deg) is assumed negligible and not corrected for.
The terrain elevation data comes from AWS Terrain Tiles (~30m resolution) via elevatr. Named peaks are whichever natural=peak features happen to be tagged in OpenStreetMap within the radius — this list may be incomplete, and their elevations are read from the DEM at each point’s coordinates rather than from (often-missing) OSM elevation tags.
The river network is watercourse-link geometry from OS Open Rivers. Contains OS data © Crown copyright and database right, available under the Open Government Licence. It is a generalised network, not a detailed hydrography product, and roughly 200 of the segments in this radius carry no watercourse_name (minor streams/ditches).
Reprojecting the elevation raster from WGS84 to British National Grid leaves a small fraction (~2%) of edge cells as NA, visible as a faint ragged border in the 3D render.
The bounding box is built as a square in degrees (±10 miles in latitude and longitude), so its corners reach roughly 14 miles from the viewing location — farther than the stated 10-mile radius. The highest point in the frame (~381 m) falls in one such corner and is ~25 km from the nearest named OSM peak, so it is almost certainly real high ground (plausibly Peak District/Pennine foothills) rather than a labeling gap — OSM just has no natural=peak point there.

title: The Complex Ginzburg-Landau Equation
text: Stir a shallow pan of fluid unevenly heated from below, run the Belousov-Zhabotinsky chemical reaction in a dish, or couple an array of lasers together, and — despite having nothing else in common — all three systems can pass through a transition where a uniform, quiescent state gives way to a sea of traveling waves. Remarkably, close to that transition, the envelope of the emerging pattern in all three systems obeys the same one equation: the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation (CGLE). This explainer works through where that equation comes from, what its two free parameters control, and what its exact plane-wave solutions predict — then checks those predictions numerically against a small 1D simulation, including a case where the amplitude field and the phase field turn out to be responsible for genuinely different pieces of the visible pattern.

title: The Complex Ginzburg-Landau Equation
section: From Landau’s theory of phase transitions to a superconducting order parameter
text:
From Landau’s theory of phase transitions to a superconducting order parameter
The story starts with Lev Landau’s 1930s mean-field theory of second-order phase transitions: expand the free energy of a system as a power series in a small “order parameter” \(\psi\) that vanishes above the critical temperature and grows continuously below it, keep only the lowest-order terms allowed by symmetry, and minimize. In 1950, Vitaly Ginzburg and Landau extended this idea to superconductivity, treating the density of superconducting charge carriers as a complex order parameter \(\psi(\mathbf{x})\) whose phase encodes the macroscopic quantum coherence of the superconducting state, and whose magnitude vanishes at the transition to the normal metal (Ginzburg and Landau 1950). The Ginzburg-Landau free energy functional, minimized over \(\psi\), gives a static nonlinear equation for \(\psi(\mathbf{x})\) — a real diffusion-like term coupling neighboring points in space, plus a cubic term that saturates the growth of \(|\psi|\).
That static, real-coefficient equation is the ancestor of the one simulated below, but two more ingredients are needed to get there: the equation has to become dynamical (an equation of motion, not just an energy to minimize), and its coefficients have to become complex.

title: The Complex Ginzburg-Landau Equation
section: Amplitude equations and the road to a complex equation
text:
Amplitude equations and the road to a complex equation
The dynamical step came from a different direction entirely: pattern formation in fluids. Near the onset of Rayleigh-Bénard convection — the striped or hexagonal patterns that appear when a fluid layer is heated from below past a critical temperature gradient — Newell and Whitehead showed that the envelope of the convection rolls (not the fast-oscillating roll pattern itself, but the slowly-varying amplitude modulating it) obeys a real Ginzburg-Landau equation, derived by a weakly nonlinear multiple-scales expansion around the instability threshold (Newell and Whitehead 1969). This is the general mechanism by which Ginzburg-Landau-type equations arise: whenever a spatially extended system crosses a bifurcation — a stationary instability (Turing-type) or an oscillatory one (Hopf-type) — sufficiently close to onset, the details of the microscopic equations wash out, and the long-wavelength, slow-time envelope of the pattern is forced by symmetry and scaling into one of a small number of universal “normal form” equations. This is the same universality argument used throughout bifurcation theory (see the companion explainer on Langevin dynamics and bifurcation for a related but distinct flavor of symmetry-breaking): the amplitude equation doesn’t care about the chemistry of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction or the viscosity of the convecting fluid, only about the type of instability and a couple of real numbers describing it.
The complex Ginzburg-Landau equation is what falls out of this same argument for an oscillatory (Hopf) instability in an extended medium: a spatially distributed field of identical, weakly coupled oscillators, each individually just past the threshold of sustained self-oscillation. Yoshiki Kuramoto derived exactly this reduction for reaction-diffusion systems modeling chemical oscillators — the mathematical root of both the CGLE and the more famous Kuramoto model of coupled-oscillator synchronization — and used it to explain the onset of “chemical turbulence” in the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction (Kuramoto 1984). Because the underlying oscillation is complex (it has both an amplitude and a phase), its slowly-varying envelope \(A(x,t)\) is a complex number too, and the coefficients that were real in the static Ginzburg-Landau theory pick up imaginary parts. Cross and Hohenberg’s canonical review of pattern formation situates the CGLE as one member of a small family of universal amplitude equations that recur across fluid dynamics, nonlinear optics, and chemical physics (Cross and Hohenberg 1993), and Aranson and Kramer’s dedicated review catalogs just how rich its behavior is — plane waves, spiral defects, and full spatiotemporal chaos, all from the same three-term equation (Aranson and Kramer 2002).

title: The Complex Ginzburg-Landau Equation
text:
The equation
The version simulated here, in one spatial dimension with periodic boundary conditions, is
\[
\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} = A + (1 + i c_1)\frac{\partial^2 A}{\partial x^2} - (1 - i c_3)\,|A|^2 A,
\]
where \(A(x,t) \in \mathbb{C}\) is the complex envelope, and \(c_1, c_3 \in \mathbb{R}\) are the two free parameters of the model (their coefficients on the linear growth and cubic terms have been rescaled to 1 by an appropriate choice of time, space, and amplitude units — the genuinely universal content of the equation is just \(c_1\) and \(c_3\)). Reading it term by term:

\(A\): linear growth. Every point is individually just past a Hopf bifurcation, so left alone (no coupling), \(|A|\) would grow exponentially from any small perturbation. This is what makes the flat \(A=0\) state in the simulation below unstable to the tiny initial noise.
\((1+ic_1)\,\partial^2_x A\): spatial coupling between neighbors. The real part (coefficient 1) is ordinary diffusion, which smooths out spatial differences in amplitude. The imaginary part, \(ic_1\,\partial^2_x A\), has no analogue in the static Ginzburg-Landau theory: it couples spatial curvature into the local phase, which is what lets a spatially extended field of oscillators lock into traveling waves rather than just synchronizing to a spatially uniform, purely time-oscillating state. \(c_1\) is often called the linear dispersion coefficient.
\(-(1-ic_3)\,|A|^2 A\): cubic self-saturation. The real part is the same amplitude-limiting nonlinearity as in the static theory — it’s what stops the linear growth term from blowing up, pinning \(|A|\) near 1 once the system saturates. The imaginary part, \(ic_3|A|^2 A\), is a nonlinear frequency shift: the local oscillation frequency depends on the local amplitude, the way a Kerr-nonlinear optical medium’s refractive index depends on light intensity. \(c_3\) is the nonlinear frequency-renormalization coefficient.


# Warm editorial-styled color map (Alabaster to Terracotta/Crimson) for |A|
col_palette <- colorRampPalette(c("#f7f5f0", "#e8e1d5", "#c5b8a5", "#a38d72", "#bd5d38", "#822c1a"))(100)
# Circular/periodic color palette for the cyclic phase variable [-pi, pi]
phase_colors <- colorRampPalette(c("#4575b4", "#e0f3f8", "#fee090", "#d73027", "#4575b4"))(100)

N   <- 200        # number of spatial grid points on the periodic ring
L   <- 100.0      # domain length
dx  <- L / N      # spatial step
dt  <- 0.04       # time step (dt < dx^2 / 2 keeps the explicit diffusion term stable)
steps <- 4000     # total time steps
save_interval <- 8 # save every 8th frame

# c1 = -1.0, c3 = 1.5: checked against the Benjamin-Feir-Newell criterion below
c1  <- -1.0
c3  <- 1.5

title: The Complex Ginzburg-Landau Equation
section: Plane waves and the Benjamin-Feir-Newell criterion
text:
Plane waves and the Benjamin-Feir-Newell criterion
Before running the simulation, it’s worth asking what the CGLE predicts analytically, because the prediction is exact and gives a sanity check for the numerics. The simplest nontrivial solutions are traveling plane waves, \(A(x,t) = R\,e^{i(kx - \omega t)}\) with constant real amplitude \(R\) and wavenumber \(k\). Substituting into the equation and separating real and imaginary parts gives
\[
R^2 = 1 - k^2, \qquad \omega = c_1 k^2 - c_3 R^2,
\]
so a family of plane-wave solutions exists for every \(|k| < 1\), with larger \(|k|\) forced to run at correspondingly smaller amplitude. But existence isn’t the same as stability: a plane wave can be an exact solution of the equation and still be destroyed by long-wavelength perturbations. Linearizing around a plane wave and analyzing the resulting perturbation growth rate gives the Benjamin-Feir-Newell instability criterion. In the sign convention used here (equation above has \(-(1-ic_3)|A|^2A\), i.e. an effective nonlinear coefficient of \(-c_3\) in the more common \((1+ib)\nabla^2A - (1+ic)|A|^2A\) convention with \(b=c_1\)), the \(k=0\) plane wave is linearly stable when
\[
1 - c_1 c_3 > 0,
\]
and unstable otherwise. When it’s unstable, small perturbations to a plane wave grow rather than decay, and the system is driven toward “defect turbulence” or “phase turbulence” — spatiotemporal chaos with proliferating phase singularities, rather than a single coherent wave. This is the source of the CGLE’s reputation as a rich generator of chaos even though it’s just one field on a line; whether the reputation is earned depends entirely on the sign of \(1-c_1c_3\).

bfn <- 1 - c1 * c3

For the parameters used here, \(1 - c_1 c_3 = 1 - (-1)(1.5) = 2.5\), which is positive — so the plane-wave regime should be linearly stable, and the simulation should settle into a single coherent traveling wave rather than turbulence. That’s the prediction to check against the numerics below.

title: The Complex Ginzburg-Landau Equation
text:
Simulating the equation
The equation is solved by explicit finite differences on a periodic ring: the spatial Laplacian at each grid point is approximated by the standard second-order central difference, with the two boundary neighbors wrapped around the ring, and the whole field is advanced in time by a single forward-Euler step. The time step (\(dt = 0.04\)) is kept comfortably below the diffusive stability limit \(dx^2/2 = 0.125\) for the explicit scheme to stay numerically stable. The field starts from the unstable state \(A \approx 0\), seeded with tiny uniform random noise — a stand-in for the fact that any real physical realization of this instability starts from some unavoidable microscopic fluctuation, not from an exact, infinitely fine-tuned zero.

set.seed(42)
A <- runif(N, -0.05, 0.05) + 1i * runif(N, -0.05, 0.05)

n_saves <- steps / save_interval
amplitude_history <- matrix(0, nrow = n_saves, ncol = N)
phase_history     <- matrix(0, nrow = n_saves, ncol = N)


save_idx <- 1
for (t_step in 1:steps) {
  # Periodic Laplacian: shift the field left/right by one grid point and
  # wrap around the ends, rather than truncating at a hard boundary.
  left_neighbor  <- c(A[N], A[1:(N - 1)])
  right_neighbor <- c(A[2:N], A[1])
  laplacian <- (left_neighbor - 2 * A + right_neighbor) / dx^2

  dA <- A + (1 + 1i * c1) * laplacian - (1 - 1i * c3) * (Mod(A)^2) * A
  A <- A + dA * dt

  if (t_step %% save_interval == 0 && save_idx <= n_saves) {
    amplitude_history[save_idx, ] <- Mod(A)
    phase_history[save_idx, ]     <- Arg(A)
    save_idx <- save_idx + 1
  }
}


time_axis  <- seq(0, steps * dt, length.out = n_saves)
space_axis <- seq(0, L, length.out = N)

to_long <- function(mat, value_name) {
  mat |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    setNames(space_axis) |>
    mutate(time = time_axis) |>
    pivot_longer(-time, names_to = "space", values_to = value_name) |>
    mutate(space = as.numeric(space))
}

amplitude_df <- to_long(amplitude_history, "amplitude")
phase_df     <- to_long(phase_history, "phase")

# Spatial spread of the amplitude field at each point in time: this is what
# quantifies the "saturation transient" discussed below.
amplitude_variance <- amplitude_df |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(sd_amplitude = sd(amplitude), .groups = "drop")

transient_end <- amplitude_variance |>
  filter(sd_amplitude < 0.01) |>
  slice(1) |>
  pull(time)


Checking the plane-wave prediction against the final state
Before plotting the full space-time history, it’s worth directly comparing the simulation’s final state to the plane-wave formula derived above. The periodic domain only permits wavenumbers \(k = 2\pi n/L\) for integer winding number \(n\), so unwrapping the final phase profile across the ring reads off exactly which \(k\) the system selected.

final_amplitude <- Mod(A)
final_phase     <- Arg(A)

unwrapped <- final_phase
for (i in 2:length(unwrapped)) {
  d <- unwrapped[i] - unwrapped[i - 1]
  if (d > pi)  unwrapped[i:length(unwrapped)] <- unwrapped[i:length(unwrapped)] - 2 * pi
  if (d < -pi) unwrapped[i:length(unwrapped)] <- unwrapped[i:length(unwrapped)] + 2 * pi
}
winding_number <- (unwrapped[length(unwrapped)] - unwrapped[1]) / (2 * pi)
k_selected     <- 2 * pi * round(winding_number) / L
R_predicted    <- sqrt(max(0, 1 - k_selected^2))

tibble(
  quantity = c("selected winding number", "selected wavenumber k", "predicted R = sqrt(1-k^2)", "observed mean |A|", "observed sd |A|"),
  value = c(round(winding_number, 3), round(k_selected, 4), round(R_predicted, 4),
            round(mean(final_amplitude), 4), round(sd(final_amplitude), 4))
)

  <chr>                      <dbl>
1 selected winding number   0.993 
2 selected wavenumber k     0.0628
3 predicted R = sqrt(1-k^2) 0.998 
4 observed mean |A|         1.02  
5 observed sd |A|           0.0013


The field settles into (almost exactly) a single winding of phase around the periodic domain — the lowest nonzero wavenumber the ring permits, \(k = 2\pi/L \approx 0.0628\) — and the observed amplitude matches the plane-wave prediction \(R=\sqrt{1-k^2}\approx 0.998\) to within about 2.4%, with the small residual coming from the finite-difference discretization and the leftover fluctuations the initial noise seeded across other, weakly-damped modes. This is the exact analytic solution derived above, reappearing as the attractor of the full nonlinear simulation.

Reading the space-time picture

Figure 1: Space-time evolution of the 1D complex Ginzburg-Landau equation. (A) The amplitude field |A(x,t)| grows from noise and saturates to a spatially uniform plane wave; the annotated ‘stripes’ and ‘waves’ language from the phase panel does not apply here. (B) The phase Arg(A(x,t)) carries the actual traveling-wave structure — this is where the diagonal stripes live. The two top panels are plotting the same complex field, split into its polar coordinates, and they show almost entirely different things. Panel A (amplitude) grows out of the noisy initial condition and then goes essentially flat — the plane-wave analysis above is exact evidence that this should happen, not a numerical artifact, since \(|A|\) genuinely is spatially uniform for an ideal plane wave. Panel C makes the transient itself legible: the spatial standard deviation of \(|A|\) collapses by roughly two orders of magnitude within the first several time units and then stays essentially at the discretization noise floor. Panel B (phase) is where the visually interesting diagonal banding actually lives, because \(\mathrm{Arg}(A) = kx - \omega t\) for a plane wave is linear in both space and time — the traveling stripes are a phase phenomenon, encoded in the winding of the argument of \(A\) around the periodic domain, not in any spatial modulation of its magnitude.

title: The Complex Ginzburg-Landau Equation
section: Extending to two dimensions: spiral defects and phase turbulence
text:
Extending to two dimensions: spiral defects and phase turbulence
Everything above stayed in one spatial dimension, where the Benjamin-Feir-Newell criterion has a clean binary reading: \(1-c_1c_3>0\) gives a stable traveling plane wave, and \(1-c_1c_3<0\) gives some form of spatiotemporal chaos. In two dimensions, the same instability opens onto a richer phase diagram, because the phase field \(\mathrm{Arg}(A)\) can now wind around a point rather than only accumulating along a line. Where the phase winds by a full \(\pm 2\pi\) around some point \((x,y)\), continuity forces the amplitude to vanish exactly at that point — these are the topological defects of the CGLE, and away from the defect core the surrounding phase field organizes itself into a rotating spiral wave. Aranson and Kramer’s review catalogs how, once \(1-c_1c_3<0\), the system can settle into two qualitatively distinct chaotic regimes depending on how far into the unstable region the parameters sit: a defect-free phase turbulence, where the phase field is chaotic but the amplitude stays bounded away from zero everywhere, and a defect (or amplitude) turbulence, where point defects continually nucleate, wander, and annihilate in pairs, each one the core of a rotating spiral (Aranson and Kramer 2002).
The equation itself only needs the Laplacian promoted to two dimensions:
\[
\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} = A + (1 + i c_1)\left(\frac{\partial^2 A}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 A}{\partial y^2}\right) - (1 - i c_3)\,|A|^2 A.
\]

Detecting a topological defect numerically
A defect is a point around which the phase winds by a full turn. On the grid, that’s checked by walking around each elementary 2x2 plaquette of grid points, summing the (wrapped, so always in \((-\pi,\pi]\)) phase differences between adjacent corners, and dividing by \(2\pi\): a plaquette encloses a defect of charge \(+1\) or \(-1\) exactly when that sum is \(\pm 2\pi\), and encloses no defect when it’s zero. This is the same discrete circulation-counting argument used to find vortices in superfluids or dislocations in a crystal lattice — a defect is, by construction, a place where a per-point quantity (the phase) is discontinuous only because the field it lives on (\(A\)) is forced through zero there.

lap2d <- function(A, dx) {
  up    <- rbind(A[nrow(A), , drop = FALSE], A[-nrow(A), , drop = FALSE])
  down  <- rbind(A[-1, , drop = FALSE], A[1, , drop = FALSE])
  left  <- cbind(A[, ncol(A), drop = FALSE], A[, -ncol(A), drop = FALSE])
  right <- cbind(A[, -1, drop = FALSE], A[, 1, drop = FALSE])
  (up + down + left + right - 4 * A) / dx^2
}

wrap_pi <- function(x) ((x + pi) %% (2 * pi)) - pi

# Topological charge of every elementary plaquette on the periodic grid,
# via the discrete phase circulation around its four corners.
defect_charge_grid <- function(A) {
  theta      <- Arg(A)
  th_ip1_j   <- rbind(theta[-1, , drop = FALSE], theta[1, , drop = FALSE])
  th_i_jp1   <- cbind(theta[, -1, drop = FALSE], theta[, 1, drop = FALSE])
  th_ip1_jp1 <- cbind(th_ip1_j[, -1, drop = FALSE], th_ip1_j[, 1, drop = FALSE])
  d1 <- wrap_pi(th_ip1_j - theta);      d2 <- wrap_pi(th_ip1_jp1 - th_ip1_j)
  d3 <- wrap_pi(th_i_jp1 - th_ip1_jp1); d4 <- wrap_pi(theta - th_i_jp1)
  round((d1 + d2 + d3 + d4) / (2 * pi))
}

simulate_cgle2d <- function(c1, c3, N, L, dt, steps, seed, save_every,
                             init = c("noise", "perturbed_plane_wave"), noise_amp = 0.05) {
  init <- match.arg(init)
  dx <- L / N
  set.seed(seed)
  if (init == "noise") {
    A <- matrix(complex(real = runif(N * N, -noise_amp, noise_amp),
                         imaginary = runif(N * N, -noise_amp, noise_amp)), nrow = N)
  } else {
    # Start from the exact k=0 plane wave (R=1) plus a small broadband
    # perturbation -- this is the state the BFN criterion is actually a
    # statement about the stability of, rather than the fully unstructured
    # A=0 noise used for the 1D run above.
    A <- matrix(1 + 0i, N, N) +
      matrix(complex(real = runif(N * N, -noise_amp, noise_amp),
                      imaginary = runif(N * N, -noise_amp, noise_amp)), nrow = N)
  }
  n_saves <- floor(steps / save_every)
  defect_count <- numeric(n_saves); time_trace <- numeric(n_saves); save_idx <- 1
  for (step in 1:steps) {
    lap <- lap2d(A, dx)
    dA  <- A + (1 + 1i * c1) * lap - (1 - 1i * c3) * (Mod(A)^2) * A
    A   <- A + dA * dt
    if (step %% save_every == 0 && save_idx <= n_saves) {
      defect_count[save_idx] <- sum(defect_charge_grid(A) != 0)
      time_trace[save_idx]   <- step * dt
      save_idx <- save_idx + 1
    }
  }
  list(A = A, defect_count = defect_count, time_trace = time_trace, dx = dx, L = L, N = N)
}



Choosing two parameter sets on the unstable side of the line
\(1-c_1c_3<0\) is necessary for either chaotic regime, but it’s a statement purely about the linear growth rate of long-wavelength perturbations to the \(k=0\) plane wave, and that growth rate vanishes continuously as the parameters approach the line from the unstable side. That has a concrete numerical consequence: sitting just barely past the line, the instability takes a very long time (and a large domain, to admit small enough wavenumbers) to grow out of infinitesimal noise, and — checked directly, by starting a run near the line and simply watching for a long time — it does not automatically produce defects. Nucleating an actual point defect is a separate, finite-amplitude event: it requires some region of the field to be driven all the way to \(A=0\), which is a much larger fluctuation than “phase is a bit ragged.” So two runs are used here, both satisfying \(1-c_1c_3<0\), chosen to sit on either side of that further, empirical threshold:

c1_defect <- 2.0;  c3_defect <- 1.5   # deep in the unstable region
c1_phase  <- 1.0;  c3_phase  <- 1.3   # only just past the line
bfn_defect <- 1 - c1_defect * c3_defect
bfn_phase  <- 1 - c1_phase * c3_phase


Defect turbulence: \(c_1=2\), \(c_3=1.5\), giving \(1-c_1c_3=-2\). Started from the same kind of small uniform noise used for the 1D run, on a \(100\times100\) periodic domain. This is deep enough into the unstable region that defects nucleate promptly and in large numbers.
Phase turbulence: \(c_1=1\), \(c_3=1.3\), giving \(1-c_1c_3=-0.3\) — unstable, but only mildly so. Started instead from the exact \(k=0\) plane wave plus a small perturbation, on a smaller \(20\times20\) domain (which restricts the accessible wavenumbers to ones large enough for the weak instability to grow within a tractable simulated time) and run for roughly three times as long. This is the regime where, empirically, no defect ever nucleates.


sim_defect <- simulate_cgle2d(c1 = c1_defect, c3 = c3_defect, N = 100, L = 100, dt = 0.04,
                               steps = 4000, seed = 909, save_every = 20,
                               init = "noise", noise_amp = 0.05)
sim_phase <- simulate_cgle2d(c1 = c1_phase, c3 = c3_phase, N = 64, L = 20, dt = 0.01,
                              steps = 45000, seed = 321, save_every = 300,
                              init = "perturbed_plane_wave", noise_amp = 0.25)


field_to_df <- function(A, L) {
  N  <- nrow(A)
  ax <- seq(0, L, length.out = N + 1)[1:N]
  expand.grid(x = ax, y = ax) |>
    mutate(amplitude = as.vector(Mod(t(A))), phase = as.vector(Arg(t(A))))
}

defect_coords <- function(A, L) {
  N <- nrow(A); dx <- L / N
  charge <- defect_charge_grid(A)
  idx <- which(charge != 0, arr.ind = TRUE)
  if (nrow(idx) == 0) return(tibble(x = numeric(0), y = numeric(0), charge = numeric(0)))
  tibble(x = (idx[, 1] - 0.5) * dx, y = (idx[, 2] - 0.5) * dx, charge = charge[idx])
}

field_defect_df <- field_to_df(sim_defect$A, sim_defect$L)
field_phase_df  <- field_to_df(sim_phase$A, sim_phase$L)
defects_final   <- defect_coords(sim_defect$A, sim_defect$L)

defect_trace_df <- bind_rows(
  tibble(time = sim_defect$time_trace, n_defects = sim_defect$defect_count,
         regime = sprintf("Defect turbulence (c1=%.1f, c3=%.1f)", c1_defect, c3_defect)),
  tibble(time = sim_phase$time_trace, n_defects = sim_phase$defect_count,
         regime = sprintf("Phase turbulence (c1=%.1f, c3=%.1f)", c1_phase, c3_phase))
)

steady_defect_stats <- defect_trace_df |>
  filter(regime == sprintf("Defect turbulence (c1=%.1f, c3=%.1f)", c1_defect, c3_defect), time > 20) |>
  summarise(mean_n = mean(n_defects), sd_n = sd(n_defects))
steady_density_pct <- round(100 * steady_defect_stats$mean_n / sim_defect$N^2, 2)



The two regimes, side by side

p_amp_defect <- ggplot(field_defect_df, aes(x, y, fill = amplitude)) +
  geom_raster() + coord_fixed() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = col_palette) +
  labs(title = "Amplitude |A|", subtitle = "Defect turbulence", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "|A|")

p_phase_defect <- ggplot(field_defect_df, aes(x, y, fill = phase)) +
  geom_raster() + coord_fixed() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = phase_colors, limits = c(-pi, pi)) +
  geom_point(data = defects_final, aes(x, y, shape = factor(sign(charge))),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "black", size = 1.4) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`-1` = 4, `1` = 1), name = "defect\ncharge") +
  labs(title = "Phase Arg(A)", subtitle = "Spiral cores marked", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Arg(A)")

p_amp_phase <- ggplot(field_phase_df, aes(x, y, fill = amplitude)) +
  geom_raster() + coord_fixed() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = col_palette, limits = range(field_phase_df$amplitude)) +
  labs(title = "Amplitude |A|", subtitle = "Phase turbulence", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "|A|")

p_phase_phase <- ggplot(field_phase_df, aes(x, y, fill = phase)) +
  geom_raster() + coord_fixed() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = phase_colors, limits = c(-pi, pi)) +
  labs(title = "Phase Arg(A)", subtitle = "No defects", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Arg(A)")

(p_amp_defect | p_phase_defect) / (p_amp_phase | p_phase_phase)







Figure 2: Final-state amplitude and phase fields for the two regimes. Top: deep in the unstable region (\(1-c_1c_3=`r round(bfn_defect,2)`\)), point defects (marked: circles and crosses for the two opposite topological charges) nucleate throughout the domain, each one the core of a spiral visible as a swirl in the surrounding phase field. Bottom: only just past the instability line (\(1-c_1c_3=`r round(bfn_phase,2)`\)), the phase field develops a smooth, slowly-evolving large-scale distortion rather than small-scale disorder, but the amplitude field never approaches zero and no defects appear – the small domain needed to make this weak instability grow in a tractable simulated time (discussed below) also limits how spatially extended the resulting chaos can look.





The amplitude field in the top-left panel makes the mechanism visible directly: it isn’t uniform the way the 1D plane wave’s amplitude was, but instead traces out a network of thin, dark troughs, and the defects sit exactly at the darkest points along that network, where \(|A|\) genuinely reaches zero. Averaged over the second half of the run, this parameter set settles into a statistically steady population of 67 \(\pm\) 6.6 defects (about 0.67% of grid plaquettes) — individual defects continually annihilate in \(\pm\) pairs and new ones nucleate elsewhere, but the population size itself is not chaotic. The bottom row is the qualitatively different outcome: the phase field deforms into a smooth large-scale swirl rather than staying flat, but the amplitude field (bottom-left) stays within 2.4% of its base value of 1 everywhere, never approaching the zero a defect would require. It’s worth being honest that this second snapshot looks more like a single large-scale deformation than “turbulence” in the everyday sense of small-scale disorder — a fair reading given how the parameters were chosen (below), and a reminder that “phase turbulence” is a technical label (chaotic in the dynamical-systems sense, i.e. sensitive to initial conditions and aperiodic in time) rather than a promise of visual complexity.

defect_trace_df |>
  filter(time > 2) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, n_defects, color = regime)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~regime, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c("#822c1a", "#4575b4"), unique(defect_trace_df$regime)), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Number of topological defects (spiral cores)")







Figure 3: Number of topological defects over time for the two regimes (each panel’s time axis is scaled to its own run). Left: after an initial transient in which spurious single-pixel defects seeded by the rough noisy start rapidly annihilate, the population settles into a statistically steady density with continual nucleation and annihilation of pairs. Right: the defect count is exactly zero for the entire run.





Both runs sit on the unstable side of the same Benjamin-Feir-Newell line derived in one dimension above — the criterion doesn’t care about dimensionality, since it comes from linearizing around the same uniform plane wave — but only one of them turns that linear instability into topological defects. This is the sense in which the two-dimensional CGLE is a genuinely richer object than its 1D restriction: a 1D “defect” would require the amplitude to hit zero at an isolated point in spacetime, an event fine-tuned enough to be essentially unobservable from generic initial conditions, whereas in 2D a defect is a robust, codimension-2 object (a point in a 2D space) that generic chaotic dynamics can and does create and destroy continually once the instability is strong enough.

title: The Complex Ginzburg-Landau Equation
section: How literal is the biological framing?
text:
How literal is the biological framing?
The comments in the original simulation script describe \(A(x,t)\) as a “morphogen field” and draw an analogy to somite segmentation clocks in vertebrate development. That framing is worth being honest about: it’s a narrative device, not a claim that this equation is a validated model of any specific developmental system. Real segmentation clocks (the traveling wavefront of Hes/Her gene expression oscillations in the vertebrate presomitic mesoderm) are usually modeled with delay-coupled genetic oscillator networks tied to a receding determination front, not a CGLE-type amplitude equation, and the classic Turing-type stripe patterns in, e.g., zebrafish pigmentation come from a stationary reaction-diffusion instability (Turing 1952), not an oscillatory one.
Where the CGLE genuinely does apply as a first-principles model — not just an analogy — is anywhere a spatially extended medium of near-identical oscillators is weakly coupled to its neighbors just past a Hopf bifurcation: coupled chemical oscillators in the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction, traveling and spiral waves in some models of cardiac tissue, arrays of coupled lasers, and convecting fluids with an oscillatory (rather than stationary) primary instability. The reason the same three-term equation keeps reappearing across such physically unrelated systems is precisely the universality argument from earlier: near onset, the equation doesn’t see the chemistry or the optics, only the bifurcation type and two real numbers.

title: The Complex Ginzburg-Landau Equation
text:
Conclusion
Three things are worth taking away. First, the historical arc: a static, real mean-field theory for superconductivity became a dynamical, complex amplitude equation once the same symmetry-and-scaling argument was applied to oscillatory rather than stationary instabilities — and that equation turned out to be universal across a wide range of unrelated physical systems. Second, the concrete numerical lesson from the 1D simulation: splitting a complex field into \(|A|\) and \(\mathrm{Arg}(A)\) is not a neutral choice of coordinates. There, essentially all of the interesting spatiotemporal structure was carried by the phase, while the amplitude did something much simpler — it grows, then locks onto the single value the exact plane-wave solution predicts. Third, moving to two dimensions changes that picture: past the same Benjamin-Feir-Newell line, the amplitude field stops being a passive, uniform background and can itself develop structure — a network of troughs pinned to point defects, each one the core of a spiral wave — and whether that happens at all is a further, empirical question beyond the sign of \(1-c_1c_3\) alone.

title: Markov Chains
text: This is the first of three short refreshers behind two earlier posts — Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models — both of which lean on ideas from Sclocchi, Favero & Wyart (2024) (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024) that are easy to gloss over if you haven’t seen them recently. This one covers Markov chains; the next two cover mean-field analysis and the generative diffusion process itself.

title: Markov Chains
text:
What makes a process “Markov”
A process is Markov if its next state depends only on its current state — not on the path that got it there. Formally, \(P(x_{t+1} \mid x_t, x_{t-1}, \dots, x_0) = P(x_{t+1} \mid x_t)\). That’s it; the entire history collapses into whatever’s true right now.
A simple weather model makes this concrete: three states, and a transition matrix giving the probability of tomorrow’s weather given today’s.

states <- c("Sunny", "Cloudy", "Rainy")
P <- matrix(
  c(0.7, 0.2, 0.1,
    0.3, 0.4, 0.3,
    0.2, 0.3, 0.5),
  nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE, dimnames = list(states, states)
)

set.seed(1)
n_steps <- 200
path <- integer(n_steps)
path[1] <- 1L
for (t in 2:n_steps) path[t] <- sample.int(3, 1, prob = P[path[t - 1], ])

data.frame(step = seq_len(n_steps), state = factor(states[path], levels = states)) |>
  ggplot(aes(step, state, colour = state)) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "step", y = NULL, colour = NULL, title = "Simulated weather path") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 1: A 200-step simulated path through the weather chain, colour-coded by state.





The same transition matrix, drawn as a state diagram, makes the “only today matters” structure visually explicit — every arrow starts from a single current state, with no memory of how the chain got there:

Figure 2: State diagram for the three-state weather chain. Edge labels are transition probabilities from the current state.





Knowing today is Sunny tells you everything relevant about tomorrow; knowing it was also Sunny for the last five days adds nothing. That’s the whole idea, and it’s what makes chains like this tractable to analyze — no exploding state space of “all possible histories” to track.

title: Markov Chains
section: Where does it settle? Two ways to find out
text:
Where does it settle? Two ways to find out
Run the chain long enough and the fraction of time spent in each state converges to a fixed stationary distribution \(\pi\), satisfying \(\pi P = \pi\) — a left eigenvector of \(P\) with eigenvalue 1. Two independent ways to find it should agree:

eig <- eigen(t(P))
pi_stat <- Re(eig$vectors[, which.min(abs(eig$values - 1))])
pi_stat <- pi_stat / sum(pi_stat)
names(pi_stat) <- states

n_long <- 5000
path_long <- integer(n_long)
path_long[1] <- 1L
for (t in 2:n_long) path_long[t] <- sample.int(3, 1, prob = P[path_long[t - 1], ])
pi_empirical <- table(factor(states[path_long], levels = states)) / n_long

df <- data.frame(
  state = rep(states, 2),
  probability = c(pi_stat, as.numeric(pi_empirical)),
  method = rep(c("eigenvector", "5000-step simulation"), each = 3)
)

ggplot(df, aes(state, probability, fill = method)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "probability", fill = NULL)







Figure 3: Stationary distribution via eigen-decomposition vs. a long simulated path’s empirical frequencies.





Eigenvector: Sunny 0.457, Cloudy 0.283, Rainy 0.261. A long simulated path lands close to the same numbers — the chain has “forgotten” where it started and settled into its long-run behaviour. This idea — a distribution that’s a fixed point of an update rule — will come back in the next post, where a self-consistency equation plays exactly the same role.

title: Markov Chains
section: Why an eigenvector, and how eigen() actually gets it
text:
Why an eigenvector, and how eigen() actually gets it
The stationary condition \(\pi P = \pi\) treats \(\pi\) as a row vector multiplying \(P\) from the left — a left eigenvector of \(P\) with eigenvalue 1. Transposing both sides turns it into an ordinary right-eigenvector problem: \(P^\top \pi^\top = \pi^\top\). That’s why the code above calls eigen(t(P)) rather than eigen(P) — R’s eigen() only ever returns right eigenvectors, so finding a left eigenvector of \(P\) means first transposing.
An eigenvalue-1 solution is guaranteed to exist. Every row of \(P\) sums to 1, so \(P\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\): the all-ones vector is a right eigenvector of \(P\) with eigenvalue 1. \(P\) and \(P^\top\) share the same eigenvalues (they have the same characteristic polynomial, since \(\det(P^\top - \lambda I) = \det((P - \lambda I)^\top) = \det(P - \lambda I)\)), so 1 is also an eigenvalue of \(P^\top\) — guaranteeing a \(\pi\) satisfying \(\pi P = \pi\) exists, though not automatically that it’s unique or non-negative (that extra guarantee comes from Perron–Frobenius, since every entry of \(P\) here is strictly positive).
Under the hood, eigen() finds all three eigenvalues of \(P^\top\) as the roots of \(\det(P^\top - \lambda I) = 0\), then for each eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) finds a vector spanning the null space of \((P^\top - \lambda_i I)\) — solved numerically via matrix decomposition rather than by hand, but conceptually just “solve \((P^\top - \lambda_i I)v = 0\).” Doing that null-space step explicitly for \(\lambda = 1\), independently of eigen()’s eigenvector output, should recover the same \(\pi\) up to scale:

eig$values

[1] 1.0000000 0.4732051 0.1267949

A <- t(P) - diag(3)
qr(A)$rank

[1] 2

pi_manual <- svd(A)$v[, 3]
pi_manual <- pi_manual / sum(pi_manual)
names(pi_manual) <- states
pi_manual

    Sunny    Cloudy     Rainy 
0.4565217 0.2826087 0.2608696 


eig$values shows one eigenvalue at 1 and two others strictly smaller in modulus — consistent with the all-ones-vector argument above and with a unique stationary distribution. A has rank 2 out of 3, meaning \((P^\top - I)\) has a 1-dimensional null space — exactly one free direction, which svd() extracts as the singular vector paired with a (numerically) zero singular value. pi_manual matches pi_stat from eigen() up to floating-point noise, since both are just different numerical routes to the same null space.
Those two smaller eigenvalues aren’t wasted information either: the second-largest one in modulus governs how fast the chain forgets its starting state and converges to \(\pi\) — larger gap to 1, faster mixing. That’s a thread this post won’t pull further, but it’s the same kind of “look at the eigenvalues away from the fixed point” reasoning that shows up when analyzing stability in the mean-field post next.

title: Markov Chains
text:
DDPM’s actual Markov chain
Diffusion models run a Markov chain too, just with a continuous state and Gaussian transition kernels rather than a lookup table. Forward and reverse processes run along the same chain of latents \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_T\), in opposite directions:
Each \(x_t\) is a latent variable — same shape as the data (an image’s pixel array, say), but not itself an observed data point except at the two ends of the chain. \(x_0\) is a real, clean data sample; \(x_T\) is (by construction, after enough steps) indistinguishable from pure Gaussian noise; everything in between, \(x_1, \dots, x_{T-1}\), is a progressively noisier, unobserved intermediate version of \(x_0\) that only exists as a mathematical construct — you never have a “true” \(x_t\) for \(0 < t < T\) the way you have a genuine image or a genuine noise sample. “Latent” here just means: a random variable in the model that generative code manipulates and a network learns to reverse, but that’s never seen directly in the training data. The subscript \(t\) indexes position along the chain (equivalently, how much noise has accumulated), not real time.

\usetikzlibrary{positioning,arrows}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  ->, >=stealth', thick, node distance=3.1cm,
  state/.style={circle, draw, minimum size=1.15cm, font=\normalsize},
  dots/.style={font=\normalsize}
]
  \node[state] (x0) {$x_0$};
  \node[state, right=of x0] (x1) {$x_1$};
  \node[dots, right=of x1] (d1) {$\cdots$};
  \node[state, right=of d1] (xtm1) {$x_{t-1}$};
  \node[state, right=of xtm1] (xt) {$x_t$};
  \node[dots, right=of xt] (d2) {$\cdots$};
  \node[state, right=of d2] (xT) {$x_T$};

  \path
    (x0)   edge node[above] {$q(x_1|x_0)$} (x1)
    (x1)   edge (d1)
    (d1)   edge (xtm1)
    (xtm1) edge node[above] {$q(x_t|x_{t-1})$} (xt)
    (xt)   edge (d2)
    (d2)   edge (xT);

  \path[dashed]
    (x1) edge[bend left=35] node[below] {$p_\theta(x_0|x_1)$} (x0)
    (xt) edge[bend left=35] node[below] {$p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t)$} (xtm1);
\end{tikzpicture}







Figure 4: The DDPM Markov chain. Forward (noising) transitions q run left to right and are fixed; reverse (denoising) transitions p_theta run right to left and are learned.





The forward (noising) process is fixed by construction, defined, exactly as in Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) (Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020), by:
\[
q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\, x_{t-1},\ \beta_t I\right)
\]
Each step nudges \(x_{t-1}\) slightly toward the origin and adds a little Gaussian noise, with \(\beta_t\) controlling how much. This is precisely the recurrence used in guided_diffusion/gaussian_diffusion.py, the codebase reproduced in the diffusion-phase-transition post.
\(\beta_t \in (0, 1)\) is the noise schedule — a small, hand-chosen number per step (Ho et al.’s schedule ramps it linearly from \(10^{-4}\) at \(t=1\) to \(0.02\) at \(t=T\)) fixing how much variance gets injected at step \(t\). It’s not learned; it’s a fixed hyperparameter sequence chosen before training even starts. \(\alpha_t := 1 - \beta_t\) is just a convenient rename — close to 1 when \(\beta_t\) is small — so that the update reads \(x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t}\, x_{t-1} + \sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon\): shrink the previous state slightly, add noise to make up the variance budget. Their product across steps, \(\bar\alpha_t := \prod_{s \le t} \alpha_s\), is what actually appears in the closed-form jump below — it tracks how much of the original signal \(x_0\) survives after \(t\) compounded steps, and it’s what decays toward 0 as \(t \to T\) in Figure 5, driving \(x_t\) toward pure \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\) noise.

T_steps <- 1000
beta <- seq(1e-4, 0.02, length.out = T_steps)
alpha <- 1 - beta
alpha_bar <- cumprod(alpha)

x0 <- 2.0
n_traj <- 8
set.seed(2)
traj <- matrix(NA_real_, T_steps + 1, n_traj)
traj[1, ] <- x0
for (t in 1:T_steps) {
  eps <- rnorm(n_traj)
  traj[t + 1, ] <- sqrt(alpha[t]) * traj[t, ] + sqrt(beta[t]) * eps
}

traj_df <- as.data.frame(traj) |>
  mutate(step = 0:T_steps) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-step, names_to = "trajectory", values_to = "x")

band_df <- data.frame(step = 0:T_steps, sd = sqrt(1 - alpha_bar[c(1, seq_len(T_steps))]))

ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = band_df, aes(step, ymin = -2 * sd, ymax = 2 * sd), fill = "grey85") +
  geom_ribbon(data = band_df, aes(step, ymin = -sd, ymax = sd), fill = "grey70") +
  geom_line(data = traj_df, aes(step, x, group = trajectory), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "t", y = expression(x[t]), title = "Forward chain trajectories vs. their theoretical envelope")







Figure 5: Eight sample trajectories of the scalar Gaussian chain, starting from x0=2, collapsing into the N(0,1) envelope (shaded bands at +-1, +-2 sd) under the real Ho et al. (2020) schedule.

title: Markov Chains
text:
The closed-form jump
Simulating 1000 sequential steps every time you need a noisy sample would be wasteful, and because each step’s kernel is Gaussian, it’s also unnecessary: the composition of \(t\) Gaussian steps is itself Gaussian, in closed form:
\[
q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_t) I\right), \qquad \bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \le t}(1-\beta_s)
\]
You can jump straight from \(x_0\) to any \(x_t\) in one draw. This is exactly q_sample in the reproduced code, and it’s what makes the “forward-diffuse-partway-then-reverse” experiment in the diffusion-phase-transition post practical on real images. Worth actually checking it’s true rather than taking it on faith:

check_t <- 30
n_mc <- 200000
set.seed(3)
x_stepwise <- rep(x0, n_mc)
for (t in 1:check_t) {
  eps <- rnorm(n_mc)
  x_stepwise <- sqrt(alpha[t]) * x_stepwise + sqrt(beta[t]) * eps
}
mean_cf <- sqrt(alpha_bar[check_t]) * x0
var_cf <- 1 - alpha_bar[check_t]

At \(t=30\), 200,000 step-by-step Monte Carlo draws give mean 1.9885 and variance 0.01163; the closed form predicts mean 1.9884 and variance 0.0116 — matching to within Monte Carlo noise.

title: Markov Chains
text:
The reverse chain
The reverse process \(p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t)\) is modelled the same way — Markov, approximately Gaussian for small \(\beta_t\) — but its mean isn’t known in closed form for real data; that’s what a neural network is trained to approximate. The next explainer is a detour into a different piece of machinery this paper needs (mean-field analysis); the third comes back to build a toy reverse chain where, unusually, the right answer is known exactly.

title: Markov Chains
text:
References

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text: Third and final part of a series behind Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models. This one assumes the first post’s closed-form jump \(q(x_t\mid x_0)\); the second is a self-contained detour and isn’t needed here.

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text:
Noising a whole distribution
The first post applied the forward chain to a single starting point, \(x_0=2\). Real data isn’t a point, it’s a distribution — so apply the same closed-form jump to a batch of samples instead. Take something with actual structure to destroy: a two-component mixture, two bumps at \(-2\) and \(+2\).

mu1 <- -2; mu2 <- 2; sd0 <- 0.4; w1 <- 0.5; w2 <- 0.5
r_data <- function(n) {
  is_mode2 <- rbinom(n, 1, w2)
  ifelse(is_mode2 == 1, rnorm(n, mu2, sd0), rnorm(n, mu1, sd0))
}

set.seed(7)
n <- 4000
x0_data <- r_data(n)

T_steps <- 400
beta <- seq(1e-4, 0.02, length.out = T_steps)
alpha <- 1 - beta
alpha_bar <- cumprod(alpha)

noise_to_t <- function(x0_vec, t) {
  sqrt(alpha_bar[t]) * x0_vec + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar[t]) * rnorm(length(x0_vec))
}
x_mid <- noise_to_t(x0_data, T_steps %/% 2)
x_T <- noise_to_t(x0_data, T_steps)

data.frame(
  x = c(x0_data, x_mid, x_T),
  t = factor(rep(c("t = 0", paste0("t = ", T_steps %/% 2), paste0("t = ", T_steps)),
                 each = n),
             levels = c("t = 0", paste0("t = ", T_steps %/% 2), paste0("t = ", T_steps)))
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, fill = t)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity") +
  facet_wrap(~t, ncol = 1) +
  labs(y = "density", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Figure 1: The bimodal starting distribution collapsing to N(0,1) as t increases, under the same schedule shape as Ho et al. (2020).





By \(t=400\), mean \(-0.0108\) and sd \(1.0414\) — the two bumps have merged into plain \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), no trace of where they started.

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
section: What a denoiser actually needs: the score
text:
What a denoiser actually needs: the score
Reversing this requires knowing which direction “more like the data” is, at every noise level. That direction is the score, \(\nabla_x \log p_t(x)\) — the gradient of the log-density of the noisy marginal at time \(t\). Tweedie’s formula relates it directly to the optimal denoiser: the best single-step estimate of the clean signal given a noisy \(x_t\) is a simple function of the score. This is the modern way to think about what a diffusion model’s network is trained to produce — not “the clean image” directly, but a time-indexed family of score estimates, one per noise level.

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
section: The one case you don’t need a network for
text:
The one case you don’t need a network for
For almost any real data distribution, the score has no closed form and has to be learned. But a Gaussian mixture is a rare exception: convolving a Gaussian mixture with Gaussian noise gives another Gaussian mixture, so the noised marginal at every \(t\) — and hence its score — stays exactly computable:
\[
p_t(x) = \sum_k w_k\, \mathcal{N}\!\left(x;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mu_k,\ \ \bar\alpha_t \sigma_0^2 + (1-\bar\alpha_t)\right)
\]

exact_score <- function(x, t) {
  abar <- alpha_bar[t]
  v <- abar * sd0^2 + (1 - abar)
  m1 <- sqrt(abar) * mu1
  m2 <- sqrt(abar) * mu2
  d1 <- dnorm(x, m1, sqrt(v))
  d2 <- dnorm(x, m2, sqrt(v))
  p <- w1 * d1 + w2 * d2
  (w1 * d1 * (-(x - m1) / v) + w2 * d2 * (-(x - m2) / v)) / p
}

log_p_t <- function(x, t) {
  abar <- alpha_bar[t]
  v <- abar * sd0^2 + (1 - abar)
  m1 <- sqrt(abar) * mu1
  m2 <- sqrt(abar) * mu2
  log(w1 * dnorm(x, m1, sqrt(v)) + w2 * dnorm(x, m2, sqrt(v)))
}

h <- 1e-5
test_x <- c(-1, 0, 0.5, 1.5)
numeric_score <- (log_p_t(test_x + h, 100) - log_p_t(test_x - h, 100)) / (2 * h)
analytic_score <- exact_score(test_x, 100)

Checked against a numerical derivative of \(\log p_t(x)\) at \(t=100\), four test points: numeric gives -2.16329, 0, 3.52389, 0.7375, the closed form gives -2.16329, 0, 3.52389, 0.7375 — matching to the precision shown.

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text:
Reversing it, exactly
The ancestral-sampling reverse update, written in terms of the score:
\[
x_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t + \beta_t\, \nabla_x \log p_t(x_t)\Big) + \sqrt{\beta_t}\, z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \text{ for } t>1
\]
Ordinarily \(\nabla_x \log p_t\) is what a trained network approximates. Here it’s the closed form from the previous section — nothing learned, nothing approximate.

n_gen <- 4000
set.seed(11)
x_gen <- rnorm(n_gen)
for (t in T_steps:1) {
  score_val <- exact_score(x_gen, t)
  noise_term <- if (t > 1) rnorm(n_gen) else 0
  x_gen <- (x_gen + beta[t] * score_val) / sqrt(alpha[t]) + sqrt(beta[t]) * noise_term
}

ks_result <- ks.test(x0_data, x_gen)

data.frame(x = c(x0_data, x_gen), source = rep(c("original data", "reverse-generated"), each = n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, fill = source)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 60, alpha = 0.55, position = "identity") +
  labs(y = "density", fill = NULL)







Figure 2: Samples generated by reverse diffusion from pure noise, using only the exact score, against the true starting distribution.





Generation recovers both modes: mean/sd of the lower cluster \(-1.9774\) / \(0.3953\) against a true \(-2\)/\(0.4\), and the upper cluster \(1.9727\) / \(0.3994\) against a true \(2\)/\(0.4\). A two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test against the original data gives \(D=0.023\), \(p=0.241\) — nowhere near rejecting “same distribution.”

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text:
What this stands in for
The diffusion-phase-transition post does exactly this same procedure — forward-diffuse partway, then reverse — but on real ImageNet images, with a trained U-Net standing in for the score computed here in closed form (Ho, Jain, and Abbeel 2020). The abrupt class-flip reported there is a direct consequence of how that (learned, not closed-form) score behaves across noise levels for hierarchically-structured data — the same mechanics as this toy, just with a far richer \(p_0\) than two Gaussian bumps (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024).

title: A Diffusion Model You Can Actually Solve
text:
Series wrap-up
Three explainers, one underlying machine: a Markov chain moves data toward noise and, run in reverse with the right score function, moves noise back toward data; mean-field/annealed averaging is how you get a tractable equation for when that reversal preserves the “shape” of the data versus loses it; and the toy model here makes both pieces concrete enough to check by hand. With all three in place, Reproducing a Phase Transition in Diffusion Models and Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models should read as engineering and analysis built on genuinely solid ground, rather than machinery taken on faith.

title: RG Functional Equations & Critical Phenomena
Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:
Note



This post’s comparative framing was originally drafted by an AI research assistant under my general direction, synthesizing my own 2022 dissertation and Sclocchi et al. (2024). The mathematics has been independently re-derived and computed in R below, rather than simply reproduced from that draft.
Two pieces of work on this blog turn out to share more mathematics than their subject headings suggest. My 2022 dissertation (Milne 2022) uses the renormalization group (RG) to describe critical phenomena in thermodynamics and financial markets. An earlier post reproduces Sclocchi, Favero & Wyart’s (2024) result (Sclocchi, Favero, and Wyart 2024) that denoising diffusion models undergo a sharp, hierarchy-dependent phase transition. Both are, underneath, the same story: a discrete iterated map, a critical parameter, and an unstable fixed point that separates two very different fates for the system.
This post makes that bridge concrete rather than just asserting it — implementing both maps in R, finding their fixed points numerically, and plotting the resulting cobweb diagrams side by side.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:
Two hierarchies, one structure
Both frameworks simplify a high-dimensional system into a multi-scale tree. In statistical mechanics, a 2D spin lattice is grouped recursively into blocks, each decimated down to a single block-spin variable — Kadanoff’s original coarse-graining move. In Sclocchi et al.’s Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), the same tree runs the other way: a class label at the root branches down through latent features to the pixels at the leaves. The parameters line up directly:







Statistical mechanics & RG
Hierarchical diffusion (RHM)




Microscopic spin configuration \(s_i \in \{-1, 1\}\)
Leaf / input variables \(X_i^{(0)}\)


Block-spin variable at level \(\ell\)
Latent feature node \(X_i^{(\ell)}\)


Lattice spacing / scale length
Tree branching factor \(s\)


Correlation length \(\xi\)
Correct reconstruction depth


Potts state dimension \(Q\)
Alphabet size \(v\)


Coupling strength \(K = J/kT\)
Belief in correct sequence \(p = 1 - \epsilon + \epsilon/v\)


Bond recursion under decimation
Production-rule density \(f\)



In both, one parameter controls order versus disorder: \(K\) above a critical value \(K_c\) gives spontaneous magnetic alignment; \(f < 1\) in the RHM gives structured, hierarchically-correlated data rather than unstructured noise.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
section: The RG side: Kadanoff decimation and the critical coupling
text:
The RG side: Kadanoff decimation and the critical coupling
For the Potts model on a hierarchical diamond lattice, decimating spin sites under a scale transformation gives an exact recurrence for the coupling strength \(K\):
\[
K_{\ell-1} = \phi(K_\ell) \equiv \left( \frac{K_\ell^2 + Q - 1}{2K_\ell + Q - 2} \right)^2
\]
The physical critical point — where the correlation length diverges — is the unstable fixed point of this map, \(K_c = \phi(K_c)\). I’ll use \(Q=3\) (a three-state Potts model): it avoids a singularity in the denominator that shows up at \(Q=2\), and it happens to give a clean, exact critical point.

phi <- function(K, Q) ((K^2 + Q - 1) / (2 * K + Q - 2))^2
Q <- 3

Kc <- uniroot(function(K) phi(K, Q) - K, interval = c(1.5, 10))$root

h <- 1e-6
dphi <- function(K) (phi(K + h, Q) - phi(K - h, Q)) / (2 * h)

curve_df <- data.frame(K = seq(0.5, 6, length.out = 400)) |>
  mutate(phiK = phi(K, Q))

fixed_points <- data.frame(
  K = c(1, Kc),
  stability = c("stable", "unstable")
)

cb_below <- cobweb_path(phi, x0 = 3.9, n = 12, Q = Q) |> mutate(traj = "K0 = 3.9")
cb_above <- cobweb_path(phi, x0 = 4.1, n = 6, Q = Q) |> mutate(traj = "K0 = 4.1")
cobweb_df <- bind_rows(cb_below, cb_above)

ggplot() +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = curve_df, aes(K, phiK), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_path(data = cobweb_df, aes(x, y, group = traj, colour = traj), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(
    data = fixed_points, aes(K, K, shape = stability, colour = stability),
    size = 3, show.legend = c(shape = TRUE, colour = FALSE)
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(stable = 16, unstable = 4)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 6), ylim = c(0.5, 6)) +
  labs(
    x = expression(K[ell]), y = expression(K[ell - 1] == phi(K[ell])),
    colour = "trajectory", shape = "fixed point",
    title = "Kadanoff-Potts RG recursion (Q = 3)"
  )







Figure 1: Kadanoff-Potts RG recursion (Q = 3). The unstable critical coupling sits at K_c = 4; trajectories starting on either side flow away from it toward one of two very different fates.





Solving numerically: \(K_c = 4\), with derivative \(\phi'(K_c) \approx 1.778\) — greater than 1, confirming it’s unstable. A trajectory starting just below \(K_c\) (green line, \(K_0=3.9\)) flows down; one starting just above (orange, \(K_0=4.1\)) flows up and diverges.
One correction to the source material is worth flagging here. The original synthesis described the disordered basin as flowing toward \(K \to 0\). Checking the map directly: \(\phi(0, 3) = 4\), not \(0\) — so \(K=0\) isn’t a fixed point of this recursion at all. The actual trivial fixed point, true for every \(Q\), is \(K=1\): \(\phi(1, Q) \equiv 1\) identically, since numerator and denominator both reduce to \(Q\). It’s also superstable (\(\phi'(1) = 0\)), which is why the “K0 = 3.9” trajectory above collapses onto it so fast.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
section: The diffusion side: belief propagation and the class transition

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:
Same bifurcation, two dictionaries
Both maps are governed by the identical mechanism: a system crosses the basin boundary set by an unstable fixed point of a nonlinear discrete map, and the outcome on the other side is qualitatively different from where it started. A magnet losing its alignment, a market crashing, and a diffusion model’s reconstructed class flipping to something else entirely are, in this sense, the same event described in three different vocabularies.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:
Schröder’s equation: the linearizing bridge
Both works lean on the same piece of machinery for handling these maps analytically: Schröder’s functional equation (Curtright and Zachos 2011),
\[
\psi(\phi(x)) = \lambda\, \psi(x)
\]
where \(\lambda = \phi'(x^*)\) is the eigenvalue at a fixed point and \(\psi\) is the (unknown) conjugating function. It linearizes the messy nonlinear dynamics of \(\phi\) into simple scaling by \(\lambda\) near \(x^*\) — which is what lets you extend a discrete iteration into a continuous-time trajectory, \(x(t) = \psi^{-1}(\lambda^t \psi(x))\).

A brief aside: the Johansen–Ledoit–Sornette crash model
In my dissertation, applying this to the Johansen-Ledoit-Sornette model of financial bubbles — where the scaling factor \(\lambda\) is complex rather than real — gives the Log-Periodic Power Law:
\[
F(x) = x^\beta\, G(\omega \log x)
\]
with \(G\) periodic and \(x = |t_c - t|\) the distance from the crash time \(t_c\) (Johansen, Ledoit, and Sornette 1998). The oscillations get faster (in \(x\)) as the crash approaches, which is the model’s signature prediction of accelerating, log-periodic herding behaviour before a crash.

lppl <- function(x, beta = 0.3, A = 1, B = 0.3, omega = 6, phase = 0) {
  x^beta * (A + B * cos(omega * log(x) + phase))
}
data.frame(x = seq(0.001, 1, length.out = 2000)) |>
  mutate(Fx = lppl(x)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, Fx)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(
    x = expression("|" * t[c] - t * "|" ~ "(time to crash, decreasing rightward)"),
    y = "F(x)  (illustrative index level)"
  )







Figure 3: Illustrative log-periodic power law approaching a critical time – not fitted to real market data, just the functional form.





Sclocchi et al. don’t solve an analogue of this — but they make a structural observation that plays a similar bridging role. The convolutional U-Net used for denoising naturally approximates belief propagation: the encoder path acts as the upward BP pass (coarse-graining noisy pixels into abstract features), and the decoder path with its skip connections acts as the downward pass, mixing global class belief back down with local detail to reconstruct clean pixels.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
section: Where the analogy breaks: scale invariance
text:
Where the analogy breaks: scale invariance
The two frameworks diverge on one point worth stating plainly rather than glossing over. In the RG picture, criticality brings true continuous scale invariance: the correlation length diverges, the lattice spacing becomes irrelevant, and the system is fractally self-similar — which is exactly why wildly different physical materials fall into the same universality class.
Diffusion models don’t have this. Scale invariance is broken during denoising: the macroscopic scale (the class label) undergoes a sharp, discontinuous transition at a critical noise level, while the microscopic scale (fine texture) changes smoothly and continuously straight through that transition — sometimes composing pieces of the old class with the new one (a wolf generated with leopard eyes, in Sclocchi et al.’s example). That’s a time-scale separation reflecting the discrete, compositional structure of real data, not the continuous scale invariance of a system at a genuine critical point. The mathematics of the fixed point is shared; the physical picture it’s describing isn’t quite the same.

title: Fixed Points, Phase Transitions, and Diffusion Models
text:
Conclusion
Kadanoff’s block-spin decimation and Sclocchi et al.’s belief propagation on the Random Hierarchy Model turn out to be the same functional-equation machinery pointed at two different problems — one asking how magnetic order emerges from a spin lattice, the other how a diffusion model recovers (or loses) a semantic class from noise. See the dissertation for the full RG derivation, and the earlier post for the diffusion side reproduced end to end on real images.

title: The Birthday Paradox
text: Put 23 people in a room and the chance that two of them share a birthday is better than 50%. It feels wrong, which is why it’s called a paradox, but it’s a true statement and the arithmetic is short.

title: The Birthday Paradox
text:
Count the complement
Assume 365 equally likely birthdays (ignore 29 February and seasonal effects). Computing “at least one match” directly is messy, so compute the opposite: no one shares a birthday.
Person 1 can have any birthday. Person 2 must avoid 1 day, so has probability \(364/365\). Person 3 must avoid 2 days, so \(363/365\), and so on. For \(n\) people,
\[
P(\text{no match}) = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{365-k}{365} = \frac{365!}{(365-n)!\,365^n},
\]
and the answer we want is
\[
P(\text{match}) = 1 - \frac{365!}{(365-n)!\,365^n}.
\]

p_match <- function(n, d = 365) {
  1 - sapply(n, function(m) prod((d - seq_len(m) + 1) / d))
}
tibble(n = c(10, 20, 23, 30, 50, 70)) |>
  mutate(P_match = round(p_match(n), 4))

# A tibble: 6 × 2
      n P_match
  <dbl>   <dbl>
1    10   0.117
2    20   0.411
3    23   0.507
4    30   0.706
5    50   0.970
6    70   0.999


The probability crosses 50% at \(n = 23\) and passes 99% by \(n = 57\).

df <- tibble(n = 1:80, p = p_match(1:80))
ggplot(df, aes(n, p)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 23, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "Number of people", y = "P(at least one shared birthday)")







Figure 1: Exact probability of at least one shared birthday as the group grows. The 50% line is crossed at n = 23.

title: The Birthday Paradox
section: Why it feels wrong: pairs, not people
text:
Why it feels wrong: pairs, not people
The intuition says “23 is small next to 365”. But we aren’t asking whether someone matches my birthday. We’re asking whether any pair matches, and the number of pairs grows quadratically:
\[
\binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n-1)}{2}, \qquad \binom{23}{2} = 253.
\]
Each pair matches with probability \(1/365\), so with 253 pairs a match is no longer surprising. (Pairs aren’t independent, so this is only a heuristic, but it points at the right scaling.)

title: The Birthday Paradox
text:
An approximation
Use \(1 - x \approx e^{-x}\) for small \(x\):
\[
P(\text{no match}) = \prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{365}\right) \approx \exp\!\left(-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{k}{365}\right) = \exp\!\left(-\frac{n(n-1)}{2\cdot 365}\right).
\]
Setting this equal to \(1/2\) and solving for \(n\) gives
\[
n \approx \sqrt{2\ln 2\; d}\;\approx\; 1.18\sqrt{d},
\]
which for \(d = 365\) is about \(22.5\). So the threshold scales as \(\sqrt{d}\) rather than \(d\). That square-root law is what makes hash collisions arrive so much sooner than people expect: a 64-bit hash has \(d = 2^{64}\) values, yet collisions become likely after only about \(2^{32}\) items.

df <- df |> mutate(approx = 1 - exp(-n * (n - 1) / (2 * 365)))
df |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(p, approx), names_to = "which", values_to = "prob") |>
  mutate(which = recode(which, p = "Exact", approx = "Approximation")) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, prob, colour = which, linetype = which)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(x = "Number of people", y = "P(match)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







Figure 2: The exponential approximation tracks the exact curve closely over the whole range.






n50 <- min(which(df$p >= 0.5))
c(exact_threshold = n50, sqrt_formula = sqrt(2 * log(2) * 365))

exact_threshold    sqrt_formula 
       23.00000        22.49439

title: The Birthday Paradox
text:
Monte Carlo check
Simulate it directly: draw \(n\) random birthdays many times and count how often a duplicate appears.

sim_match <- function(n, trials = 20000) {
  mean(replicate(trials, anyDuplicated(sample.int(365, n, replace = TRUE)) > 0))
}
ns <- seq(5, 70, by = 5)
mc <- tibble(n = ns, p = sapply(ns, sim_match))

ggplot(df, aes(n, p)) +

title: The Birthday Paradox
text:
Takeaways

Count the complement: “no shared birthday” is a clean product.
The surprise comes from \(\binom{n}{2}\) pairs, not \(n\) people.
Collision thresholds scale as \(\sqrt{d}\), a fact that shows up well beyond birthdays, in hashing and cryptographic collision attacks.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Every statistics course repeats that correlation is not causation. Almost none of them say what causation is, or how to get from data to a causal answer when you can’t run an experiment. Judea Pearl spent forty years building the missing machinery: a language for causal assumptions (diagrams), an algebra for answering causal questions (the do-calculus), and a hierarchy that says which questions each kind of data can answer (the ladder of causation).
This post is a tour of that machinery. It covers the person, the three rungs, the mathematics, working R checks of each idea, and why the work matters for artificial intelligence, both in how modern AI began and in what it is still missing.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Who is Judea Pearl?
Judea Pearl was born in Tel Aviv in 1936 and trained as an electrical engineer at the Technion, later taking graduate degrees in the United States, including a PhD from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn. After industrial research work on electronic devices he joined UCLA in 1970, where he built the Cognitive Systems Laboratory and has worked ever since.
His career has two distinct halves, and the second grew out of the limits of the first.

Probabilistic reasoning for AI (1980s). At the time, AI reasoned with logic rules and ad-hoc “certainty factors”. Pearl argued that uncertainty should be handled by probability theory, and made that practical by representing a joint distribution as a Bayesian network: a directed graph in which each variable depends only on its parents. His 1982 paper on message passing in trees and his 1988 book Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems introduced belief propagation, an efficient way to compute posteriors by passing local messages along the graph.
Causality (1990s onward). Pearl came to think that a Bayesian network, however good at prediction, says nothing reliable about what happens when you act. His 1995 Biometrika paper “Causal diagrams for empirical research” introduced the do-calculus, and his book Causality (2000, second edition 2009) set out the full theory. The Book of Why (2018, written with Dana Mackenzie) is the popular version and the source of the “ladder of causation”.

He received the ACM Turing Award for 2011 “for fundamental contributions to artificial intelligence through the development of a calculus for probabilistic and causal reasoning”. The citation names both halves.
Pearl is also known beyond science. His son Daniel, a Wall Street Journal reporter, was kidnapped and murdered in Pakistan in 2002, and the family set up the Daniel Pearl Foundation in his memory.

What came before
Pearl did not invent causal thinking from nothing. The pieces he unified were scattered across fields that barely spoke to each other.

Sewall Wright (1921) drew path diagrams for guinea-pig coat colours, the first causal graphs, but the method stayed inside genetics and econometrics.
R. A. Fisher gave the randomised experiment its modern form in the 1920s and 30s. Randomisation works because it deletes the arrows into treatment, which we’ll see is exactly what Pearl’s \(do(\cdot)\) operator does to a diagram.
Jerzy Neyman (1923) and Donald Rubin (1970s) developed potential outcomes, the other major formalism, in which each unit has an outcome under each treatment.
Trygve Haavelmo (1940s) argued that structural equations in economics describe how a system responds to intervention, not just how it is distributed.
Statisticians such as Simpson (1951) documented paradoxes, but statistics had no vocabulary to say which of the two conflicting answers was right.

Pearl’s contribution was to put these into one framework with a precise graphical language, and to prove which causal quantities can be computed from which data.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
The ladder of causation
Pearl sorts all causal reasoning into three levels, which he calls rungs. Each rung asks a qualitatively different question, and, crucially, data on a lower rung can never answer a higher-rung question without extra assumptions.


Show code
rungs <- tibble(
  ymin = c(0, 1.1, 2.2),
  ymax = c(1, 2.1, 3.2),
  fill = c("#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#2171b5"),
  txt  = c("#08306b", "#08306b", "white"),
  title = c("1. Seeing  (association)",
            "2. Doing  (intervention)",
            "3. Imagining  (counterfactuals)"),
  q = c("What does observing X tell me about Y?",
        "What happens to Y if I set X?",
        "What would Y have been, had X been different?"),
  sym = c("P(y | x)", "P(y | do(x))", "P(y_x | x', y')"),
  ex = c("Do people who take aspirin have fewer headaches?",
         "If I take aspirin, will my headache go?",
         "My headache went after aspirin. Was it the aspirin?")
)
ggplot(rungs) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = 0, xmax = 10, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax, fill = fill)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.3, y = ymax - 0.2, label = title, colour = txt),
            hjust = 0, vjust = 1, fontface = "bold", size = 4.6) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.3, y = ymax - 0.52, label = q, colour = txt),
            hjust = 0, vjust = 1, size = 3.6) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.3, y = ymin + 0.18, label = ex, colour = txt),
            hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.3, fontface = "italic") +
  geom_text(aes(x = 9.7, y = (ymin + ymax) / 2, label = sym, colour = txt),
            hjust = 1, size = 5, family = "mono") +
  scale_fill_identity() + scale_colour_identity() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 3.2), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_void()








Figure 1: The three rungs of the ladder of causation. Each rung needs strictly more causal knowledge than the one below it.





Rung 1, seeing. Pure statistics lives here: conditional probabilities, regression, and today most of machine learning. Bayes’ theorem, as in the prosecutor’s fallacy, is a rung-1 tool. It tells you how to update beliefs on evidence, but not what would happen if you changed something.
Rung 2, doing. Here we ask about the consequences of deliberate action. The key notation is \(P(y \mid do(x))\): the distribution of \(Y\) in a world where \(X\) has been forced to \(x\), not merely observed there. A randomised trial measures it directly. Observational data can too, if the causal structure is known.
Rung 3, imagining. Counterfactuals concern a specific individual and a specific alternative history: “Would this patient have recovered had they not been treated?” The quantity \(P(y_x \mid x', y')\) reads “the probability that \(Y\) would have been \(y\) had \(X\) been \(x\), given that we actually saw \(x'\) and \(y'\)”. Responsibility, blame, regret and explanation all live here.
A tidy way to remember the difference: the rooster’s crow predicts sunrise (rung 1) but silencing the rooster doesn’t stop the sun (rung 2), and “had the rooster not crowed, would the sun still have risen?” is a counterfactual (rung 3) with an obvious answer that no dataset contains.

title: Judea Pearl, the do-Calculus and the Ladder of Causation
text:
Same data, different worlds
Why can’t rung-1 data reach rung 2? Because very different causal worlds can produce identical observational distributions. Here are two models with the same joint distribution of \((X, Y)\).

Model A: \(X\) is a fair coin; \(Y\) depends on \(X\): \(P(Y{=}1 \mid X) = 0.3 + 0.4X\).
Model B: a hidden coin \(U\); \(X\) is just a copy of \(U\); \(Y\) depends on \(U\) with the same formula, and \(X\) has no effect on \(Y\).



Show code
n <- 1e6
# Model A: X causes Y
xa <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
ya <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.4 * xa)
# Model B: hidden U drives both; X is a copy of U
ub <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
xb <- ub
yb <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.4 * ub)

# intervening: set X by an outside coin
do_a <- function(x) mean(rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.4 * x))
do_b <- function(x) mean(rbinom(n, 1, 0.3 + 0.4 * ub))   # X has no arrow into Y

tibble(
  model = c("A: X causes Y", "B: X is a copy of a hidden cause"),
  `P(Y=1 | X=1)` = c(mean(ya[xa == 1]), mean(yb[xb == 1])),
  `P(Y=1 | X=0)` = c(mean(ya[xa == 0]), mean(yb[xb == 0])),
  `P(Y=1 | do(X=1))` = c(do_a(1), do_b(1)),
  `P(Y=1 | do(X=0))` = c(do_a(0), do_b(0))
) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(v) round(v, 3))) |> knitr::kable()












model
P(Y=1 | X=1)
P(Y=1 | X=0)
P(Y=1 | do(X=1))
P(Y=1 | do(X=0))




A: X causes Y
0.700
0.300
0.700
0.299


B: X is a copy of a hidden cause
0.699
